theory.title: The alphabet and spelling out loud
theory.summary: Spanish spelling is almost perfectly regular, so learning the letter names lets you write down anything you hear.
theory.body:
Spanish has 27 letters — the English 26 plus **ñ**. The letter names that catch English speakers out are **e** (said *eh*), **i** (said *ee*), **g** (*heh*), **h** (*ah-cheh*, and always silent in words), **j** (*hota*), **y** (*i griega* or *ye*) and **ll** (*elle*).

The payoff is big: unlike English, Spanish is written as it sounds. Once you know the letters and the five pure vowel sounds, you can spell almost any word you hear correctly on the first try. That is why dictation works as a learning tool in Spanish and barely works in English.

When spelling out loud, people distinguish **b de burro** from **v de vaca**, because the two letters sound identical in most of the Spanish-speaking world.

examples.target: ¿Cómo se escribe tu apellido?
examples.native: How do you spell your surname?

examples.target: García: ge, a, erre, ce, i con tilde, a.
examples.native: García: G, A, R, C, I with an accent, A.

examples.target: Con be de burro, no con uve.
examples.native: With a B, not a V.

theory.watch_out: H is never pronounced. 'Hola' starts with the O sound, and 'hola'/'ola' sound identical.

theory.title: Days, months and dates
theory.summary: Days and months are lowercase in Spanish, and 'on Monday' is expressed with an article, not a preposition.
theory.body:
The days are **lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo**, and the week starts on Monday — a calendar printed in Spain or Argentina puts *lunes* in the first column.

Unlike English, days and months are written in **lowercase**: *el lunes*, *en marzo*. Writing *Lunes* marks you as a foreigner faster than almost any pronunciation error.

There is no word for *on* with days. English *on Monday* is simply **el lunes**; *on Mondays* is **los lunes**. Five of the seven days already end in -s, so their plural does not change: *el lunes* / *los lunes*.

For dates, the order is day-month-year and the number is a plain cardinal: **el 5 de mayo**, not *the fifth of*.

examples.target: Nos vemos el jueves.
examples.native: See you on Thursday.

examples.target: Los sábados no trabajo.
examples.native: I don't work on Saturdays.

examples.target: Mi cumpleaños es el 12 de octubre.
examples.native: My birthday is October 12th.

theory.watch_out: No preposition with days: 'el lunes', never 'en lunes'. And never capitalise them.

theory.title: Greetings and goodbyes
theory.summary: Spanish splits greetings by time of day more strictly than English does, and the split is not where you would guess.
theory.body:
The three basic greetings are **hola** (any time), **buenos días** (morning), **buenas tardes** (afternoon) and **buenas noches** (night). Two things surprise English speakers. First, *buenas tardes* starts after lunch — which in Spain and much of Latin America means around 2 or 3 pm, not noon. Second, **buenas noches** is both *good evening* and *good night*: you use the same phrase arriving at a dinner and leaving it.

For goodbyes, **adiós** is heavier than *goodbye* — it hints you will not see the person soon. For everyday partings people say **hasta luego**, **chau** or **nos vemos**. And **¿qué tal?** is a greeting, not a real question: the expected answer is *bien, ¿y tú?*, not an account of your week.

examples.target: Buenos días, ¿qué tal?
examples.native: Good morning, how are you?

examples.target: Buenas noches, hasta mañana.
examples.native: Good night, see you tomorrow.

examples.target: Chau, nos vemos el lunes.
examples.native: Bye, see you on Monday.

theory.watch_out: Saying 'adiós' to a colleague you will see in an hour sounds oddly final. Use 'hasta luego'.

theory.title: Numbers 0 to 100
theory.summary: The only genuinely hard stretch is 16 to 29; after 30 the pattern never changes again.
theory.body:
**Uno** to **quince** have to be memorised. From **dieciséis** to **veintinueve** the numbers are written as one word (*dieciséis, diecisiete, veintiuno, veintidós*) — this is the part that trips people up, because it looks irregular but is just *diez y seis* and *veinte y uno* fused together.

From thirty on, Spanish is more regular than English: **treinta y uno, cuarenta y dos, noventa y nueve** — always the ten, then **y**, then the unit, as three separate words. There is no equivalent of the English *-teen/-ty* confusion.

One trap: **uno** becomes **un** before a masculine noun and **una** before a feminine one. *Veintiún libros*, *veintiuna sillas*.

examples.target: Tengo veintiún años.
examples.native: I am twenty-one years old.

examples.target: Son treinta y cinco euros.
examples.native: That's thirty-five euros.

examples.target: Hay dieciséis personas en la clase.
examples.native: There are sixteen people in the class.

theory.watch_out: 16-29 are one word; 31 and up are three. 'Dieciséis' but 'treinta y seis'.

theory.title: Ser and estar: two verbs for 'to be'
theory.summary: English has one verb where Spanish has two, so this is not a memory problem — it is a distinction English never asked you to make.
theory.body:
**Ser** is for what something *is*: identity, origin, profession, nationality, material, the time. **Estar** is for where something is and how it is right now: location, physical state, mood.

The rule usually taught is *permanent vs temporary*, and it is close enough to start with but it leaks. *Estar muerto* — being dead — is about as permanent as it gets, and it takes **estar**. A better instinct: **ser** answers *what is it?*, **estar** answers *how/where is it at the moment?*

Some adjectives change meaning with each verb, and the shift is real: **es aburrido** = he is boring, **está aburrido** = he is bored. **Es listo** = he is clever, **está listo** = he is ready.

Both are irregular and worth memorising cold: *soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son* — *estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están*.

examples.target: Soy profesor y soy de Irlanda.
examples.native: I'm a teacher and I'm from Ireland.

examples.target: Estoy en casa y estoy cansado.
examples.native: I'm at home and I'm tired.

examples.target: La sopa es buena, pero está fría.
examples.native: The soup is good, but it's cold.

theory.watch_out: Location of a thing always takes 'estar' — 'Madrid está en España' — even though a city's position is permanent.

theory.title: Family members
theory.summary: The masculine plural covers mixed groups, so 'los hermanos' may well mean a brother and a sister.
theory.body:
The core words are **padre/madre, hijo/hija, hermano/hermana, abuelo/abuela, tío/tía, primo/prima, nieto/nieta**.

The grammatical point hiding here matters more than the vocabulary: the **masculine plural stands for a mixed group**. *Mis hermanos* can be two brothers, or a brother and a sister. *Los padres* usually means *the parents*, not *the fathers*. English has separate words — *siblings*, *parents* — and Spanish just reuses the masculine.

**Padres** vs **parientes** is a classic false friend: *padres* = parents, *parientes* = relatives. And **esposo/esposa** (spouse) coexists with **marido/mujer**, where *mujer* means both *woman* and *wife* depending on context.

examples.target: Tengo dos hermanos: un chico y una chica.
examples.native: I have two siblings: a boy and a girl.

examples.target: Mis padres viven en Sevilla.
examples.native: My parents live in Seville.

examples.target: Vienen todos mis parientes.
examples.native: All my relatives are coming.

theory.watch_out: 'Parientes' means relatives, not parents. 'Mis parientes' is not 'my parents'.

theory.title: Countries and nationalities
theory.summary: Nationalities are lowercase and they agree in gender and number, unlike the fixed English adjectives.
theory.body:
Nationality adjectives are written in **lowercase**: *español, mexicana, francés, alemanes*. Country names keep their capital: *España, México, Francia*.

They agree like any adjective. Ones ending in **-o** switch to **-a**: *italiano/italiana*. Ones ending in a consonant add **-a**: *español/española*, *francés/francesa* — and note the written accent disappears in the feminine and plural because the stress falls naturally there. Ones ending in **-e** or **-í** do not change: *estadounidense*, *marroquí*.

To say where you are from, **ser de** + country: *soy de Canadá*. To say the language, the masculine singular doubles as the noun: *hablo español*.

examples.target: Soy irlandés y ella es irlandesa.
examples.native: I'm Irish and she's Irish.

examples.target: Somos estadounidenses, de Chicago.
examples.native: We're American, from Chicago.

examples.target: En Brasil se habla portugués.
examples.native: In Brazil they speak Portuguese.

theory.watch_out: Lowercase always: 'soy americano', not 'soy Americano'. The country keeps its capital.

theory.title: My, your, his, her
theory.summary: Spanish possessives agree with the thing owned, not the owner — so 'su' can mean his, her, their or your.
theory.body:
The forms are **mi, tu, su, nuestro, vuestro, su**. They agree with **what is owned**, never with who owns it: *mis libros* (my books) is plural because the books are plural, not because there are several of me.

Only **nuestro** and **vuestro** change for gender: *nuestra casa*, *nuestros hijos*. The rest only add **-s** for plural.

The hard one is **su**. It covers *his*, *her*, *their*, and formal *your* all at once, so *su casa* is genuinely ambiguous. Spanish resolves it when needed with **de + person**: *la casa de él*, *la casa de ellos*.

Also: Spanish uses the plain article where English uses a possessive, especially with body parts and clothes — *me duele **la** cabeza*, not *mi cabeza*.

examples.target: Mis padres y nuestra casa.
examples.native: My parents and our house.

examples.target: Su hermana vive en Lima.
examples.native: His (or her, or their) sister lives in Lima.

examples.target: Me lavo las manos.
examples.native: I wash my hands.

theory.watch_out: 'Mis' is plural because of the books, not because of you. 'Mi libros' is wrong.

theory.title: Jobs and professions
theory.summary: Spanish drops the article before a profession — 'soy médico', never 'soy un médico'.
theory.body:
With **ser**, a bare profession takes **no article**: *soy médico*, *es abogada*, *somos estudiantes*. English requires *a/an* here, so *soy un médico* is one of the most persistent English-speaker errors. The article comes back only when the profession is modified: *es **un** médico excelente*.

Most professions have a feminine form. Some change the ending (*abogado/abogada*, *enfermero/enfermera*), some only change the article (*el/la periodista*, *el/la estudiante*, *el/la artista*), and a few are still in flux — *la médica* and *la médico* are both heard.

To ask, use **¿a qué te dedicas?** or **¿en qué trabajas?**. *¿Qué eres?* sounds blunt, closer to *what ARE you?*

examples.target: Soy ingeniera.
examples.native: I'm an engineer.

examples.target: ¿A qué te dedicas?
examples.native: What do you do for a living?

examples.target: Es un profesor buenísimo.
examples.native: He's a really good teacher.

theory.watch_out: No 'un/una' before a plain profession. 'Soy un profesor' sounds like 'I am one of the teachers'.

theory.title: Asking questions
theory.summary: Spanish has no 'do/does', so a question can be identical to a statement — the difference lives in the intonation and the punctuation.
theory.body:
English builds questions with an auxiliary: *do you work?*, *are you tired?*. Spanish has **no equivalent of do/does**, and this is liberating once it clicks: the statement itself becomes the question.

There are three ways to ask a yes/no question. Keep the word order and raise your voice at the end: **¿Trabajas aquí?** Invert the subject and verb: **¿Trabaja Ana aquí?** Or tag the end: **Trabajas aquí, ¿verdad?**

Spanish writes an **inverted question mark** at the start, and it is not decorative — it tells the reader to use question intonation from the first word, which matters in a language where nothing else marks the question.

Question words all carry a written accent: **qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cómo, por qué, cuál**.

examples.target: ¿Eres de aquí?
examples.native: Are you from here?

examples.target: ¿Dónde trabaja tu hermana?
examples.native: Where does your sister work?

examples.target: Hablas francés, ¿verdad?
examples.native: You speak French, right?

theory.watch_out: Never translate 'do' — '¿Haces tú trabajar?' is not Spanish. The verb alone carries the question.

theory.title: Daily routine verbs
theory.summary: Half the routine verbs are reflexive, and the -se is not decoration — it changes who receives the action.
theory.body:
The everyday set: **levantarse** (get up), **ducharse** (shower), **vestirse** (get dressed), **desayunar** (have breakfast), **ir** (go), **volver** (come back), **acostarse** (go to bed), **dormirse** (fall asleep).

Notice how many end in **-se**. These are reflexive: the subject does the action to itself. **Levantar** means to lift something; **levantarse** means to lift yourself, i.e. get up. **Despertar** is to wake someone; **despertarse** is to wake up.

The pronoun changes with the person and normally sits before the verb: *me levanto, te levantas, se levanta, nos levantamos, os levantáis, se levantan*.

English hides this distinction — *I wash* and *I wash the car* look the same — which is why English speakers drop the pronoun and say *levanto a las siete*, which means *I lift (something) at seven*.

examples.target: Me levanto a las siete y media.
examples.native: I get up at half past seven.

examples.target: Se ducha antes de desayunar.
examples.native: He showers before having breakfast.

examples.target: Nos acostamos muy tarde.
examples.native: We go to bed very late.

theory.watch_out: Dropping the pronoun changes the meaning, it doesn't just sound off: 'lavo' is 'I wash something', 'me lavo' is 'I wash myself'.

theory.title: Places and prepositions of place
theory.summary: 'En' does the work of English in, on and at all by itself, so the guessing goes the other way around.
theory.body:
The workhorse is **en**, which covers English *in*, *on* and *at*: *en la mesa* (on the table), *en Madrid* (in Madrid), *en casa* (at home). Where English makes you choose, Spanish does not — this is one of the rare places Spanish is simpler.

The others: **sobre / encima de** (on top of), **debajo de** (under), **al lado de** (next to), **entre** (between), **delante de** (in front of), **detrás de** (behind), **cerca de / lejos de** (near / far from), **enfrente de** (opposite).

Notice how many end in **de**. That *de* is not optional: *al lado **de** la puerta*. Dropping it is a very common English-speaker slip, because English says *next to the door* with no second preposition.

And remember location takes **estar**: *El banco **está** al lado del cine*.

examples.target: El libro está encima de la mesa.
examples.native: The book is on the table.

examples.target: Vivo cerca del centro.
examples.native: I live near the centre.

examples.target: La farmacia está enfrente del banco.
examples.native: The pharmacy is opposite the bank.

theory.watch_out: 'De' + 'el' always contracts to 'del'. 'Cerca de el banco' is wrong; it is 'cerca del banco'.

theory.title: The present tense: -ar, -er, -ir
theory.summary: The ending carries the subject, which is why Spanish normally leaves the pronoun out entirely.
theory.body:
Spanish verbs come in three families by infinitive ending. Regular present endings:

**-ar** (hablar): *hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan*
**-er** (comer): *como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen*
**-ir** (vivir): *vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven*

The -er and -ir sets are identical except in *nosotros* and *vosotros*.

Because the ending already says who is acting, **the subject pronoun is normally omitted**: *hablo español*, not *yo hablo español*. Including *yo* is not wrong, but it adds emphasis — *YO hablo español (whatever the others do)*. English speakers who say *yo* every time sound as if they are constantly contrasting themselves with someone.

The Spanish present also covers the English present continuous: **como** is both *I eat* and *I am eating*.

examples.target: Hablo español y estudio francés.
examples.native: I speak Spanish and I'm studying French.

examples.target: ¿Dónde vives?
examples.native: Where do you live?

examples.target: Comemos a las dos.
examples.native: We eat at two.

theory.watch_out: Leave out 'yo' unless you mean to stress it. Repeating it sounds like you're arguing with someone.

theory.title: Hay: there is and there are
theory.summary: One invariable word covers both, and it never agrees with what follows.
theory.body:
**Hay** means both *there is* and *there are*, and it does **not change for number**: *hay un libro*, *hay tres libros*. English speakers instinctively look for a plural form; there isn't one. (In other tenses it behaves the same way: *había* for both *there was* and *there were*.)

The important distinction is **hay vs está**. Use **hay** to say something *exists* — it introduces new, unknown information, and takes an indefinite article or none at all: *hay **un** banco por aquí*. Use **estar** to locate something already known, with a definite article: *el banco **está** en la esquina*.

So *¿hay un baño?* asks whether one exists; *¿dónde está el baño?* asks where the known one is. Saying *hay el baño* is ungrammatical: **hay** never takes *el/la*.

examples.target: Hay dos supermercados en mi barrio.
examples.native: There are two supermarkets in my neighbourhood.

examples.target: ¿Hay una farmacia por aquí?
examples.native: Is there a pharmacy around here?

examples.target: La farmacia está en la calle Mayor.
examples.native: The pharmacy is on Mayor Street.

theory.watch_out: 'Hay' never takes a definite article. 'Hay el problema' is wrong — it's 'hay un problema'.

theory.title: Telling the time
theory.summary: The verb is plural for every hour except one o'clock, because you are literally counting hours.
theory.body:
Spanish says **son las tres** — *they are the three (hours)*. Because you are counting hours, the verb is plural for everything except one: **es la una**.

Minutes past take **y**: *son las tres y diez*. Minutes to take **menos**: *son las tres menos cuarto* (2:45). Half is **y media**, quarter is **y cuarto**. In much of Latin America *faltan diez para las tres* is more common than *menos diez*.

To say *at* a time, use **a**: *la clase es **a** las nueve*. Do not confuse this with **son las nueve**, which states what time it is.

For am/pm Spanish uses **de la mañana / de la tarde / de la noche** — with **de**, not *por*. *Por la mañana* means *in the morning* generally, without a specific hour.

examples.target: Son las cinco y veinte.
examples.native: It's twenty past five.

examples.target: Es la una menos cuarto.
examples.native: It's a quarter to one.

examples.target: Trabajo a las ocho de la mañana.
examples.native: I work at eight in the morning.

theory.watch_out: 'Son las' for telling the time, 'a las' for scheduling. 'La reunión son las tres' is wrong.

theory.title: This, that and that over there
theory.summary: Spanish has three degrees of distance where English has two.
theory.body:
English splits the world into *this* and *that*. Spanish splits it three ways:

**este/esta/estos/estas** — near me (this)
**ese/esa/esos/esas** — near you (that, by the listener)
**aquel/aquella/aquellos/aquellas** — far from both (that one over there)

The middle one is the surprise: **ese** is anchored to *the person you are talking to*, not to a measured distance. Handing something over you say *ese libro que tienes* — that book you're holding.

There are also neuter forms — **esto, eso, aquello** — used for something unidentified or for a whole situation: *¿qué es esto?*, *eso no me gusta*. They never carry an accent and never change form.

**Aquel** is also used for distance in time: *en aquella época* — back in those days.

examples.target: Este libro es mío.
examples.native: This book is mine.

examples.target: ¿Me pasas esa silla?
examples.native: Can you pass me that chair?

examples.target: ¿Qué es eso?
examples.native: What's that?

theory.watch_out: Use 'eso/esto' when you don't know what the thing is. Once you name it, it needs gender: 'esa mesa'.

theory.title: Asking for and giving directions
theory.summary: Directions are normally given with the impersonal usted command, which is why they sound like a different tense.
theory.body:
To ask: **¿Dónde está…?**, **¿Cómo se llega a…?**, **Perdone, ¿hay un banco por aquí?**

The answer usually comes in **usted** commands, because you are addressing a stranger: **siga** (carry on), **gire** / **doble** (turn), **cruce** (cross), **tome** (take), **baje/suba** (go down/up). These look irregular because they are the subjunctive-based formal imperative — you do not need to analyse it yet, just recognise the shape.

The vocabulary: **a la derecha** (right), **a la izquierda** (left), **todo recto / todo derecho** (straight on), **la esquina** (corner), **la manzana / la cuadra** (block), **el semáforo** (traffic light).

Watch **derecha** (right, the direction) against **derecho** (straight on). One vowel apart, opposite instructions.

examples.target: Perdone, ¿cómo se llega a la estación?
examples.native: Excuse me, how do I get to the station?

examples.target: Siga todo recto y gire a la derecha.
examples.native: Go straight on and turn right.

examples.target: Está a dos manzanas de aquí.
examples.native: It's two blocks from here.

theory.watch_out: 'A la derecha' is right; 'todo derecho' is straight ahead. Mixing them sends you the wrong way.

theory.title: Poder: can, could and may
theory.summary: One verb covers ability, permission and polite requests, and it is always followed by a bare infinitive.
theory.body:
**Poder** is *o→ue* stem-changing: *puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden*. The change happens wherever the stress falls on the stem, which is why *nosotros* and *vosotros* keep the plain *o*.

It is always followed directly by an **infinitive**, with nothing in between: *puedo ir*, *¿puedes ayudarme?*. There is no *to*, and no conjugation of the second verb — a relief coming from English *I can go* / *I am able to go*.

It covers three meanings English separates: ability (*puedo nadar*), permission (*¿puedo pasar?*) and polite request (*¿puede repetir, por favor?*).

For learned skills, Spanish often prefers **saber**: *sé nadar* means *I know how to swim*, while *puedo nadar* suggests the circumstances allow it right now.

examples.target: ¿Puedes ayudarme, por favor?
examples.native: Can you help me, please?

examples.target: No puedo ir mañana.
examples.native: I can't go tomorrow.

examples.target: Sé tocar la guitarra.
examples.native: I can play the guitar.

theory.watch_out: For a skill you learned, use 'saber': 'sé conducir'. 'Puedo conducir' means nothing is stopping you right now.

theory.title: Prices and shopping
theory.summary: The price question uses a plural verb, and the decimal separator is a comma.
theory.body:
To ask a price: **¿Cuánto cuesta?** for one item, **¿Cuánto cuestan?** for several, or the catch-all **¿Cuánto es?**. In a shop, **¿Me cobra, por favor?** asks them to ring it up.

The answer normally uses **son**: *son doce euros con cincuenta*. Spanish writes the decimal with a **comma** and thousands with a **point** — *1.250,50* — the exact opposite of English convention, which matters the moment you read a price tag.

Useful shop language: **¿Tiene…?** (do you have), **¿Puedo probármelo?** (can I try it on), **está rebajado** (it's on sale), **en efectivo / con tarjeta** (cash / card), **el cambio** (the change), **la vuelta** (change given back, in Latin America).

And **barato/caro** for cheap/expensive — *barato* is not *cheap* in the pejorative sense; for that Spanish says *de mala calidad*.

examples.target: ¿Cuánto cuestan estos zapatos?
examples.native: How much are these shoes?

examples.target: Son cuarenta y cinco euros.
examples.native: That's forty-five euros.

examples.target: ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?
examples.native: Can I pay by card?

theory.watch_out: The decimal separator is a comma: '2,50 euros'. A price written '2.50' reads as two hundred and fifty.

theory.title: Tener and the expressions built on it
theory.summary: Spanish uses 'have' where English uses 'be' — for age, hunger, cold and fear.
theory.body:
**Tener** is irregular: *tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen*. Note the *e→ie* change in everything except *nosotros/vosotros*, and the odd first person *tengo*.

Beyond possession, tener carries a set of expressions where **English uses *to be***, and translating literally produces nonsense:

**tener … años** — to be … years old (*tengo treinta años*, never *soy treinta*)
**tener hambre / sed** — to be hungry / thirsty
**tener frío / calor** — to be cold / hot
**tener miedo** — to be afraid
**tener razón** — to be right
**tener sueño** — to be sleepy
**tener prisa** — to be in a hurry

These take **no article**: *tengo hambre*, not *tengo una hambre*. And because *hambre* is a noun, it is intensified with **mucho/mucha**, not *muy*: *tengo **mucha** hambre*.

examples.target: Tengo veintiocho años.
examples.native: I'm twenty-eight.

examples.target: Tenemos mucha hambre.
examples.native: We're very hungry.

examples.target: Tienes razón.
examples.native: You're right.

theory.watch_out: 'Muy hambre' is wrong. Hunger is a noun here, so it takes 'mucha': 'mucha hambre'.

theory.title: Gustan: when the thing liked is plural
theory.summary: Because the liked thing is the subject, a plural thing makes the verb plural — regardless of who likes it.
theory.body:
Once you accept that **gustar** agrees with the thing liked, the plural follows automatically: *me gusta**n** los libros* — *the books are pleasing to me*.

Only two forms matter in practice: **gusta** for a singular thing or an infinitive, **gustan** for a plural thing.

*Me gusta el perro* — I like the dog.
*Me gustan los perros* — I like dogs.
*Nos gustan las películas españolas* — we like Spanish films.

The pronoun (*me, te, le…*) tells you **who likes**; the verb ending tells you **how many things are liked**. They are independent, which is exactly what English speakers keep merging.

A trap: an infinitive is always singular, even a list of them. *Me gusta leer y escribir* — two activities, still *gusta*.

examples.target: Me gustan las películas de terror.
examples.native: I like horror films.

examples.target: A mis padres les gusta el cine.
examples.native: My parents like the cinema.

examples.target: ¿Te gustan los gatos?
examples.native: Do you like cats?

theory.watch_out: 'Me gustan leer y escribir' is wrong. Infinitives never make the verb plural.

theory.title: Gustar: the sentence turns around
theory.summary: Gustar does not mean 'to like' — it means 'to be pleasing to', and that flips who the subject is.
theory.body:
This is the single most reorganising piece of beginner Spanish grammar. **Gustar** does not work like *to like*. It works like the English verb *to please*: the thing liked is the **subject**, and the person is an **indirect object**.

*Me gusta el café* is literally *the coffee is pleasing to me*. So:

**me / te / le / nos / os / les** + **gusta** + the singular thing

That means the verb agrees with the **coffee**, not with you. *Me gusta* stays *gusta* no matter who is doing the liking — only the little pronoun in front changes.

When the liked thing is a verb, it stays in the infinitive and the verb stays singular: *me gusta leer*, *me gusta nadar y correr* (still singular — liking is one activity).

To emphasise or clarify who, add **a + person** at the front: *a mí me gusta*, *a Juan le gusta*. The *a mí* is not redundant; it is how Spanish stresses the person.

examples.target: Me gusta el chocolate.
examples.native: I like chocolate.

examples.target: A ella le gusta cocinar.
examples.native: She likes cooking.

examples.target: No nos gusta este restaurante.
examples.native: We don't like this restaurant.

theory.watch_out: 'Yo gusto' means 'people find me attractive'. It is not how you say 'I like'.

theory.title: Other verbs that work like gustar
theory.summary: Once the pattern clicks, a whole family of everyday verbs comes free.
theory.body:
**Gustar** is not a one-off. A group of common verbs uses the same backwards structure — indirect object pronoun + verb agreeing with the thing:

**encantar** — to love (*me encanta este libro*)
**interesar** — to interest (*me interesa la historia*)
**molestar** — to bother (*me molesta el ruido*)
**doler** — to hurt (*me duele la cabeza*)
**parecer** — to seem (*me parece bien*)
**faltar** — to be missing (*me faltan dos euros*)
**quedar** — to have left (*me quedan tres días*)
**apetecer** — to fancy (*¿te apetece un café?*)

**Encantar** is worth a note: it is already the maximum, so it never takes *mucho*. *Me encanta mucho* is like saying *I absolutely love it a lot* — Spanish speakers do not say it.

Also notice **doler**: Spanish says *me duele la cabeza*, using the article, where English says *my head hurts*.

examples.target: Me encanta la música clásica.
examples.native: I love classical music.

examples.target: Me duelen los pies.
examples.native: My feet hurt.

examples.target: ¿Te apetece salir esta noche?
examples.native: Do you fancy going out tonight?

theory.watch_out: 'Me encanta mucho' is redundant. 'Encantar' already means the most.

theory.title: Question words
theory.summary: They all carry a written accent, and 'qué' vs 'cuál' does not divide the way 'what' vs 'which' does.
theory.body:
The set: **qué** (what), **quién/quiénes** (who), **dónde** (where), **cuándo** (when), **cómo** (how), **por qué** (why), **cuánto/a/os/as** (how much/many), **cuál/cuáles** (which/what).

All carry a **written accent** when they ask a question, direct or indirect. The same words without the accent are relative pronouns: *¿**qué** quieres?* against *lo **que** quiero*.

The hard pair is **qué vs cuál**. It does not map onto *what vs which*:

- **qué + noun**: *¿qué libro prefieres?*
- **cuál + ser**: *¿cuál es tu nombre?*, *¿cuál es el problema?*

So *what is your name?* is **¿cuál es tu nombre?**, not *¿qué es tu nombre?* — which asks for the *definition* of a name. **Qué + ser** is reserved for asking what something fundamentally is: *¿qué es la democracia?*

**Cuánto** is the only one that agrees: *¿cuántas personas?*

examples.target: ¿Cuál es tu número de teléfono?
examples.native: What's your phone number?

examples.target: ¿Qué película quieres ver?
examples.native: Which film do you want to see?

examples.target: ¿Cuántos hermanos tienes?
examples.native: How many siblings do you have?

theory.watch_out: '¿Qué es tu nombre?' asks what a name IS, philosophically. Use '¿cuál es tu nombre?'

theory.title: Review: tener, poder and gustar
theory.summary: The three verbs that most often get built like English, and the three places that breaks.
theory.body:
These three carry most of everyday A1 conversation, and each one breaks a different English habit.

**Tener** takes over where English uses *to be*: age, hunger, cold, fear, being right. *Tengo veinte años*, *tengo frío*, *tienes razón*. Intensify with **mucho/mucha**, never *muy*, because what follows is a noun.

**Poder** takes a bare infinitive with nothing between: *puedo ir*, *¿puedes venir?*. For a learned skill, prefer **saber**: *sé conducir*.

**Gustar** turns the sentence around: the thing liked is the subject. *Me gusta el libro*, *me gustan los libros*. The pronoun says who, the ending says how many.

The common thread: in all three, translating word by word from English produces something that is not merely awkward but wrong. It helps to learn the whole expression as one block — *tengo hambre*, *me gustan*, *sé nadar* — rather than assembling it from parts each time.

examples.target: Tengo mucho frío y no puedo dormir.
examples.native: I'm very cold and I can't sleep.

examples.target: ¿Te gusta bailar? Yo sé bailar salsa.
examples.native: Do you like dancing? I can dance salsa.

examples.target: No tienen tiempo, tienen mucha prisa.
examples.native: They don't have time, they're in a big hurry.

theory.watch_out: The three classic slips: 'soy 20 años', 'puedo nadar' for a skill, and 'yo gusto'.

theory.title: Adjectives agree in gender
theory.summary: The adjective takes its gender from the noun, so the same quality is spelled two ways.
theory.body:
An adjective ending in **-o** changes to **-a** for a feminine noun: *el coche roj**o***, *la casa roj**a***.

Adjectives ending in **-e** or in most consonants do **not** change: *un libro interesante*, *una película interesante*; *un examen difícil*, *una tarea difícil*.

The exceptions worth knowing: adjectives of **nationality** add -a even after a consonant (*español/española*), and adjectives ending in **-or, -ón, -ín** do the same (*trabajador/trabajadora*).

What makes this hard is not the rule, it is that English has no equivalent at all — *red* is *red* forever — so there is no habit to transfer, only one to build. The agreement is not decoration: it is what tells a listener which noun a distant adjective refers to.

examples.target: Es una casa muy bonita.
examples.native: It's a very pretty house.

examples.target: Mi hermana es alta y trabajadora.
examples.native: My sister is tall and hard-working.

examples.target: Un problema difícil y una solución difícil.
examples.native: A hard problem and a hard solution.

theory.watch_out: 'Problema' ends in -a but is masculine: 'un problema difícil'. The -ma words from Greek all behave this way.

theory.title: Adjectives agree in number
theory.summary: Plural is added on top of gender, and a mixed group defaults to masculine.
theory.body:
After gender comes number. Add **-s** to a vowel ending, **-es** to a consonant ending: *rojos*, *interesantes*, *difíciles*, *españoles*.

A spelling detail: a final **-z** becomes **-ces** (*feliz → felices*), and words ending in stressed vowel + consonant may lose a written accent in the plural because the stress now falls naturally (*joven → jóvenes* gains one, *examen → exámenes* gains one).

When one adjective describes **several nouns of different genders**, it goes **masculine plural**: *el libro y la revista son nuev**os***. English speakers find this arbitrary; it is simply the default gender doing the work of a neutral.

Agreement travels: *son* is plural too. Everything in the phrase lines up with the noun, which is why changing one word can force three changes.

examples.target: Son unos zapatos muy caros.
examples.native: They're very expensive shoes.

examples.target: Los niños están felices.
examples.native: The children are happy.

examples.target: La mesa y el sofá son nuevos.
examples.native: The table and the sofa are new.

theory.watch_out: 'Feliz' pluralises to 'felices', not 'felizes'. Z becomes c before e.

theory.title: Where the adjective goes
theory.summary: The default is after the noun, and moving it forward changes the meaning rather than the style.
theory.body:
Spanish puts the adjective **after** the noun by default: *una casa grande*, *un coche rojo*. This is the opposite of English and it is the safe choice in almost every sentence.

But position carries meaning. Before the noun, the adjective becomes **subjective or expected** rather than distinguishing. *Un amigo viejo* is a friend who is old; *un viejo amigo* is a long-standing friend. *Un hombre pobre* has no money; *un pobre hombre* is a pitiable one. *Un coche nuevo* is brand new; *un nuevo coche* is another one, new to you.

So the position is not a stylistic flourish — placing it after **distinguishes this one from others**, placing it before **comments on it**.

A few adjectives shorten before a masculine singular noun: **bueno → buen**, **malo → mal**, **grande → gran** (before any gender, and with the meaning *great* rather than *large*).

examples.target: Es un buen amigo.
examples.native: He's a good friend.

examples.target: Vivo en una casa grande.
examples.native: I live in a big house.

examples.target: Fue un gran día.
examples.native: It was a great day.

theory.watch_out: 'Una gran mujer' is a great woman; 'una mujer grande' is a large one. The position is the whole difference.

theory.title: Comparisons: more, less, as
theory.summary: One pattern covers every adjective — there is no Spanish equivalent of the -er ending.
theory.body:
Spanish has no *-er* suffix. Everything uses the same frame:

**más + adjective + que** — *más alto que* (taller than)
**menos + adjective + que** — *menos caro que* (less expensive than)
**tan + adjective + como** — *tan alto como* (as tall as)

For quantities: **más/menos + noun + que**, and **tanto/a/os/as + noun + como** (agreeing with the noun).

Four irregulars replace *más + adjective*: **mejor** (better), **peor** (worse), **mayor** (older/bigger), **menor** (younger/smaller). Saying *más bueno* is not impossible but usually means morally good.

One trap: before a **number**, *than* is **de**, not *que*: *más **de** veinte personas*. Using *que* there is a very common error.

The superlative just adds the article: *el más alto de la clase* — and note *de*, where English uses *in*.

examples.target: Madrid es más grande que Sevilla.
examples.native: Madrid is bigger than Seville.

examples.target: Este libro es tan bueno como el otro.
examples.native: This book is as good as the other one.

examples.target: Hay más de cien personas.
examples.native: There are more than a hundred people.

theory.watch_out: Before a number it's 'más de', not 'más que'. 'Más que cien' means 'more than [merely] a hundred'.

theory.title: How often: frequency adverbs
theory.summary: Spanish word order is far freer here than English, but 'nunca' brings a double negative with it.
theory.body:
The scale: **siempre** (always), **casi siempre**, **a menudo / muchas veces** (often), **a veces** (sometimes), **casi nunca / rara vez** (rarely), **nunca / jamás** (never).

Unlike English, these move freely: *siempre llego tarde*, *llego siempre tarde*, *llego tarde siempre* are all fine.

The grammatical point is **negation**. If a negative word comes **after** the verb, Spanish requires **no** before it: *No como carne **nunca***. If it comes **before**, the *no* disappears: ***Nunca** como carne*. Both are correct; what is wrong is *nunca no como*.

This double negative is not sloppiness — it is required. The same applies to *nada*, *nadie*, *ninguno*: *no veo a **nadie*** is the standard way to say *I see nobody*.

To ask, use **¿con qué frecuencia?** or **¿cada cuánto?**

examples.target: Siempre desayuno a las ocho.
examples.native: I always have breakfast at eight.

examples.target: No voy nunca al gimnasio.
examples.native: I never go to the gym.

examples.target: A veces salgo con mis amigos.
examples.native: Sometimes I go out with my friends.

theory.watch_out: 'No veo nada' is correct Spanish, not a mistake. Two negatives reinforce, they don't cancel.

theory.title: Direct object pronouns: lo, la, los, las
theory.summary: They go before the verb, not after it — the opposite of English word order.
theory.body:
These replace the thing receiving the action: **me, te, lo/la, nos, os, los/las**.

The placement is the shock. They go **before** the conjugated verb: *lo veo* (*I see it*), *la compré* (*I bought it*). English puts the object after; Spanish puts the pronoun in front, always.

With an infinitive or gerund there is a choice, and both are equally correct: *voy a comprar**lo*** or ***lo** voy a comprar*; *estoy leyéndo**lo*** or ***lo** estoy leyendo*. Attaching it may add a written accent to keep the stress: *leyéndolo*.

**Lo** also works as a neuter, standing for a whole idea: *no **lo** sé* — *I don't know it (that fact)*.

In much of Spain, **le** replaces *lo* for a male person (*le vi* rather than *lo vi*). This is *leísmo*, it is accepted for people, and you will hear it constantly — but *lo* is correct everywhere.

examples.target: ¿El libro? Lo compré ayer.
examples.native: The book? I bought it yesterday.

examples.target: Te llamo mañana.
examples.native: I'll call you tomorrow.

examples.target: Voy a hacerlo esta tarde.
examples.native: I'm going to do it this afternoon.

theory.watch_out: Never after a conjugated verb: 'veo lo' is wrong. It's 'lo veo'.

theory.title: Hace: saying how long ago
theory.summary: 'Hace' goes at the front where English puts 'ago' at the end, and it never changes form.
theory.body:
To say *two years ago*, Spanish says **hace dos años** — the word comes **first**, and it is always *hace*, never pluralised.

The frame: **hace + time + que + verb**, or the simpler **verb + hace + time**.

*Hace dos años que vivo aquí* / *Vivo aquí desde hace dos años* — I've lived here for two years.
*Llegué hace una hora* — I arrived an hour ago.

Notice the second big difference: for something **still going on**, Spanish uses the **present** tense where English uses the present perfect. *Hace tres años que estudio español* = *I have been studying Spanish for three years*. Using a past tense there would mean you stopped.

To ask: **¿cuánto (tiempo) hace que…?** or **¿desde cuándo…?**

Do not confuse with **desde** (since a point in time): *desde 2020*, *desde el lunes*.

examples.target: Llegué hace veinte minutos.
examples.native: I arrived twenty minutes ago.

examples.target: Hace tres años que vivo en Madrid.
examples.native: I've been living in Madrid for three years.

examples.target: ¿Cuánto hace que estudias español?
examples.native: How long have you been studying Spanish?

theory.watch_out: For something still happening, use the present: 'hace dos años que trabajo aquí', not 'trabajé'.

theory.title: Ir a + infinitive: the near future
theory.summary: This is how Spanish speakers actually talk about the future; the future tense is rarer than the textbooks suggest.
theory.body:
**Ir a + infinitive** is the everyday future, exactly parallel to English *going to*: *voy a comer*, *vamos a salir*.

**Ir** is irregular: *voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van*. The **a** is obligatory — *voy comer* is wrong — and the second verb stays in the infinitive.

In conversation this construction is far more common than the true future tense (*comeré*). If you learn only one way to talk about the future, learn this one.

Be careful with **ir** on its own: it needs a destination. *Voy* alone sounds unfinished; you say *me voy* (I'm off) or *voy a casa*.

And note **ir a + place** vs **ir a + verb** look identical: *voy al cine* (to the cinema), *voy a ver una película* (going to watch a film). The **a + el** contraction to **al** applies only to the place version.

examples.target: Voy a llamarte esta noche.
examples.native: I'm going to call you tonight.

examples.target: ¿Qué vas a hacer el fin de semana?
examples.native: What are you going to do at the weekend?

examples.target: Vamos a comer al restaurante nuevo.
examples.native: We're going to eat at the new restaurant.

theory.watch_out: The 'a' is not optional. 'Voy comer' is wrong; it's 'voy a comer'.

theory.title: Irregular preterites
theory.summary: The common irregulars share one trick: a new stem plus a set of endings with no accents at all.
theory.body:
The most-used verbs are irregular in the preterite, and they follow a pattern that makes them learnable as a group.

They take a **new stem** and then one shared set of endings: **-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron** — with **no written accents**, unlike the regular preterite.

Stems: *tener → tuv-*, *estar → estuv-*, *poder → pud-*, *poner → pus-*, *saber → sup-*, *hacer → hic-* (with *hizo* in the third person), *querer → quis-*, *venir → vin-*, *decir → dij-*, *traer → traj-*.

When the stem ends in **j** (*dij-, traj-*), the third person plural drops the i: *dijeron*, not *dijieron*.

Two verbs share one form completely: **ser** and **ir** are both *fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron*. Context alone separates *fui médico* (I was a doctor) from *fui a Madrid* (I went to Madrid).

**Dar** takes -er endings: *di, diste, dio*.

examples.target: Tuve que trabajar el sábado.
examples.native: I had to work on Saturday.

examples.target: Fuimos a Barcelona en tren.
examples.native: We went to Barcelona by train.

examples.target: No pude venir porque estuve enfermo.
examples.native: I couldn't come because I was ill.

theory.watch_out: These endings carry no accent: it's 'tuve' and 'tuvo', never 'tuvé' or 'tuvó'.

theory.title: The preterite: finished past actions
theory.summary: The accent marks are not optional here — they are the only thing separating 'I speak' from 'he spoke'.
theory.body:
The preterite reports an action as **completed**, viewed as a whole event.

**-ar** (hablar): *hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablasteis, hablaron*
**-er/-ir** (comer, vivir): *comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comisteis, comieron*

The -er and -ir endings are identical, which halves the work.

The **written accents carry meaning**, they are not ornament. *Hablo* is *I speak*; *habló* is *he spoke*. *Hablé* is *I spoke*. Leave the accent off and you have written a different tense and a different person. This is one of the few places where an accent error changes the sentence rather than just looking untidy.

Another detail: for **-ar** and **-ir** verbs, *nosotros* is identical in present and preterite — *hablamos*, *vivimos*. Context decides. (For -er verbs they differ: *comemos* vs *comimos*.)

Signal words: *ayer, anoche, la semana pasada, en 2019, hace dos años*.

examples.target: Ayer hablé con mi jefe.
examples.native: Yesterday I spoke to my boss.

examples.target: Comimos en un restaurante muy bueno.
examples.native: We ate at a very good restaurant.

examples.target: ¿A qué hora saliste de casa?
examples.native: What time did you leave the house?

theory.watch_out: 'Hablo' and 'habló' are different tenses AND different people. The accent is doing real work.

theory.title: Obligation: tener que, deber, hay que
theory.summary: Three ways to say 'must', separated by who exactly is obliged.
theory.body:
**Tener que + infinitive** is the everyday one: a concrete, personal obligation. *Tengo que estudiar* — I have to study.

**Deber + infinitive** is weightier — moral duty or strong advice. *Debes decirle la verdad* — you ought to tell him the truth. In the conditional it softens into advice: *deberías descansar* — you should rest.

**Hay que + infinitive** is **impersonal**: it obliges nobody in particular. *Hay que llegar temprano* — one has to arrive early. There is no subject, so it cannot be conjugated for a person; that is the whole point of it.

A distinction worth keeping: **deber** (must) vs **deber de** (must, as a guess). *Debe estar en casa* = he must be at home (obligation); *debe de estar en casa* = he's probably at home (deduction). In speech the two blur, but in writing the *de* is the difference between an order and a hunch.

examples.target: Tengo que terminar esto hoy.
examples.native: I have to finish this today.

examples.target: Hay que reservar con antelación.
examples.native: You have to book in advance.

examples.target: Deberías hablar con ella.
examples.native: You should talk to her.

theory.watch_out: 'Hay que' has no subject. You cannot say 'yo hay que' — use 'tengo que'.

theory.title: The three irregular imperfects
theory.summary: Ser, ir and ver — and that is the complete list for the entire language.
theory.body:
The imperfect has exactly **three** irregular verbs. Not three groups: three verbs.

**ser**: *era, eras, era, éramos, erais, eran*
**ir**: *iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, ibais, iban*
**ver**: *veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veíais, veían*

*Ver* is barely irregular — it just keeps the **e** of the stem (*veía* rather than *vía*).

Even verbs that are wildly irregular elsewhere behave here: *tener → tenía*, *hacer → hacía*, *poder → podía*, *decir → decía*. After the preterite this feels like a gift.

**Era** and **estaba** both translate *was*, and the ser/estar split holds: *era alto* (he was tall, a characteristic), *estaba cansado* (he was tired, a state).

**Iba a + infinitive** is the *was going to* construction: *iba a llamarte* — I was going to call you (and didn't).

examples.target: Cuando era pequeño, iba al colegio en bici.
examples.native: When I was little, I used to cycle to school.

examples.target: Éramos cinco en casa.
examples.native: There were five of us at home.

examples.target: Iba a llamarte, pero se me olvidó.
examples.native: I was going to call you, but I forgot.

theory.watch_out: Only ser, ir and ver are irregular. If you're tempted to invent another one, you're wrong.

theory.title: The imperfect: how things used to be
theory.summary: The easiest tense in Spanish — only three irregular verbs exist in the whole language.
theory.body:
The imperfect describes the past **without a boundary**: what used to happen, what was going on, what things were like.

**-ar** (hablar): *hablaba, hablabas, hablaba, hablábamos, hablabais, hablaban*
**-er/-ir** (comer, vivir): *comía, comías, comía, comíamos, comíais, comían*

Every -er and -ir verb carries an accent on the **í** in every form. Every -ar verb has the *-aba* shape.

This tense translates three different English structures: *I used to eat*, *I was eating*, and plain *I ate* when it means habitually. That breadth is why English speakers under-use it.

Use it for: repeated past habits (*de niño jugaba al fútbol*), descriptions and background (*hacía frío y llovía*), age and time in the past (*tenía diez años*, *eran las tres*), and ongoing actions interrupted by something else.

Note *hablaba* is both *I* and *he/she* — the only ambiguity in the tense.

examples.target: De niño jugaba al fútbol todos los días.
examples.native: As a child I used to play football every day.

examples.target: Hacía frío y no había nadie en la calle.
examples.native: It was cold and there was nobody in the street.

examples.target: Cuando vivíamos en Lima, comíamos pescado.
examples.native: When we lived in Lima, we used to eat fish.

theory.watch_out: Age in the past is always imperfect: 'tenía veinte años', never 'tuve veinte años'.

theory.title: Indirect object pronouns: le and les
theory.summary: Spanish states the pronoun even when the person is already named — the redundancy is compulsory, not clumsy.
theory.body:
The forms: **me, te, le, nos, os, les**. They mark **to whom** or **for whom**.

Only the third person differs from the direct object set, and *le/les* do **not** change for gender.

The surprise is that Spanish uses the pronoun **even when the person is spelled out**: ***Le** di el libro **a Juan***. In English that doubling would be an error; in Spanish leaving it out sounds wrong.

When both pronouns appear, order is **indirect then direct**: *me lo dio* (he gave it to me).

And one hard rule: **le/les becomes se** before *lo/la/los/las*. *Le di el libro* → ***Se** lo di*, never *le lo di*. Spanish simply refuses two l-words in a row.

Because *se lo* is ambiguous about who received it, clarify with **a + person**: *se lo di **a ella***.

examples.target: Le di el regalo a mi madre.
examples.native: I gave the present to my mother.

examples.target: ¿Me lo puedes explicar?
examples.native: Can you explain it to me?

examples.target: Se lo dije ayer.
examples.native: I told him (or her, or them) yesterday.

theory.watch_out: 'Le lo' never exists. It becomes 'se lo'.

theory.title: Preterite or imperfect?
theory.summary: The choice is not about how long ago or how long it lasted — it is about whether you see the action closed.
theory.body:
This is the hardest single decision in Spanish past tense, because **English has one simple past** covering both.

The usual shortcut — *completed vs ongoing* — is right but badly worded. Better: **preterite = a whole event, seen from outside; imperfect = the inside of a situation, no edges in view.**

Duration is irrelevant. *Viví en Madrid diez años* is preterite despite lasting a decade, because you are treating the decade as one closed block.

The classic pairing is background plus interruption: **imperfect sets the scene, preterite breaks it.** *Yo **leía** cuando **sonó** el teléfono* — I was reading (background) when the phone rang (event).

Some verbs shift meaning with the tense, which is the clearest proof it is about viewpoint rather than time:

*Sabía* = I knew · *Supe* = I found out
*Conocía* = I knew (a person) · *Conocí* = I met
*Quería* = I wanted · *Quise* = I tried · *No quise* = I refused
*Podía* = I was able · *Pude* = I managed to

examples.target: Leía tranquilamente cuando sonó el teléfono.
examples.native: I was reading quietly when the phone rang.

examples.target: Conocí a Ana en 2015; ya conocía a su hermano.
examples.native: I met Ana in 2015; I already knew her brother.

examples.target: Viví diez años en Madrid.
examples.native: I lived in Madrid for ten years.

theory.watch_out: Length of time decides nothing. 'Viví diez años' is preterite; 'eran las tres' is imperfect.

theory.title: Doler and talking about pain
theory.summary: It works like gustar, and Spanish uses 'the' where English uses 'my'.
theory.body:
**Doler** follows the *gustar* pattern exactly: the body part is the subject, and the person is an indirect object.

*Me duele la cabeza* — literally *the head hurts to me*.
*Me duelen los pies* — plural body part, plural verb.

Only two forms matter: **duele** and **duelen**. It is *o→ue* stem-changing, hence the *ue*.

The second point is the article. Spanish says **la cabeza**, not *mi cabeza*. With body parts and clothing, the indirect pronoun already tells you whose it is, so a possessive would be redundant — and *me duele mi cabeza* sounds wrong to a native ear.

Related ways to talk about health: **tener dolor de** (*tengo dolor de espalda*), **estar mareado** (dizzy), **tener fiebre** (a temperature), **encontrarse mal** (to feel unwell), **me siento mal**.

To ask: **¿qué te pasa?** or **¿dónde te duele?**

examples.target: Me duele mucho la garganta.
examples.native: My throat really hurts.

examples.target: ¿Te duelen las piernas?
examples.native: Do your legs hurt?

examples.target: Le duele la espalda desde ayer.
examples.native: His back has been hurting since yesterday.

theory.watch_out: 'Me duele mi cabeza' is redundant. The 'me' already says it's yours: 'me duele la cabeza'.

theory.title: Giving instructions: the tú command
theory.summary: The affirmative tú command is just the he/she form of the present, which makes it the easiest command to build.
theory.body:
To tell someone *tú* to do something, take the **third person singular of the present**: *hablar → habla*, *comer → come*, *escribir → escribe*. That is all.

Eight verbs are irregular, and they are short and frequent enough to learn as a block:

**decir → di · hacer → haz · ir → ve · poner → pon · salir → sal · ser → sé · tener → ten · venir → ven**

Pronouns **attach to the end** of an affirmative command, and a written accent usually appears to preserve the stress: *dime* (tell me), *háblame* (talk to me), *levántate* (get up), *dámelo* (give it to me).

Be careful with tone. A bare command is more normal in Spanish than in English — *pásame la sal* is not rude — but adding **por favor** or phrasing it as a question (*¿me pasas la sal?*) is softer and very common.

examples.target: Habla más despacio, por favor.
examples.native: Speak more slowly, please.

examples.target: Ven aquí y dime qué pasó.
examples.native: Come here and tell me what happened.

examples.target: Levántate, que es tarde.
examples.native: Get up, it's late.

theory.watch_out: Pronouns attach to the end here: 'dímelo', not 'me lo di'.

theory.title: Telling someone not to do something
theory.summary: The negative command looks nothing like the affirmative one — it borrows a whole different set of endings.
theory.body:
The negative *tú* command does **not** come from the affirmative. It is built from the **subjunctive**, and in practice that means: take the *yo* form of the present, drop the **-o**, and add the **opposite vowel** ending, then put **no** in front.

*hablar*: hablo → **no hables**
*comer*: como → **no comas**
*escribir*: escribo → **no escribas**

So -ar verbs take **-es** and -er/-ir verbs take **-as**. The vowels swap, which is the single most useful thing to remember about the subjunctive later on.

Because it starts from the *yo* form, irregular verbs stay irregular: *tener → tengo → no tengas*; *hacer → hago → no hagas*; *venir → vengo → no vengas*. Only *ir (no vayas)*, *ser (no seas)*, *dar (no des)* and *estar (no estés)* have to be learned separately.

And the pronouns move back **in front**: *no me hables*, *no te levantes*, *no me lo digas*.

examples.target: No hables tan rápido.
examples.native: Don't speak so fast.

examples.target: No te preocupes, no pasa nada.
examples.native: Don't worry, it's fine.

examples.target: No me lo digas ahora.
examples.native: Don't tell me now.

theory.watch_out: The pronoun jumps sides: 'dímelo' but 'no me lo digas'.

theory.title: Por and para
theory.summary: Both translate as 'for', and the split is roughly cause behind you versus goal ahead of you.
theory.body:
The most useful mental image: **para points forward** — destination, purpose, deadline, recipient. **Por points backward or through** — cause, motive, means, exchange, movement across.

**Para**: destination (*salgo para Madrid*), purpose (*estudio para aprender*), deadline (*para el lunes*), recipient (*es para ti*), opinion (*para mí, está bien*).

**Por**: cause (*lo hice por ti* — because of you), exchange (*lo compré por veinte euros*), duration (*por dos horas*), means (*por teléfono*), movement through (*paseo por el parque*), the agent in a passive (*escrito por Cervantes*), and approximate location (*por aquí*).

The pair that shows the difference: *lo hice **para** ti* = I made it to give to you. *Lo hice **por** ti* = I did it on your behalf, because of you.

Some expressions are simply fixed and worth memorising whole: *por favor, por supuesto, por fin, por eso, para siempre, por ahora*.

examples.target: Este regalo es para ti.
examples.native: This present is for you.

examples.target: Gracias por tu ayuda.
examples.native: Thanks for your help.

examples.target: Estudio español para trabajar en Chile.
examples.native: I'm studying Spanish in order to work in Chile.

theory.watch_out: Before an infinitive of purpose, it's always 'para': 'para aprender', never 'por aprender'.

theory.title: Se: saying what people do in general
theory.summary: Where English reaches for a vague 'you' or 'they', Spanish uses se and names nobody.
theory.body:
English has several vague subjects: *you can't park here*, *they say it's good*, *one never knows*. Spanish uses one construction: **se + third person verb**.

*Se habla español* — Spanish is spoken / people speak Spanish.
*No se puede fumar aquí* — you can't smoke here.
*¿Cómo se dice…?* — how do you say…?

The verb agrees with the **thing**, not with the invisible people: *se vende **casa*** (singular), *se venden **casas*** (plural). This trips up English speakers, who hear *se vende* as a fixed phrase.

This is everywhere in public language — shop signs, instructions, rules — precisely because it names no one and blames no one.

A close relative is the **accidental se**: *se me cayó el vaso* — the glass fell (on me). Spanish prefers this to *dejé caer el vaso*, which would assign blame. It is not evasion; it is the normal way to report an accident.

examples.target: Aquí se habla inglés.
examples.native: English is spoken here.

examples.target: ¿Cómo se dice 'window' en español?
examples.native: How do you say 'window' in Spanish?

examples.target: Se me olvidó el paraguas.
examples.native: I forgot my umbrella.

theory.watch_out: The verb agrees with the thing: 'se venden pisos', not 'se vende pisos'.

theory.title: The conditional: would
theory.summary: Same stems as the future, but the endings of the imperfect -er verbs.
theory.body:
The conditional is built from the **future stem** plus the **-ía endings** of the imperfect:

**-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían**

*hablaría, comerías, viviría, tendríamos, harían*

Every form carries the accent on the **í**. And every irregular future stem is irregular here too — *tendría, saldría, podría, diría, haría* — so there is nothing new to memorise.

Its jobs:

**Politeness.** *¿Podría ayudarme?* is markedly more courteous than *¿puede?* — this is the most frequent use in daily life.
**Advice.** *Yo que tú, hablaría con él* — if I were you, I'd talk to him. *Deberías* — you should.
**Hypothesis.** *Sería genial* — that would be great.
**The future seen from the past.** *Dijo que vendría* — he said he would come.

Beware: English *would* also marks past habit (*we would go every summer*). That is **not** the conditional in Spanish — it is the imperfect: *íbamos todos los veranos*.

examples.target: ¿Podría hablar con el gerente?
examples.native: Could I speak to the manager?

examples.target: Yo que tú, no iría.
examples.native: If I were you, I wouldn't go.

examples.target: Dijo que llegaría a las ocho.
examples.native: He said he'd arrive at eight.

theory.watch_out: English 'would' for a past habit is the imperfect in Spanish: 'de niño iba', not 'iría'.

theory.title: Irregular futures
theory.summary: Twelve verbs change the stem, and the same twelve stems reappear in the conditional.
theory.body:
The endings never change; only the stem does. Twelve verbs are affected, in three tidy groups.

**Drop the vowel**: *poder → podr-*, *querer → querr-*, *saber → sabr-*, *haber → habr-*, *caber → cabr-*

**Vowel becomes d**: *tener → tendr-*, *poner → pondr-*, *salir → saldr-*, *venir → vendr-*, *valer → valdr-*

**Fully irregular**: *hacer → har-*, *decir → dir-*

So: *tendré, saldrás, pondrá, habrá, diremos, harán*.

The payoff is that these **same stems serve the conditional** — *tendría, saldría, haría* — so learning them once covers two tenses.

**Habrá** is worth singling out: it is the future of *hay*, and like *hay* it never pluralises. *Habrá mucha gente* — there will be a lot of people.

examples.target: Tendremos que salir temprano.
examples.native: We'll have to leave early.

examples.target: ¿Qué harás el domingo?
examples.native: What will you do on Sunday?

examples.target: Habrá mucha gente en la fiesta.
examples.native: There'll be a lot of people at the party.

theory.watch_out: 'Habrá' covers 'there will be' singular and plural alike. 'Habrán muchas personas' is a common error.

theory.title: The future tense
theory.summary: The endings attach to the whole infinitive, so there is one set for all three verb families.
theory.body:
Unlike every other tense, the future does not drop the infinitive ending. The endings go straight onto the **full infinitive**:

**-é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án**

*hablar → hablaré, hablarás, hablará, hablaremos, hablaréis, hablarán*
*comer → comeré* · *vivir → viviré*

One set of endings for all three families, and every form except *nosotros* carries a written accent.

In everyday speech, **ir a + infinitive is more common** for plans. The future tense turns up in writing, in predictions, in promises, and in formal registers.

It has a second job that surprises learners: expressing **probability in the present**. *¿Qué hora será?* — what time do you think it is? *Estará en casa* — he's probably at home. This is not the future at all; it is a guess about now, and it is extremely common in speech.

examples.target: Mañana hablaré con el director.
examples.native: Tomorrow I'll speak with the director.

examples.target: ¿Dónde estará mi teléfono?
examples.native: Where can my phone be?

examples.target: El año que viene viviremos en Chile.
examples.native: Next year we'll be living in Chile.

theory.watch_out: The endings go on the whole infinitive: 'comeré', not 'comré'.

theory.title: Relative clauses: que, quien, donde
theory.summary: 'Que' covers people and things alike, and unlike English it can never be left out.
theory.body:
**Que** is the workhorse — it means *that, which, who* and *whom*, for people and things alike: *el libro **que** compré*, *la chica **que** vive aquí*.

The big difference from English: **que can never be omitted**. English happily drops it — *the book I bought* — but Spanish requires it: *el libro **que** compré*. This is one of the most common English-speaker errors at this level.

**Quien/quienes** is only for people, and mainly after a preposition or between commas: *la persona **con quien** hablé*.

**Donde** replaces *en que* for places: *la ciudad **donde** nací*.

**El que / el cual** and their feminine and plural forms are used after prepositions or to remove ambiguity, and belong to a more formal register: *la razón **por la que** vine*.

And **lo que** stands for a whole idea rather than a noun: *no entiendo **lo que** dices*.

examples.target: El libro que me prestaste es buenísimo.
examples.native: The book you lent me is excellent.

examples.target: Esa es la ciudad donde nací.
examples.native: That's the city where I was born.

examples.target: No entiendo lo que dices.
examples.native: I don't understand what you're saying.

theory.watch_out: You cannot drop 'que'. 'El libro compré' is not a sentence.

theory.title: The passive with se
theory.summary: Spanish avoids the full passive; this is what it uses instead, and it is much more natural.
theory.body:
Spanish has a true passive — *la casa **fue construida** en 1920* — but it is far less used than the English one. In everyday language, the **pasiva refleja** does the job:

**se + verb in the third person + the thing**

*Se construyó la casa en 1920.*
*Se venden pisos.*
*Se publicaron tres libros.*

The verb agrees with the **thing**, singular or plural. That agreement is what separates this from the impersonal *se*.

Use it when the doer is unknown or irrelevant. The moment you want to name the doer, you need the true passive with **por**: *la casa fue construida **por** mi abuelo* — or, more naturally still, just an active sentence: *mi abuelo construyó la casa*.

As a rule of thumb: where English reaches for a passive, Spanish reaches for **se** or for an active sentence with an unstated subject (*dicen que…* — they say that…).

examples.target: Se venden coches usados.
examples.native: Used cars are sold here.

examples.target: Se publicó el año pasado.
examples.native: It was published last year.

examples.target: Dicen que va a llover.
examples.native: They say it's going to rain.

theory.watch_out: If you name who did it, 'se' no longer works. 'Se vendió por Juan' is wrong — use 'Juan lo vendió'.

theory.title: Irregular past participles
theory.summary: About a dozen, and they double as adjectives — which is where the agreement comes back.
theory.body:
The list is short enough to learn outright:

**abrir → abierto · escribir → escrito · ver → visto · poner → puesto · hacer → hecho · decir → dicho · volver → vuelto · morir → muerto · romper → roto · cubrir → cubierto · resolver → resuelto**

Compounds inherit them: *describir → descrito*, *devolver → devuelto*, *componer → compuesto*, *deshacer → deshecho*.

A handful take a written accent to break a vowel cluster: *leer → leído*, *traer → traído*, *oír → oído*, *caer → caído*.

The second life of the participle is as an **adjective**, and there it **does agree**: *la puerta está abiert**a***, *los platos están rot**os***. So the same word is invariable after *haber* and variable after *ser* or *estar*. That contrast — *he abierto la puerta* vs *la puerta está abierta* — is the clearest way to see that agreement follows the grammar, not the word.

examples.target: He escrito tres cartas hoy.
examples.native: I've written three letters today.

examples.target: La ventana está abierta.
examples.native: The window is open.

examples.target: No he visto esa película.
examples.native: I haven't seen that film.

theory.watch_out: After 'haber' it never agrees; after 'estar' it always does. 'Han abierto' but 'están abiertas'.

theory.title: The present perfect: he hablado
theory.summary: Built like the English one, but its territory is different — and it varies by country.
theory.body:
Form: **haber** in the present + past participle.

*he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han* + *hablado / comido / vivido*

Participles: **-ar → -ado**, **-er/-ir → -ido**.

Two rules English does not have. The participle **never changes** for gender or number here — *ellas han llegado*, not *llegadas*. And **nothing may come between** *haber* and the participle: *no **he** terminado*, and pronouns go in front of *haber* — *lo he visto*, never *he lo visto*.

The usage is where it gets interesting. In **Spain**, the present perfect covers today and the recent past: *hoy he comido tarde*, *esta mañana he hablado con él*. In most of **Latin America**, the preterite does that work: *hoy comí tarde*. Neither is wrong; they are regional.

Signal words: *ya, todavía no, alguna vez, nunca, hoy, esta semana, últimamente*.

examples.target: ¿Has estado alguna vez en México?
examples.native: Have you ever been to Mexico?

examples.target: Todavía no he terminado el informe.
examples.native: I haven't finished the report yet.

examples.target: Esta semana hemos trabajado mucho.
examples.native: We've worked a lot this week.

theory.watch_out: Nothing goes between 'haber' and the participle: 'lo he visto', never 'he lo visto'.

theory.title: Estar + gerund: what is happening right now
theory.summary: Spanish uses it far less than English does, and never for the future.
theory.body:
Form: **estar** + gerund. **-ar → -ando**, **-er/-ir → -iendo**: *hablando, comiendo, viviendo*.

Spelling shifts: a vowel before the ending turns *-iendo* into **-yendo** (*leyendo, oyendo, cayendo*), and -ir stem-changers shift the vowel (*decir → diciendo*, *dormir → durmiendo*, *pedir → pidiendo*).

The crucial difference: **Spanish uses this much less than English.** The simple present already covers ongoing action, so *¿qué haces?* is the normal way to ask what someone is doing. Reserve *estar + gerundio* for stressing that something is in progress **at this moment**: *ahora mismo estoy comiendo*.

And it is **never** used for the future. *I'm flying to Madrid tomorrow* is *mañana **vuelo** a Madrid* or *voy a volar* — *estoy volando mañana* is wrong.

Other verbs take the gerund with a nuance: **seguir/continuar** (still doing), **llevar** (doing it for a time — *llevo dos horas esperando*), **ir** (gradually).

examples.target: Ahora mismo estoy trabajando.
examples.native: Right now I'm working.

examples.target: Llevo dos horas esperando.
examples.native: I've been waiting for two hours.

examples.target: Mañana voy a Sevilla.
examples.native: I'm going to Seville tomorrow.

theory.watch_out: Never for future plans. 'Estoy yendo mañana' is wrong — say 'voy mañana'.

theory.title: Reporting what someone said
theory.summary: The tense shift is the same idea as in English, and 'que' is compulsory.
theory.body:
To report speech, use **decir que**, **comentar que**, **explicar que** — and **que can never be dropped**, unlike English *he said he was tired*.

If the reporting verb is in the **present**, nothing shifts: *dice que **está** cansado*.

If it is in the **past**, the reported verb moves back one step:

present → imperfect (*estoy* → *dijo que estaba*)
preterite/perfect → pluperfect (*fui* → *dijo que había ido*)
future → conditional (*iré* → *dijo que iría*)
imperative → imperfect subjunctive (*ven* → *me dijo que viniera*)

The imperfect and the conditional do not shift further — they are already as far back as it goes.

Other things move too: *aquí → allí*, *hoy → aquel día*, *mañana → al día siguiente*, *este → ese*, and the person changes (*yo → él*).

For questions, use **preguntar si** for yes/no, and keep the question word (with its accent) otherwise: *me preguntó **dónde** vivía*.

examples.target: Dijo que estaba muy cansado.
examples.native: He said he was very tired.

examples.target: Me preguntó si quería café.
examples.native: She asked me if I wanted coffee.

examples.target: Nos dijo que llegaría tarde.
examples.native: He told us he'd arrive late.

theory.watch_out: 'Que' is compulsory: 'dijo que estaba', never 'dijo estaba'.

theory.title: The subjunctive: what it actually is
theory.summary: Not a tense and not a list of triggers — it is the mood you use when you are not reporting the world.
theory.body:
English speakers meet the subjunctive as a list of phrases to memorise, and that is why it stays hard. The idea underneath is simpler.

**The indicative reports on reality.** *Sé que **viene*** — I know he is coming; I am telling you a fact.
**The subjunctive does not report.** It wishes, doubts, denies, reacts emotionally, or projects something not yet real. *Espero que **venga*** — I hope he comes; I am not stating that he does.

The form is the vowel swap you already met in negative commands: take the **yo** form of the present, drop the -o, and use the **opposite vowel**.

*hablar*: hablo → **hable, hables, hable, hablemos, habléis, hablen**
*comer*: como → **coma, comas, coma, comamos, comáis, coman**

Because it starts from *yo*, irregulars carry over: *tengo → tenga*, *hago → haga*, *digo → diga*, *salgo → salga*.

Six must be learned alone: **ser → sea · ir → vaya · saber → sepa · haber → haya · estar → esté · dar → dé**.

examples.target: Espero que tengas un buen día.
examples.native: I hope you have a good day.

examples.target: Quiero que vengas a la fiesta.
examples.native: I want you to come to the party.

examples.target: Sé que viene mañana.
examples.native: I know he's coming tomorrow.

theory.watch_out: It normally needs two different subjects. Same subject takes an infinitive: 'quiero ir', not 'quiero que yo vaya'.

theory.title: Making suggestions and giving advice
theory.summary: The conditional is the politeness dial; a bare command is not rude, but it is not soft either.
theory.body:
Ways to suggest something, roughly from softest to most direct:

**¿Y si + present/imperfect?** — *¿y si vamos al cine?* The most casual.
**Podrías / deberías + infinitive** — *deberías descansar*. Advice.
**Yo que tú / yo en tu lugar + conditional** — *yo que tú, no iría*. The classic advice frame.
**¿Por qué no…?** — *¿por qué no le llamas?*
**Te recomiendo que / te aconsejo que + subjunctive** — *te recomiendo que vayas*. Note the subjunctive, because two subjects are involved.
**Hay que / tienes que** — the direct end.

The conditional is what does the softening. *¿Puedes ayudarme?* is fine among friends; *¿podrías ayudarme?* is what you say to a stranger; *¿podría ayudarme?* is the formal version of that.

For offering rather than advising: **¿Quieres que…?** + subjunctive — *¿quieres que te ayude?*

examples.target: Yo que tú, hablaría con ella.
examples.native: If I were you, I'd talk to her.

examples.target: ¿Y si vamos al cine esta noche?
examples.native: What if we go to the cinema tonight?

examples.target: Te recomiendo que llegues temprano.
examples.native: I recommend you arrive early.

theory.watch_out: 'Yo que tú' is followed by the conditional, not the subjunctive: 'yo que tú iría'.

theory.title: Talking about plans: ir a, pensar, querer
theory.summary: Three degrees of commitment, from a firm arrangement to a vague intention.
theory.body:
Spanish separates plans by how settled they are.

**Ir a + infinitive** — the decision is made. *Voy a comprar un coche.*
**Pensar + infinitive** — you intend to, but it is not fixed. *Pienso comprar un coche.* Note there is **no *en*** here: *pienso ir*, not *pienso en ir* (which means *I'm thinking about the idea of going*).
**Querer + infinitive** — you want to, nothing arranged. *Quiero comprar un coche.*
**Tener pensado / tener la intención de** — more formal versions of *pensar*.

Also useful: **estar a punto de** (about to), **acabar de** (to have just — *acabo de llegar*, present tense for a past event), and **quedar en** (to agree to — *quedamos en vernos el lunes*).

Careful with **quedar**: *quedar con alguien* is to arrange to meet, *quedarse* is to stay, and *quedar* alone can mean to be left over. Three different verbs sharing a shape.

examples.target: Pienso estudiar medicina.
examples.native: I'm planning to study medicine.

examples.target: Acabo de hablar con ella.
examples.native: I've just spoken to her.

examples.target: Quedamos en vernos el viernes.
examples.native: We agreed to meet on Friday.

theory.watch_out: 'Pienso ir' is I plan to go. 'Pienso en ir' is I'm mulling it over. The 'en' changes the meaning.

theory.title: B1 review: the four past tenses
theory.summary: By this point four ways to talk about the past coexist, and each answers a different question.
theory.body:
Spanish has four past forms in ordinary use, and the choice is about **viewpoint**, not distance in time.

**Preterite** — a finished event, seen whole. *Ayer **comí** paella.*
**Imperfect** — background, habit, description, no edges. *De niño **comía** paella todos los domingos.*
**Present perfect** — connected to now; in Spain, also today. *Hoy **he comido** paella.*
**Pluperfect** — before another past point. *Cuando llegué, ya **habían comido**.*

The pluperfect (**había + participle**) is the easiest of the four and works exactly like English *had eaten*.

The two that genuinely compete are the preterite and the imperfect. A working test: if you could add *while* or *used to*, it is imperfect. If you could add *and then*, it is preterite.

And remember the tense shifts meaning in a few verbs — *supe* (found out) vs *sabía* (knew), *conocí* (met) vs *conocía* (knew) — which is the strongest evidence that the choice is about how you frame the event.

examples.target: Cuando llegué, ya habían cenado.
examples.native: When I arrived, they had already had dinner.

examples.target: Llovía cuando salimos de casa.
examples.native: It was raining when we left the house.

examples.target: Esta mañana he hablado con el médico.
examples.native: This morning I spoke to the doctor.

theory.watch_out: Not distance in time but viewpoint. 'Viví allí veinte años' is preterite; 'eran las tres' is imperfect.

theory.title: Cuando with the subjunctive
theory.summary: The same word takes a different mood depending on whether the event is habitual or still ahead.
theory.body:
**Cuando** takes the indicative for something habitual or already past, and the subjunctive for something **still in the future**:

*Cuando **llego** a casa, me ducho.* — habitual, indicative.
*Cuando **llegue** a casa, me ducharé.* — not yet happened, subjunctive.

This is not an exception. It follows the core idea: the future has not happened, so it is not being reported as fact.

The same applies to every time conjunction: **en cuanto** (as soon as), **hasta que** (until), **después de que**, **mientras**, **tan pronto como**, **siempre que**.

*Te llamo en cuanto **llegue***.
*Espera aquí hasta que **vuelva***.

English hides this because it uses a plain present for the future in these clauses — *when I get home, I'll shower* — so there is no signal to transfer.

One exception worth noting: **antes de que** always takes the subjunctive, in every context, because what follows it has by definition not happened yet.

examples.target: Cuando llegue, te aviso.
examples.native: When I arrive, I'll let you know.
