examples.target: Cuando llego tarde, ceno solo.
examples.native: When I get home late, I eat alone.

examples.target: Antes de que te vayas, firma esto.
examples.native: Before you go, sign this.

theory.watch_out: 'Cuando llego' is a habit; 'cuando llegue' is a plan. Same word, different mood, different meaning.

theory.title: The subjunctive after wanting and hoping
theory.summary: The rule that decides everything is whether the two halves have the same subject.
theory.body:
Verbs of **wanting, hoping, asking and advising** take the subjunctive: *querer, esperar, desear, pedir, recomendar, aconsejar, sugerir, necesitar, preferir*.

But only when there are **two different subjects**. This is the switch English speakers keep missing, because English uses an infinitive in both cases:

*I want to go* → **quiero ir** (one subject: infinitive)
*I want you to go* → **quiero que vayas** (two subjects: subjunctive)

English says *I want you to go*, so learners produce *quiero tú ir*, which is not Spanish. The moment a second person appears, you need **que** and the subjunctive.

**Ojalá** always takes the subjunctive, with or without *que*: *ojalá venga*. It comes from Arabic *law šāʾ Allāh* — *if God wills* — which explains why the mood is baked in.

Same with **que** alone at the start of a wish: *¡Que te mejores!*, *¡Que tengas suerte!* — a very common everyday construction.

examples.target: Quiero que me llames mañana.
examples.native: I want you to call me tomorrow.

examples.target: Ojalá haga buen tiempo.
examples.native: Hopefully the weather will be good.

examples.target: ¡Que tengas un buen viaje!
examples.native: Have a good trip!

theory.watch_out: One subject means infinitive: 'espero llegar'. Two subjects means subjunctive: 'espero que llegues'.

theory.title: Connectors of contrast
theory.summary: 'Pero' and 'sino' are both 'but', and choosing wrong is one of the most audible errors.
theory.body:
**Pero** adds a qualification: *es caro, **pero** me gusta*.

**Sino** corrects a negative — *not X but Y*. It only appears after a negative statement: *no es caro, **sino** barato*. When a conjugated verb follows, it becomes **sino que**: *no lo compré, **sino que** lo alquilé*.

English uses *but* for both, so *no es caro pero barato* is an extremely common learner sentence — and it sounds clearly wrong to a native.

The rest of the family:

**sin embargo / no obstante** — however (formal, usually after a full stop or semicolon)
**aunque** — although
**a pesar de (que)** — in spite of
**mientras que** — whereas (contrast between two things)
**en cambio / por el contrario** — on the other hand

Note **mientras** alone means *while* in time; **mientras que** contrasts. *Mientras cocino, escucho música* against *él es tranquilo, mientras que ella es nerviosa*.

examples.target: No es difícil, sino aburrido.
examples.native: It's not difficult, but boring.

examples.target: Es caro, pero merece la pena.
examples.native: It's expensive, but it's worth it.

examples.target: Sin embargo, no todos están de acuerdo.
examples.native: However, not everyone agrees.

theory.watch_out: After a negative, correcting it takes 'sino': 'no es caro, sino barato'.

theory.title: Irregular imperfect subjunctives
theory.summary: There are none of its own — every irregularity is inherited from the preterite.
theory.body:
Strictly speaking this tense has **no irregular verbs**. Every oddity comes from the preterite, and the rule *ellos-form minus -ron* absorbs all of them.

*ser / ir*: fueron → **fuera** (shared, exactly as in the preterite)
*estar*: estuvieron → **estuviera**
*tener*: tuvieron → **tuviera**
*hacer*: hicieron → **hiciera**
*decir*: dijeron → **dijera**
*poder*: pudieron → **pudiera**
*saber*: supieron → **supiera**
*haber*: hubieron → **hubiera**
*dar*: dieron → **diera**
*querer*: quisieron → **quisiera**

So the practical advice is: if you are unsure of an imperfect subjunctive, do not try to derive it from the infinitive — recall the preterite first.

**Quisiera** deserves a note of its own. It is used as an extra-polite *I would like*: *quisiera reservar una mesa*. Softer than *quiero*, and slightly more formal than *me gustaría*. In a hotel or a restaurant it is the phrase to have ready.

examples.target: Quisiera reservar una mesa para dos.
examples.native: I'd like to book a table for two.

examples.target: Si fuera rico, viajaría por el mundo.
examples.native: If I were rich, I'd travel the world.

examples.target: No creía que supieras la respuesta.
examples.native: I didn't think you knew the answer.

theory.watch_out: If you don't know the form, recall the preterite first. 'Ellos dijeron' is what gives you 'dijera'.

theory.title: The imperfect subjunctive
theory.summary: Built from the third person plural of the preterite, which makes every irregular free.
theory.body:
The recipe never fails: take the **ellos form of the preterite**, remove **-ron**, and add the endings.

*hablar → hablaron → **habla-*** 
*comer → comieron → **comie-***

Then: **-ra, -ras, -ra, -´ramos, -rais, -ran**
→ *hablara, hablaras, hablara, habláramos, hablarais, hablaran*

There is a second, fully equivalent set: **-se, -ses, -se, -´semos, -seis, -sen** → *hablase, hablases…*. The **-ra** forms dominate in speech and in Latin America; **-se** sounds more literary or peninsular. Either is correct.

The *nosotros* form always carries a written accent: *habláramos, comiéramos, tuviéramos*.

The beauty of the rule is that **every preterite irregularity comes along automatically**: *tuvieron → tuviera*, *fueron → fuera*, *dijeron → dijera*, *hicieron → hiciera*, *pudieron → pudiera*. Nothing extra to learn.

It is used where the subjunctive is required but the frame is past or hypothetical.

examples.target: Quería que vinieras conmigo.
examples.native: I wanted you to come with me.

examples.target: Me pidió que le ayudara.
examples.native: He asked me to help him.

examples.target: Si tuviera tiempo, iría.
examples.native: If I had time, I'd go.

theory.watch_out: Build it from the preterite, never from the infinitive: 'tener' gives 'tuviera', not 'teniera'.

theory.title: The pluperfect: había hablado
theory.summary: The one compound tense that maps cleanly onto English, with no regional variation.
theory.body:
Form: the **imperfect of haber** + past participle.

*había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían* + *hablado / comido / vivido*

It means the same as English *had spoken*: something completed **before another point in the past**. Because both languages agree here, it is the easiest compound tense to acquire.

*Cuando llegué, ya **habían cenado**.* — they finished before I arrived.
*No sabía que **habías estado** en Perú.*

As with the present perfect, nothing goes between *haber* and the participle, the participle never agrees, and pronouns sit before *haber*: *ya lo había visto*.

Useful companions: **ya** (already), **todavía no** (not yet), **antes de** and **cuando**.

There is a literary alternative, the pretérito anterior (*hubo llegado*), which you will meet in nineteenth-century novels and effectively nowhere else. Recognise it, do not use it.

examples.target: Cuando llegamos, la película ya había empezado.
examples.native: When we arrived, the film had already started.

examples.target: No sabía que habías vivido en Perú.
examples.native: I didn't know you had lived in Peru.

examples.target: Nunca había probado ese plato.
examples.native: I had never tried that dish.

theory.watch_out: Pronouns go before 'haber': 'ya lo había visto', not 'había lo visto'.

theory.title: Subjunctive with doubt and denial
theory.summary: Negating a verb of thinking flips the mood — 'creo que' and 'no creo que' behave differently.
theory.body:
Expressions of **doubt, denial or improbability** take the subjunctive: *dudar que, no creer que, no pensar que, negar que, no es verdad que, es posible que, puede que, es improbable que*.

The cleanest demonstration is the flip:

*Creo que **tiene** razón.* — indicative; I am asserting it.
*No creo que **tenga** razón.* — subjunctive; I am not asserting anything.

Same verb, and the negation alone changes the mood. English gives no hint of this.

Careful in the reverse direction: **no dudar que** and **no negar que** take the **indicative**, because denying a doubt is an assertion. *No dudo que **es** verdad.*

**Quizá / tal vez / probablemente** take either mood, and the choice is a real nuance: subjunctive for more doubt, indicative for less. *Quizá **venga*** (maybe, who knows) against *quizá **viene*** (I rather think he will).

**Puede que** always takes the subjunctive: *puede que llueva*.

examples.target: No creo que sea buena idea.
examples.native: I don't think it's a good idea.

examples.target: Es posible que llegue tarde.
examples.native: It's possible he'll arrive late.

examples.target: No dudo que tienes razón.
examples.native: I don't doubt that you're right.

theory.watch_out: 'Creo que viene' but 'no creo que venga'. The negation alone changes the mood.

theory.title: The conditional perfect: habría hecho
theory.summary: For the thing that did not happen — the regret tense.
theory.body:
Form: **habría** + past participle. *habría, habrías, habría, habríamos, habríais, habrían* + participle.

It describes something that **would have happened but didn't**: *yo **habría ido**, pero estaba enfermo*.

Its natural home is the third conditional, paired with the pluperfect subjunctive: *Si **hubiera sabido**, te **habría llamado*** — if I had known, I would have called you.

In that structure the two halves are interchangeable in one direction: *hubiera llamado* is widely used in place of *habría llamado* in speech (*si hubiera sabido, te hubiera llamado*), and is perfectly standard. The reverse — *habría* in the *si* clause — is not: ***si habría sabido*** is a well-known error, marked as uneducated in Spain.

It also expresses **a guess about a past event**: *ya habrían salido cuando llamaste* — they had probably already left. Same probability use as the future, moved back in time.

examples.target: Si hubiera sabido, te habría llamado.
examples.native: If I had known, I would have called you.

examples.target: Yo habría hecho lo mismo.
examples.native: I would have done the same.

examples.target: Habrían salido ya cuando llegaste.
examples.native: They had probably already left when you arrived.

theory.watch_out: 'Si habría sabido' is wrong. The 'si' half takes 'hubiera'.

theory.title: The gerund and its limits
theory.summary: Spanish forbids the gerund exactly where English uses it most — as a noun and as a modifier.
theory.body:
The gerund (*-ando / -iendo*) expresses an action **in progress** or **the manner** of another action: *entró **corriendo***, *aprendo **practicando***.

The restrictions matter more than the uses, because English pushes learners straight into them.

**Never as a noun.** English *smoking is bad* becomes ***fumar** es malo* — the infinitive is the noun in Spanish. *Fumando es malo* is wrong.

**Never as an adjective modifying a noun.** English *a box containing books* is *una caja **que contiene** libros*. The only two exceptions in the whole language are *hirviendo* (boiling) and *ardiendo* (burning).

**Never for the future**, as covered earlier.

**Not for a subsequent action.** *Se cayó rompiéndose el brazo* is poor Spanish; the arm broke as a result, not simultaneously — say *se cayó y se rompió el brazo*.

What it does well: simultaneity (*desayuno **viendo** las noticias*), manner (*me lo dijo **sonriendo***), and cause (***siendo** tan tarde, nos fuimos*).

examples.target: Fumar es malo para la salud.
examples.native: Smoking is bad for your health.

examples.target: Entró corriendo en la sala.
examples.native: He ran into the room.

examples.target: Aprendo español practicando todos los días.
examples.native: I learn Spanish by practising every day.

theory.watch_out: As a subject, use the infinitive: 'nadar es divertido', never 'nadando es divertido'.

theory.title: Turning things into nouns
theory.summary: An article plus almost anything becomes a noun — including 'lo' plus an adjective, which English cannot do at all.
theory.body:
Spanish makes nouns very cheaply: put an **article** in front of something.

**Article + adjective** drops the repeated noun: *¿el coche rojo o el azul?* — the red car or the blue one? Spanish has no equivalent of *one*; the article carries it.

**Article + de** shows possession or origin: *el de Juan* (Juan's), *la de la esquina* (the one on the corner).

**Article + que**: *el que llegó primero* — the one who arrived first.

**El + infinitive** makes an abstract noun: *el comer, el dormir*.

The one with no English equivalent is **lo + adjective**, which creates an abstract quality: **lo bueno** (the good thing/part), **lo importante**, **lo difícil**. *Lo bueno es que ya terminó* — the good thing is that it's over.

And **lo + adjective + que** intensifies: *no sabes **lo difícil que** es* — you don't know how difficult it is. Note the adjective agrees with the noun it describes: *lo guapa que es*.

examples.target: Lo importante es participar.
examples.native: The important thing is to take part.

examples.target: ¿Prefieres el rojo o el azul?
examples.native: Do you prefer the red one or the blue one?

examples.target: No sabes lo difícil que fue.
examples.native: You have no idea how hard it was.

theory.watch_out: 'Lo' never goes with a noun. It's 'lo bueno' but 'el libro bueno'.

theory.title: Relatives after prepositions
theory.summary: Spanish cannot strand a preposition at the end, so the whole phrase moves to the front.
theory.body:
English happily ends a clause with a preposition: *the man I spoke to*. Spanish **cannot**. The preposition must travel with the relative:

*el hombre **con el que** hablé*
*la razón **por la que** vine*
*la casa **en la que** vivo*

After a preposition, plain **que** needs an article: **el que, la que, los que, las que**. For people, **quien/quienes** is also available and slightly more formal: *el hombre **con quien** hablé*.

**El cual / la cual / los cuales** belongs to formal writing, and is preferred after longer prepositions (*a pesar de la cual*, *frente al cual*) where *el que* would be clumsy.

**Cuyo** means *whose* and — a detail that catches everyone — agrees with **the thing possessed**, not the owner: *el escritor **cuyas** novelas leí*. It is written language; in speech people rephrase.

And **lo cual** refers back to a whole clause: *llegó tarde, **lo cual** me molestó*.

examples.target: Ese es el hombre con el que hablé.
examples.native: That's the man I spoke to.

examples.target: La razón por la que vine es simple.
examples.native: The reason I came is simple.

examples.target: Es un autor cuyas novelas me encantan.
examples.native: He's an author whose novels I love.

theory.watch_out: You cannot leave the preposition at the end. 'El hombre que hablé con' is not Spanish.

theory.title: Reported speech: the full tense shift
theory.summary: Two tenses do not move because they are already at the back, and knowing which saves half the work.
theory.body:
With a past reporting verb, the whole system shifts back one notch:

present → **imperfect**
preterite / present perfect → **pluperfect**
future → **conditional**
future perfect → **conditional perfect**
present subjunctive → **imperfect subjunctive**
imperative → **imperfect subjunctive**

And two do **not** shift, because there is nowhere further back: the **imperfect** and the **conditional** stay as they are. *«Estaba cansado»* → *dijo que estaba cansado*.

The pluperfect also stays put, for the same reason.

Commands become subjunctive: *«Ven»* → *me dijo que **viniera***. This is where the imperfect subjunctive earns its keep in everyday speech.

Time and place markers move with the tense: *hoy → aquel día*, *ayer → el día anterior*, *mañana → al día siguiente*, *aquí → allí*, *ahora → entonces*, *este → aquel*.

And if what was said is **still true**, native speakers often leave the present alone: *dijo que **se llama** Ana*.

examples.target: Me dijo que viniera a las ocho.
examples.native: He told me to come at eight.

examples.target: Comentó que ya lo había visto.
examples.native: He mentioned he had already seen it.

examples.target: Dijo que se llama Ana.
examples.native: She said her name is Ana.

theory.watch_out: The imperfect and the conditional don't shift. 'Dijo que estaba' stays 'estaba'.

theory.title: The -ísimo ending
theory.summary: A one-word intensifier with no English equivalent, and it is everywhere in speech.
theory.body:
Adding **-ísimo** to an adjective means *extremely*: *bueno → buenísimo*, *caro → carísimo*, *grande → grandísimo*.

Spelling rules: drop the final vowel first (*alto → altísimo*). A **c** becomes **qu** (*rico → riquísimo*), a **g** becomes **gu** (*largo → larguísimo*), a **z** becomes **c** (*feliz → felicísimo*). A few are irregular in a Latinate way: *fuerte → fortísimo*, *antiguo → antiquísimo*.

It agrees like any adjective: *buenísima, carísimos*.

It can also attach to some adverbs: *muchísimo, tardísimo, cerquísima*.

The important thing is register. This is **conversational** and warm, not formal. *La comida estaba buenísima* is what you say to a host; *la comida estaba extremadamente buena* sounds like a report.

And it does not stack: *muy buenísimo* is wrong. The ending already contains the *muy*.

examples.target: La comida estaba buenísima.
examples.native: The food was absolutely delicious.

examples.target: Es un libro larguísimo.
examples.native: It's an extremely long book.

examples.target: Te lo agradezco muchísimo.
examples.native: Thank you so very much.

theory.watch_out: 'Muy buenísimo' is wrong. The -ísimo already means 'very'.

theory.title: Mejor, peor, mayor, menor
theory.summary: Four forms that replace 'más + adjective', and two of them mean age rather than size.
theory.body:
Four adjectives have their own comparative and reject *más*:

**bueno → mejor** (better) · **malo → peor** (worse) · **grande → mayor** · **pequeño → menor**

They have one form for both genders and add **-es** for plural: *mejores, peores*.

**Mayor** and **menor** refer to **age** far more often than to size: *mi hermano mayor* is my older brother, not my bigger one. For physical size, Spanish uses *más grande / más pequeño*. So *una casa mayor* sounds odd; say *una casa más grande*.

**Mejor** and **peor** double as adverbs: *canta mejor que yo* (sings better).

*Más bueno* and *más malo* do exist, but they refer to moral character or, with food, to taste: *este niño es más bueno que el otro*.

The superlative just adds the article: *el mejor restaurante de la ciudad* — and note **de**, where English uses *in*. *El mejor en la ciudad* is a common error.

examples.target: Mi hermana mayor vive en Bogotá.
examples.native: My older sister lives in Bogotá.

examples.target: Es el mejor restaurante de la ciudad.
examples.native: It's the best restaurant in the city.

examples.target: Hoy me siento peor que ayer.
examples.native: Today I feel worse than yesterday.

theory.watch_out: The superlative takes 'de', not 'en': 'el mejor de la clase'.

theory.title: The pluperfect subjunctive: hubiera hecho
theory.summary: For the past that never was — and it is the required form after 'si'.
theory.body:
Form: the **imperfect subjunctive of haber** + participle: *hubiera* (or *hubiese*) + *hablado / comido / ido*.

It refers to something that **would have been true but wasn't**, or to a subjunctive context set before another past point.

Its main home is the third conditional: *Si **hubiera estudiado**, habría aprobado.*

Also after any subjunctive trigger pointing further back: *No creía que **hubiera llegado***; *Me alegré de que **hubieras venido***.

Two points worth fixing in memory. First, **si never takes habría** — *si habría estudiado* is a marked error. The *si* half takes *hubiera*. Second, in the result half both are acceptable: *habría aprobado* and *hubiera aprobado* are both standard, the second being very common in speech.

**Ojalá hubiera** expresses regret about the past: *ojalá hubiera ido* — I wish I had gone. Compare *ojalá fuera* (present wish) and *ojalá vaya* (future hope). Three regrets at three distances.

examples.target: Si hubiera estudiado más, habría aprobado.
examples.native: If I had studied more, I would have passed.

examples.target: Ojalá hubiera ido a esa fiesta.
examples.native: I wish I had gone to that party.

examples.target: No creía que hubieras terminado.
examples.native: I didn't think you had finished.

theory.watch_out: After 'si', always 'hubiera'. 'Si habría sabido' is a well-known error.

theory.title: Subjunctive after emotion
theory.summary: The oddity is that the fact is true and still takes the subjunctive — because you are reacting, not reporting.
theory.body:
Expressions of **emotion and value judgement** take the subjunctive: *me alegro de que, siento que, me molesta que, me sorprende que, temo que, es una pena que, qué raro que, es bueno/malo/lógico/normal que*.

What makes this group philosophically odd is that **the fact is usually true**. *Me alegro de que **estés** aquí* — you are demonstrably here. So why the subjunctive?

Because the sentence is not asserting that you are here. The assertion is *I'm glad*; your presence is the presupposed backdrop being reacted to. The subjunctive marks information that is **not the point of the sentence**.

Once you see it that way, the whole mood becomes coherent rather than a list.

As always, the two-subject rule applies. Same subject → infinitive: *me alegro de **estar** aquí*. Different subject → subjunctive: *me alegro de que **estés** aquí*.

Impersonal judgements work the same way: *es importante que **vengas***, but *es importante **venir*** when nobody in particular is meant.

examples.target: Me alegro de que estés mejor.
examples.native: I'm glad you're better.

examples.target: Es una pena que no puedas venir.
examples.native: It's a shame you can't come.

examples.target: Me sorprende que no lo sepas.
examples.native: I'm surprised you don't know.

theory.watch_out: The fact being true doesn't matter here. Reacting to it is what triggers the subjunctive.

theory.title: Time conjunctions and the mood they take
theory.summary: The rule is one question: has it happened yet?
theory.body:
Every time conjunction — **cuando, en cuanto, tan pronto como, hasta que, después de que, mientras, siempre que, una vez que** — takes:

**Indicative** for something habitual or already past.
**Subjunctive** for something still ahead.

*Siempre que **vengo**, comemos juntos.* (habit)
*Siempre que **vengas**, avísame.* (future)

Two behave differently and are worth memorising:

**Antes de que** — **always** subjunctive, no exceptions, because what follows has not happened. *Antes de que **salgas**, cierra la ventana.*

**Después de que** — subjunctive for the future, but in practice you will hear the indicative for past events too: *después de que **llegó***. Both circulate.

And when there is only **one subject**, drop the *que* and use an **infinitive**: *antes de **salir***, *después de **comer***, *hasta **terminar***. That is the more natural construction, and learners tend to over-use the *que* version.

examples.target: Llámame en cuanto llegues.
examples.native: Call me as soon as you arrive.

examples.target: Antes de que te vayas, dame tu número.
examples.native: Before you leave, give me your number.

examples.target: Después de comer, salimos a pasear.
examples.native: After eating, we go out for a walk.

theory.watch_out: One subject means no 'que': 'antes de salir', not 'antes de que yo salga'.

theory.title: Saying why: porque, como, ya que
theory.summary: They differ by position and by whether the reason is new information.
theory.body:
**Porque** — the default, and it can never start a sentence. The reason is new: *no fui **porque** estaba enfermo*.

**Como** — must go **first**, and presents the reason as already known or agreed: ***Como** estaba enfermo, no fui.* Using *como* in the middle changes its meaning to *as/like*.

**Ya que / puesto que / dado que** — the reason is shared knowledge; they can go either side. *Ya que estás aquí, ayúdame.*

**Por + noun or infinitive** — compact: *lo despidieron **por llegar** tarde*.

**Debido a / a causa de + noun** — formal, written.

**Es que** — the spoken excuse: *no puedo, **es que** tengo que trabajar*. Extremely common and worth having.

For consequence rather than cause: **así que** (so), **por eso** (that's why), **por lo tanto / en consecuencia** (therefore, formal), **de ahí que** + subjunctive.

And distinguish **por qué** (why, question), **porque** (because), **por que** (for which) and **el porqué** (the reason). Four spellings, four jobs.

examples.target: Como llovía, nos quedamos en casa.
examples.native: As it was raining, we stayed at home.

examples.target: No voy porque tengo que estudiar.
examples.native: I'm not going because I have to study.

examples.target: Ya que estás aquí, échame una mano.
examples.native: Since you're here, give me a hand.

theory.watch_out: 'Porque' can never open a sentence. Use 'como' there.

theory.title: The second conditional: si tuviera, iría
theory.summary: Hypothetical present. The 'si' half never takes a conditional, and never the present subjunctive either.
theory.body:
For something imagined, unlikely or contrary to fact **now**:

**Si + imperfect subjunctive, + conditional**

*Si **tuviera** dinero, **viajaría** por el mundo.*
*Si **fuera** tú, no lo **haría**.*

The two halves can swap order without a comma: *viajaría por el mundo si tuviera dinero*.

Two hard prohibitions, and they cause most of the errors:

**Si never takes the conditional.** *Si tendría dinero* is wrong — badly wrong, the way *if I would have* is in English.
**Si never takes the present subjunctive.** *Si tenga* does not exist in modern Spanish.

The present subjunctive after *si* is simply not a thing; the imperfect subjunctive is what does hypothesis.

Contrast with the **first conditional**, which is about real possibility and takes the plain **present**: *Si **tengo** tiempo, **iré*** — if I have time, I'll go. So *si tengo* (likely) against *si tuviera* (imagined).

**Como si** always takes the imperfect subjunctive: *habla como si **fuera** experto*.

examples.target: Si tuviera más tiempo, aprendería a tocar el piano.
examples.native: If I had more time, I'd learn to play the piano.

examples.target: Si tengo tiempo, te llamo.
examples.native: If I have time, I'll call you.

examples.target: Habla como si fuera el jefe.
examples.native: He talks as if he were the boss.

theory.watch_out: 'Si tendría' and 'si tenga' are both wrong. After 'si' it's 'tuviera' or the plain present.

theory.title: The third conditional: what never happened
theory.summary: Past regret, and the one construction where two different forms are equally acceptable in the result half.
theory.body:
For an unreal past — something that did not happen and now cannot:

**Si + pluperfect subjunctive, + conditional perfect**

*Si **hubiera estudiado**, **habría aprobado**.*

In the result half, **hubiera aprobado** is just as standard and is more common in speech: *si hubiera estudiado, hubiera aprobado*. Both are correct. What remains wrong is *si habría estudiado*.

**Mixed conditionals** work exactly as in English, and are worth practising because they are frequent:

Past cause, present result: *Si **hubiera estudiado** medicina, ahora **sería** médico.*
Present cause, past result: *Si **fuera** más organizado, no **habría perdido** el tren.*

Related ways to say the same regret: **de haber + participle** (*de haberlo sabido, no habría venido*), which is compact and slightly literary, and **ojalá + pluperfect subjunctive** (*ojalá hubiera ido*).

examples.target: Si hubiéramos salido antes, no habríamos perdido el tren.
examples.native: If we'd left earlier, we wouldn't have missed the train.

examples.target: Si hubiera estudiado medicina, ahora sería médico.
examples.native: If I'd studied medicine, I'd be a doctor now.

examples.target: De haberlo sabido, no habría venido.
examples.native: Had I known, I wouldn't have come.

theory.watch_out: In the result half both 'habría' and 'hubiera' work. In the 'si' half only 'hubiera' does.

theory.title: The gerund for simultaneous actions
theory.summary: It only works when the two actions genuinely overlap — otherwise Spanish uses two verbs.
theory.body:
The gerund links an action happening **at the same time** as the main verb: *desayuno **viendo** las noticias*; *salió **cerrando** la puerta*.

The test is strict: the two must genuinely overlap. If one follows the other, the gerund is wrong. *Se cayó **rompiéndose** el brazo* is poor Spanish because the break came after the fall; say *se cayó **y se rompió** el brazo*.

The gerund also carries **manner** (*me lo dijo **llorando***), **means** (*se gana la vida **enseñando***) and **cause** (***siendo** tan tarde, decidimos volver*).

Some verbs take a gerund and add aspect:

**seguir / continuar** + gerund — still doing it: *sigue lloviendo*
**llevar** + time + gerund — has been doing it: *llevo dos años estudiando*
**ir** + gerund — gradually: *va mejorando*
**venir** + gerund — building up over time: *viene diciéndolo desde hace meses*
**acabar / terminar** + gerund — ending up: *acabó aceptando*

That *llevar* one is worth memorising: it replaces the English present perfect continuous, which Spanish has no direct equivalent of.

examples.target: Llevo tres años estudiando español.
examples.native: I've been studying Spanish for three years.

examples.target: Sigue lloviendo desde ayer.
examples.native: It's still raining since yesterday.

examples.target: Se gana la vida enseñando música.
examples.native: He makes a living teaching music.

theory.watch_out: The actions must overlap. If one caused the other, use two verbs joined by 'y'.

theory.title: Describing something that may not exist
theory.summary: The mood tells the listener whether the thing you are describing is real or still wanted.
theory.body:
When a relative clause describes a noun, the mood reveals whether that noun **exists**:

*Busco un piso que **tiene** balcón.* — a specific flat, I know it exists.
*Busco un piso que **tenga** balcón.* — any flat with a balcony; it may not exist.

This is a genuinely useful distinction with no English equivalent. English *I'm looking for a flat that has a balcony* is ambiguous between the two; Spanish forces you to say which you mean.

The subjunctive is required when the antecedent is:

**Unknown or hypothetical**: *necesito alguien que **hable** ruso*.
**Negated**: *no hay nadie que **sepa** la respuesta*. *No conozco a ningún médico que **trabaje** los domingos*.
**Questioned**: *¿conoces a alguien que **pueda** ayudarme?*

Note that with a non-specific person, the personal **a** disappears: *busco **un** secretario que hable inglés*, but *busco **a la** secretaria que habla inglés*. Two grammatical signals moving together.

examples.target: Busco un piso que tenga terraza.
examples.native: I'm looking for a flat with a terrace.

examples.target: No hay nadie que sepa la respuesta.
examples.native: There's nobody who knows the answer.

examples.target: Conozco a una chica que habla cinco idiomas.
examples.native: I know a girl who speaks five languages.

theory.watch_out: 'Que tiene' means it exists; 'que tenga' means you're still looking. The mood is the whole message.

theory.title: Impersonal expressions and the subjunctive
theory.summary: Almost all take the subjunctive — except the ones that assert something is true.
theory.body:
The frame is **es + adjective + que**. Most take the subjunctive, because they evaluate rather than report:

*es importante que **vengas***, *es necesario que **lo sepas***, *es posible que **llueva***, *es raro que **no haya llamado***, *es mejor que **te vayas***, *más vale que **te abrigues***.

The exceptions are the ones that **assert truth**, and they take the **indicative**:

*es verdad que…*, *es cierto que…*, *es evidente que…*, *está claro que…*, *es obvio que…*

*Es verdad que **tiene** razón.*

And if you negate one of those, it flips back to the subjunctive — the same mechanism as *creo / no creo*:

*No es verdad que **tenga** razón.*

When no particular person is involved, drop the *que* and use an **infinitive**: *es importante **llegar** a tiempo*. That is the more natural form for a general statement, and learners over-use the *que* version.

examples.target: Es importante que llegues a tiempo.
examples.native: It's important that you arrive on time.

examples.target: Es evidente que tiene razón.
examples.native: It's obvious he's right.

examples.target: No es cierto que sea imposible.
examples.native: It's not true that it's impossible.

theory.watch_out: 'Es verdad que es' but 'no es verdad que sea'. Asserting takes indicative; denying doesn't.

theory.title: Indirect questions
theory.summary: The question word keeps its accent even without question marks, and the word order does not invert.
theory.body:
An indirect question is one embedded in a sentence: *no sé **dónde vive***.

Two things to get right.

**The accent stays.** Even with no question marks, the interrogative keeps its written accent: *dónde, qué, cuándo, cómo, quién, cuánto*. This is precisely what distinguishes *no sé **qué** dice* (I don't know what he's saying) from *no sé **que** dice* (I'm unaware that he says).

**The word order does not invert.** English says *I don't know where he lives* and learners of Spanish sometimes over-correct; Spanish keeps the ordinary order too, though it allows the subject to move to the end: *no sé dónde vive **Juan*** is fine.

For yes/no questions, use **si**: *me preguntó **si** quería café*. Not *que* — a very common slip.

Common frames: *no sé…, me pregunto…, ¿sabes…?, ¿me puedes decir…?, no tengo ni idea de…, depende de…*

And note *¿me puedes decir dónde está?* is a request, not a question about your ability — the same politeness move as English.

examples.target: No sé dónde está el hotel.
examples.native: I don't know where the hotel is.

examples.target: Me preguntó si hablaba francés.
examples.native: He asked me whether I spoke French.

examples.target: ¿Me puedes decir cuánto cuesta?
examples.native: Can you tell me how much it costs?

theory.watch_out: For yes/no questions it's 'si', not 'que': 'preguntó si venías'.

theory.title: Connectors of opposition
theory.summary: The register ladder from 'pero' to 'no obstante' matters more than the meaning, which barely changes.
theory.body:
They all mean roughly *however*, and the choice is about **register and position**.

**Pero** — neutral, joins two clauses, never opens a paragraph.
**Sin embargo** — the standard written *however*. Opens a sentence, followed by a comma.
**No obstante** — more formal still; common in legal and academic prose.
**Ahora bien** — introduces a qualification in argumentative writing: *ahora bien, conviene matizar…*
**En cambio / por el contrario** — sets two things against each other.
**Aun así / con todo** — concedes and continues anyway.
**Eso sí** — spoken, adds a caveat: *es caro. Eso sí, dura años.*

Using *sin embargo* three times in a paragraph is the most recognisable sign of a learner text; native writers vary them, and often just use punctuation.

Note the spelling trap: **aún** with an accent means *still/yet*; **aun** without means *even*. *Aun así* (even so) has no accent; *aún no ha llegado* (he hasn't arrived yet) does.

examples.target: Es caro. Sin embargo, merece la pena.
examples.native: It's expensive. However, it's worth it.

examples.target: Él es tranquilo; en cambio, ella es muy nerviosa.
examples.native: He's calm; she, on the other hand, is very edgy.

examples.target: Aun así, prefiero intentarlo.
examples.native: Even so, I'd rather try.

theory.watch_out: 'Aun así' (even so) has no accent; 'aún' (still, yet) does. Different words.

theory.title: The full passive with ser
theory.summary: It exists, it agrees, and it is much rarer than the English passive — which is the real lesson.
theory.body:
Form: **ser** + past participle, and here the participle **agrees** with the subject: *la casa fue **construida***, *los libros fueron **publicados***.

The agent takes **por**: *la novela fue escrita **por** Cervantes*.

All tenses are available: *es publicado, fue publicado, será publicado, ha sido publicado, sería publicado*.

The real point is **when not to use it**. Spanish uses the full passive far less than English — mainly in journalism, academic writing and formal reports. In ordinary language it prefers:

**Se + verb**: *se publicó el año pasado*
**Active with an unstated subject**: *dicen que…*, *me robaron el móvil* (literally *they stole my phone from me*)

So *my phone was stolen* is **me robaron el móvil**, not *mi móvil fue robado*, which sounds like a police report.

A restriction worth knowing: **estar + participle** describes the resulting state, not the action. *La puerta **fue** cerrada* (someone closed it) against *la puerta **está** cerrada* (it is shut).

examples.target: La novela fue escrita por Cervantes.
examples.native: The novel was written by Cervantes.

examples.target: Me robaron el móvil en el metro.
examples.native: My phone was stolen on the underground.

examples.target: La puerta está cerrada.
examples.native: The door is closed.

theory.watch_out: For everyday events prefer the active: 'me robaron el móvil', not 'mi móvil fue robado'.

theory.title: Ordering a text
theory.summary: The connectors that turn a list of sentences into an argument someone can follow.
theory.body:
**Opening**: *en primer lugar, para empezar, ante todo, lo primero que…*
**Continuing**: *en segundo lugar, a continuación, además, asimismo, por otra parte, igualmente*
**Adding weight**: *es más, de hecho, incluso, cabe destacar que*
**Giving examples**: *por ejemplo, en concreto, tal como, pongamos por caso*
**Reformulating**: *es decir, o sea, dicho de otro modo, en otras palabras*
**Closing**: *en conclusión, en definitiva, en resumen, para terminar, por último*

**Finalmente** and **por último** both close a list; **al final** does not — it means *in the end*, about how something turned out. *Al final no fuimos* — in the end we didn't go. Mixing them is a frequent error.

**O sea** is the spoken *I mean*; **es decir** its written equivalent.

A register note: in Spanish, connectors are placed at the head of the sentence and followed by a comma much more consistently than in English. A well-connected paragraph is expected in formal Spanish writing, not seen as heavy-handed.

examples.target: En primer lugar, hay que definir el problema.
examples.native: First of all, we need to define the problem.

examples.target: Es decir, no tenemos suficiente tiempo.
examples.native: That is to say, we don't have enough time.

examples.target: Al final decidimos no ir.
examples.native: In the end we decided not to go.

theory.watch_out: 'Por último' closes a list; 'al final' says how things turned out. They are not interchangeable.

theory.title: B2 review: choosing the mood
theory.summary: One question resolves most subjunctive decisions: am I asserting this, or doing something else with it?
theory.body:
By B2 the subjunctive stops being a list and becomes a single question: **is this clause being asserted as fact?**

**Indicative** — you are reporting: *sé que viene*, *es verdad que llueve*, *dice que está bien*, *cuando llego* (habit).

**Subjunctive** — you are doing something other than reporting:
- wanting or influencing: *quiero que vengas*
- reacting emotionally: *me alegro de que vengas*
- doubting or denying: *no creo que venga*
- projecting into the future: *cuando venga*
- describing something that may not exist: *busco alguien que venga*
- hypothesising: *si viniera*

The two structural rules that catch most errors:

**Same subject → infinitive.** *Quiero ir*, not *quiero que yo vaya*.
**Negation flips the mood** on verbs of thinking: *creo que es* / *no creo que sea*.

And the sequence of tenses: a **present** main verb takes the present subjunctive; a **past or conditional** main verb takes the imperfect subjunctive. *Quiero que vengas* / *Quería que vinieras*.

examples.target: Sé que viene, pero no creo que llegue a tiempo.
examples.native: I know he's coming, but I don't think he'll make it on time.

examples.target: Quería que vinieras conmigo.
examples.native: I wanted you to come with me.

examples.target: Busco a alguien que sepa alemán.
examples.native: I'm looking for someone who knows German.

theory.watch_out: A past main verb pulls the subjunctive back too: 'quería que vinieras', not 'quería que vengas'.

theory.title: The future perfect: habré terminado
theory.summary: Used more for guessing about the past than for talking about the future.
theory.body:
Form: **habré** + participle. *habré, habrás, habrá, habremos, habréis, habrán* + participle.

Its textbook use is an action finished **before a future point**: *para el viernes **habré terminado** el informe*. It usually appears with *para* or *cuando*: *cuando llegues, ya **habré salido***.

But its most frequent use in real speech is **conjecture about the past** — the same probability trick as the simple future, shifted back:

*¿Dónde está Juan? — **Habrá perdido** el tren.* (He must have missed the train.)
*No contesta. **Se habrá dormido**.*

That is how a Spanish speaker says *he must have…*. There is no separate modal construction for it, so if you translate *must have* literally you get *debe haber*, which exists but sounds heavier and more deductive.

The pattern is consistent across the language: **future = guess about now**, **future perfect = guess about the past**, **conditional = guess about the past too, but more tentative**.

examples.target: Para junio habré terminado la carrera.
examples.native: By June I'll have finished my degree.

examples.target: No contesta; se habrá dormido.
examples.native: He's not answering; he must have fallen asleep.

examples.target: Cuando llegues, ya habremos cenado.
examples.native: By the time you arrive, we'll have had dinner.

theory.watch_out: 'Habrá salido' usually means 'he must have left', not 'he will have left'.

theory.title: Reporting a whole conversation
theory.summary: Beyond the tense shift, this is about choosing a reporting verb that says how it was said.
theory.body:
Reporting a real exchange needs more than *dijo que* repeated. Spanish has a rich set of reporting verbs, and each carries an attitude:

**Neutral**: *decir, comentar, señalar, indicar, explicar, añadir, contar*
**Asserting**: *afirmar, sostener, insistir en, asegurar, subrayar, destacar*
**Hedging**: *sugerir, apuntar, dar a entender, insinuar*
**Reacting**: *quejarse de, admitir, reconocer, negar, replicar, protestar*
**Asking**: *preguntar, querer saber, interesarse por*

Choosing the verb is how a writer takes a position without saying so. *Afirmó que* and *insinuó que* report the same words very differently.

Mechanically: **negar que** takes the subjunctive (*negó que **fuera** verdad*), while **reconocer que** and **admitir que** take the indicative, because they concede a fact.

And Spanish keeps the reported clause introduced by **que** even after a long chain: *dijo que había llegado tarde y que no había podido avisar* — the second *que* is not optional.

examples.target: Aseguró que no sabía nada del asunto.
examples.native: He insisted he knew nothing about the matter.

examples.target: Negó que hubiera hablado con ella.
examples.native: He denied having spoken to her.

examples.target: Reconoció que se había equivocado.
examples.native: He admitted he had been wrong.

theory.watch_out: 'Negar que' takes the subjunctive; 'reconocer que' takes the indicative. Denying and conceding behave oppositely.

theory.title: Reporting without naming a source
theory.summary: How Spanish says 'it is said that' — and why the impersonal is preferred to the passive.
theory.body:
To report something without attributing it, Spanish offers several impersonal frames:

**Se dice que / se cree que / se sabe que** — *se dice que va a dimitir*. The commonest.
**Dicen que** — third person plural with no subject, the spoken version.
**Según + source** — *según el periódico*, *según fuentes oficiales*.
**Al parecer / por lo visto** — apparently. Both very frequent in speech.
**Parece ser que** — it seems that.

The English *he is said to be…* has **no direct equivalent**. *Se dice que **es**…* is the way, with a full clause.

A mood note: **se dice que** and **se sabe que** take the **indicative**, because they report an assertion. But **se duda que** and **se teme que** take the subjunctive.

Journalistic Spanish also uses the conditional for unconfirmed information: *el ministro **habría dimitido*** — the minister has reportedly resigned. English marks that with *reportedly*; Spanish marks it with a tense. Reading a newspaper, that conditional is a signal not to take the claim as verified.

examples.target: Se dice que va a dimitir.
examples.native: It's said he's going to resign.

examples.target: Al parecer, no había nadie en casa.
examples.native: Apparently, there was nobody at home.

examples.target: Según el informe, las cifras han bajado.
examples.native: According to the report, the figures have fallen.

theory.watch_out: In the press, a conditional means 'reportedly'. 'Habría dimitido' is not confirmed.

theory.title: Verbs of influence
theory.summary: Trying to change what someone else does always takes the subjunctive — with a few verbs that allow an infinitive instead.
theory.body:
Verbs that attempt to **influence another person's behaviour** take the subjunctive: *pedir, rogar, exigir, ordenar, mandar, permitir, prohibir, recomendar, aconsejar, sugerir, insistir en, lograr, conseguir, hacer que, evitar que, impedir que*.

*Te pido que **vengas***. *Me prohibieron que **entrara***. *Insisto en que **lo pruebes***.

A small group allows **either** the subjunctive or an infinitive, even with two subjects: **permitir, prohibir, dejar, mandar, hacer, obligar a, impedir**.

*Me permitió **entrar*** = *me permitió que **entrara***. Both correct; the infinitive is shorter and more common.

Watch **decir**, which changes meaning with the mood:

*Me dijo que **venía*** — he told me he was coming (reporting).
*Me dijo que **viniera*** — he told me to come (an order).

The same applies to *insistir en* — reporting a fact takes the indicative, pressing for an action takes the subjunctive. The mood is doing the work that English does with a completely different sentence structure.

examples.target: Te pido que me escuches.
examples.native: I'm asking you to listen to me.

examples.target: Me dijo que viniera a las ocho.
examples.native: He told me to come at eight.

examples.target: No me dejaron entrar.
examples.native: They didn't let me in.

theory.watch_out: 'Dijo que venía' reports; 'dijo que viniera' orders. Same verb, different mood, different message.

theory.title: Aunque with the indicative
theory.summary: The indicative says the obstacle is real and known — you are conceding a fact.
theory.body:
**Aunque** takes the indicative when what follows is a **real, known fact** that you are conceding:

*Aunque **llueve**, voy a salir.* — It is raining, and I'm going anyway.
*Aunque **es** caro, lo voy a comprar.* — It is expensive; I know.

English makes no distinction here — *although it's raining* covers both readings — so the choice has to be made consciously.

The test: if you could add *y lo sé* (and I know it), use the indicative.

The same applies to **a pesar de que**, **si bien** (formal), and **y eso que** (spoken, always indicative and always about something real): *no vino, **y eso que** se lo pedí*.

With a past fact: *aunque **estudió** mucho, suspendió* — he did study, and still failed.

Note the difference from **pero**: *aunque* subordinates the concession, *pero* coordinates. *Aunque es caro, lo compro* and *es caro, pero lo compro* mean the same, but the *aunque* version front-loads the concession, which is the more formal shape.

examples.target: Aunque llueve, voy a salir.
examples.native: Even though it's raining, I'm going out.

examples.target: Aunque estudió mucho, suspendió el examen.
examples.native: Although he studied a lot, he failed the exam.

examples.target: No vino, y eso que se lo pedí.
examples.native: He didn't come, and that's despite my asking him.

theory.watch_out: Indicative means you know it's true. 'Aunque llueve' means it IS raining right now.

theory.title: Aunque with the subjunctive
theory.summary: The subjunctive turns the same word into 'even if' — the obstacle is hypothetical or irrelevant.
theory.body:
**Aunque** + subjunctive means **even if**: the fact is unknown, hypothetical, or being dismissed as not mattering.

*Aunque **llueva**, voy a salir.* — Even if it rains (I don't know yet), I'm going.
*Aunque **fuera** caro, lo compraría.* — Even if it were expensive, I'd buy it.
*Aunque **hubiera estudiado**, habría suspendido.* — Even if he had studied, he'd have failed.

The present subjunctive covers the unknown future, the imperfect subjunctive the hypothetical present, the pluperfect subjunctive the unreal past.

There is a third use worth knowing: the subjunctive also appears when the fact **is** known but the speaker wants to **minimise** it. *Aunque **sea** caro, lo compro* — yes, it's expensive, so what. A native speaker hears that as dismissal rather than ignorance.

So *aunque* gives you three shades from one word: conceding a fact (indicative), supposing (subjunctive), and brushing a fact aside (subjunctive again). That range is exactly why it appears in every C1 exam.

examples.target: Aunque llueva, iremos a la playa.
examples.native: Even if it rains, we'll go to the beach.

examples.target: Aunque fuera millonario, no compraría eso.
examples.native: Even if I were a millionaire, I wouldn't buy that.

examples.target: Aunque sea difícil, hay que intentarlo.
examples.native: Even if it's hard, we have to try.

theory.watch_out: 'Aunque llueve' = it is raining. 'Aunque llueva' = if it should rain. One letter, different situation.

theory.title: El hecho de que
theory.summary: It presents a fact as a topic rather than as news, and that is why it takes the subjunctive despite being true.
theory.body:
**El hecho de que** turns a whole clause into a noun phrase: *el hecho de que **llegara** tarde me molestó*.

It normally takes the **subjunctive**, even though the fact is true — the same logic as verbs of emotion. The fact is not being asserted; it is being presented as the known ground on which a comment is built.

The indicative appears when the speaker wants to **insist that it really happened**: *el hecho de que **llegó** tarde es indiscutible*.

Related structures at the same register:

**El que + subjunctive** — the compact version: *el que no vinieras me dolió*.
**Que + subjunctive** at the start of a sentence: *que no me avisaras fue un error*.
**De ahí que + subjunctive** — hence: *de ahí que sea tan caro*.

A common error is **dequeísmo** — inserting *de* where it does not belong: *pienso **de** que* is wrong; it is *pienso que*. The mirror error is **queísmo**, dropping a *de* that is required: *me alegro **de** que*, not *me alegro que*. Both are noticed by educated speakers.

examples.target: El hecho de que llegara tarde me molestó.
examples.native: The fact that he arrived late annoyed me.

examples.target: Que no me avisaras fue un error.
examples.native: Your not telling me was a mistake.

examples.target: Me alegro de que estés aquí.
examples.native: I'm glad you're here.

theory.watch_out: 'Pienso de que' is wrong; 'me alegro que' is also wrong. One adds a 'de' it shouldn't, the other drops one it needs.

theory.title: Lo que for emphasis
theory.summary: Spanish cannot stress a word with the voice as freely as English, so it rebuilds the sentence instead.
theory.body:
English emphasises by stressing a word: *I want **coffee**, not tea.* Spanish word stress is fixed, so it **restructures**:

**Lo que + verb + es** — *lo que quiero es café*.
**Lo que pasa es que** — introduces an explanation: *lo que pasa es que no tengo tiempo*.
**Lo que + verb + es que** — *lo que me molesta es que no avisó*.

This is the everyday version of the cleft sentence, and it is extremely common in speech — far more than the English *what I want is…*, which sounds formal.

Related emphasis tools:

**Fronting**: *café es lo que quiero*.
**Sí que** — contradicts a denial: *sí que lo sabía* (I did know).
**Es que** — justifies: *es que no me avisaste*.
**Ni + noun** — not even: *ni un euro*.

And the doubled pronoun for contrast: *a mí me parece bien* — where *a mí* adds the stress English would put on *I*.

Note the mood: *lo que quiero es que **vengas*** — the subordinate clause after *es que* takes the subjunctive when it expresses a wish.

examples.target: Lo que quiero es que me escuches.
examples.native: What I want is for you to listen to me.

examples.target: Lo que pasa es que no tengo tiempo.
examples.native: The thing is, I don't have time.

examples.target: Sí que lo sabía.
examples.native: I did know.

theory.watch_out: Spanish stresses by restructuring, not by raising the voice. 'Lo que quiero es café' is the natural form.

theory.title: Por más que and other concessions
theory.summary: A family of 'no matter how much' structures, all built on the subjunctive.
theory.body:
**Por más que / por mucho que** — no matter how much: *por más que **lo intente**, no lo consigo*.

**Por muy + adjective + que** — no matter how: *por muy caro que **sea**, lo compro*. Note the *muy*, which is obligatory.

**Por poco que** — however little: *por poco que **ganes**, algo es algo*.

These normally take the **subjunctive**. They take the indicative only when the speaker asserts the fact as verified: *por mucho que **estudió**, no aprobó* — he really did study a lot.

Related emphatic concessions, all subjunctive, and all built by **repeating the verb**:

*digas lo que **digas*** — whatever you say
*pase lo que **pase*** — whatever happens
*sea como **sea*** — one way or another
*cueste lo que **cueste*** — whatever it takes

That doubled-verb pattern is very idiomatic and instantly raises the register of spoken Spanish. It has no English structural equivalent, which is why learners rarely produce it unprompted.

examples.target: Por más que lo intento, no lo entiendo.
examples.native: No matter how hard I try, I don't understand it.

examples.target: Por muy caro que sea, lo voy a comprar.
examples.native: However expensive it is, I'm going to buy it.

examples.target: Pase lo que pase, te apoyaré.
examples.native: Whatever happens, I'll support you.

theory.watch_out: 'Por muy' needs the 'muy': 'por muy difícil que sea', not 'por difícil que sea'.

theory.title: Talking about imminence
theory.summary: The expressions for something about to happen, and one that means the opposite of what it looks like.
theory.body:
**Estar a punto de + infinitive** — to be about to: *estaba a punto de salir cuando llamaste*.

**Estar para + infinitive** — the same, more colloquial: *está para llover*.

**Faltar poco para que + subjunctive** — *falta poco para que empiece*.

**Estar al caer** — imminent, said of an event or a person's arrival: *ya está al caer*.

And the trap: **por poco** and **casi** + **present tense** describe something that **nearly happened but didn't**:

*Por poco **me caigo**.* — I nearly fell (and didn't).
*Casi **pierdo** el tren.* — I almost missed the train.

The present tense there is not an error; it is the required form. Using a past tense (*por poco me caí*) is heard but considered less correct.

Related, for something that stopped: **estar a punto de + infinitive + cuando** is the standard frame for an interrupted intention, and it pairs naturally with the imperfect: *estaba a punto de irme cuando llegó*.

examples.target: Estaba a punto de salir cuando me llamaste.
examples.native: I was about to leave when you called me.

examples.target: Por poco pierdo el vuelo.
examples.native: I nearly missed the flight.

examples.target: Falta poco para que empiece la película.
examples.native: The film is about to start.

theory.watch_out: 'Por poco' takes the present even about the past: 'por poco me caigo', not 'me caí'.

theory.title: Softening what you say
theory.summary: How to disagree, refuse or complain in Spanish without sounding blunt.
theory.body:
Direct Spanish is not rude the way direct English is, but there is still a full hedging apparatus, and using none of it marks you as foreign.

**Softening an opinion**: *me parece que…, diría que…, tengo la impresión de que…, hasta cierto punto…, en principio…, si no me equivoco…*

**Disagreeing**: *no estoy del todo de acuerdo…, entiendo lo que dices, pero…, sí, aunque…, bueno, depende…*

**Refusing**: *me temo que no…, lo siento, pero…, es que…, me encantaría, pero…*

**Complaining**: *no sé si sabes que…, quizá haya habido un malentendido…, ¿podrías…?*

The grammatical tools are the **conditional** (*diría, sería, podríamos*), the **imperfect** for tentative requests (*quería preguntarte…*, literally *I wanted to ask you*), and **quisiera**.

That use of the imperfect is worth noting: *venía a preguntarte* and *quería pedirte un favor* put the request slightly in the past to make it less pressing. English does the same with *I was wondering if…* — one of the rare places the two languages hedge identically.

examples.target: Me temo que no va a ser posible.
examples.native: I'm afraid it won't be possible.

examples.target: Quería pedirte un favor.
examples.native: I wanted to ask you a favour.

examples.target: No estoy del todo de acuerdo.
examples.native: I don't entirely agree.

theory.watch_out: The imperfect softens a request: 'quería preguntarte' is politer than 'quiero preguntarte'.

theory.title: Infinitive or subjunctive?
theory.summary: One question decides it: is there one subject or two?
theory.body:
This single rule prevents a large share of remaining errors.

**One subject → infinitive.** *Quiero **ir***. *Espero **llegar** a tiempo*. *Me alegro de **estar** aquí*. *Antes de **salir**, cierra*.

**Two subjects → que + subjunctive.** *Quiero que **vayas***. *Espero que **llegues***. *Me alegro de que **estés** aquí*. *Antes de que **salgas**, cierra*.

English uses an infinitive in both cases — *I want to go*, *I want you to go* — which is exactly why learners produce *quiero tú ir*.

A group of verbs of influence breaks the rule and allows an infinitive even with two subjects: **dejar, permitir, prohibir, mandar, hacer, obligar a, impedir**. *Me dejó **entrar*** = *me dejó que **entrara***.

And impersonal expressions drop the *que* when nobody in particular is meant: *es importante **llegar** temprano* (in general) against *es importante que **llegues** temprano* (you specifically).

When in doubt, count the subjects first. The mood follows.

examples.target: Quiero ir contigo.
examples.native: I want to go with you.

examples.target: Quiero que vengas conmigo.
examples.native: I want you to come with me.

examples.target: Es importante llegar temprano.
examples.native: It's important to arrive early.

theory.watch_out: Count the subjects before choosing. 'Quiero que yo vaya' is never right.

theory.title: Verbal periphrases
theory.summary: Small verb combinations that express aspect Spanish has no tense for.
theory.body:
Spanish adds nuance by pairing a verb with an infinitive, gerund or participle. The most useful:

**acabar de + infinitive** — to have just: *acabo de llegar*. Note the **present** tense for a past event.
**volver a + infinitive** — to do again: *volvió a llamar*. Spanish has no prefix like *re-*; this is how *again* is expressed.
**ponerse a + infinitive** — to start suddenly: *se puso a llorar*.
**empezar a / echarse a** — to begin.
**dejar de + infinitive** — to stop doing: *dejé de fumar*.
**llegar a + infinitive** — to get as far as: *llegó a ser director*.
**venir a + infinitive** — to amount to roughly: *viene a costar unos cien euros*.
**andar + gerund** — to be going around doing: *anda buscando piso*.
**tener + participle** — accumulated result: *tengo escritas tres cartas*.

**Volver a** is the one worth drilling: English speakers reach for *otra vez* every time, and while that works, *volvió a llamar* is what a native says.

Careful with **dejar**: *dejar de fumar* is to quit; *dejar fumar* is to allow someone to smoke.

examples.target: Acabo de hablar con ella.
examples.native: I've just spoken to her.

examples.target: Volvió a llamar por la tarde.
examples.native: He called again in the afternoon.

examples.target: Dejé de fumar hace dos años.
examples.native: I stopped smoking two years ago.

theory.watch_out: 'Dejar de fumar' is to quit; 'dejar fumar' is to let someone smoke. The 'de' is the whole difference.

theory.title: Expressing possibility
theory.summary: A ladder from almost certain to barely possible, and only some rungs take the subjunctive.
theory.body:
From most to least certain:

**Seguro que + indicative** — *seguro que viene*. Despite meaning *surely*, it takes the indicative.
**Seguramente + indicative** — probably.
**A lo mejor + indicative** — maybe. Spoken, and notably **always indicative** despite the meaning.
**Igual + indicative** — spoken Spain: *igual viene*.
**Quizá / tal vez / posiblemente** — either mood; subjunctive adds doubt.
**Puede que + subjunctive** — always subjunctive: *puede que llueva*.
**Es posible que + subjunctive**.
**Dudo que + subjunctive**.

The two that catch learners are **a lo mejor** and **seguro que**: both feel like they should trigger the subjunctive and neither does.

Also available: the **future for present conjecture** (*estará en casa*) and the **future perfect for past conjecture** (*habrá salido*), which are more natural in speech than any of the above.

**Deber de + infinitive** is the explicit deduction: *debe de estar enfermo* — he must be ill.

examples.target: Puede que llueva esta tarde.
examples.native: It might rain this afternoon.

examples.target: A lo mejor viene mañana.
examples.native: Maybe he'll come tomorrow.

examples.target: Debe de estar enfermo.
examples.native: He must be ill.

theory.watch_out: 'A lo mejor' takes the indicative; 'puede que' takes the subjunctive. Same meaning, opposite grammar.

theory.title: Academic connectors
theory.summary: Spanish academic prose connects more explicitly than English, and under-connecting reads as careless.
theory.body:
Formal Spanish signposts its argument far more openly than academic English, which prizes economy. A Spanish paper that omits connectors reads as abrupt, not elegant.

**Adding**: *asimismo, además, por otra parte, cabe añadir que, a ello se suma que*
**Specifying**: *concretamente, en particular, más concretamente, a saber*
**Explaining**: *es decir, esto es, dicho de otro modo, en otros términos*
**Consequence**: *por consiguiente, por lo tanto, de ahí que* (+ subjunctive), *en consecuencia*
**Contrast**: *sin embargo, no obstante, ahora bien, por el contrario, si bien*
**Concluding**: *en definitiva, en suma, a modo de conclusión, cabe concluir que*

**Cabe + infinitive** is characteristic of this register: *cabe destacar*, *cabe señalar*, *cabe preguntarse*. It means *it is worth…* and has no compact English equivalent.

**De ahí que** always takes the **subjunctive**: *de ahí que **resulte** tan complejo*.

And formal Spanish prefers **nominal style** — *la implementación del sistema* over *implementar el sistema* — the mirror image of the plain-English advice.

examples.target: Cabe señalar que los datos son preliminares.
examples.native: It is worth noting that the data are preliminary.

examples.target: De ahí que resulte tan difícil de medir.
examples.native: Hence its being so difficult to measure.

examples.target: Si bien el método es válido, la muestra es reducida.
examples.native: While the method is valid, the sample is small.

theory.watch_out: 'De ahí que' always takes the subjunctive: 'de ahí que sea', never 'de ahí que es'.

theory.title: Verbs for citing sources
theory.summary: The verb you choose tells the reader how much you believe the source.
theory.body:
In academic Spanish, the reporting verb is where the writer's stance leaks out.

**Neutral**: *señalar, indicar, apuntar, exponer, describir, observar*
**Endorsing**: *demostrar, evidenciar, constatar, poner de manifiesto, establecer*
**Attributing without committing**: *afirmar, sostener, defender, argumentar, plantear*
**Distancing**: *alegar, pretender, dar por sentado, asumir sin más*

*Demostró que* accepts the finding; *alegó que* quietly withholds. Choosing between them is an argumentative move disguised as a verb.

Standard framing: **según + author**, **de acuerdo con**, **tal como señala X**, **siguiendo a X**, **en palabras de X**.

Two false friends to avoid. **Pretender** means *to claim* or *to intend*, **not** *to pretend* (that is *fingir*). And **asumir** means *to take on* a role or responsibility; for *to assume* a premise Spanish prefers *suponer* or *dar por sentado*.

With **negar** the subjunctive returns: *el autor niega que **exista** relación*.

examples.target: Según el autor, los resultados son concluyentes.
examples.native: According to the author, the results are conclusive.

examples.target: El estudio pone de manifiesto una relación clara.
examples.native: The study reveals a clear relationship.

examples.target: El informe niega que exista tal vínculo.
examples.native: The report denies that such a link exists.

theory.watch_out: 'Pretender' means to claim or intend, not to pretend. 'Fingir' is to pretend.

theory.title: Markers of formal register
theory.summary: The vocabulary swap that separates a letter from a message, item by item.
theory.body:
Register in Spanish is carried by specific lexical choices, and the pairs are learnable:

*pero* → **sin embargo** · *así que* → **por consiguiente** · *pasa que* → **sucede que** · *hablar de* → **abordar / tratar** · *empezar* → **iniciar** · *terminar* → **concluir / finalizar** · *pedir* → **solicitar** · *decir* → **manifestar / exponer** · *mandar* → **remitir** · *dar* → **facilitar / proporcionar** · *bastante* → **considerable** · *un montón de* → **numerosos**

Formal correspondence has its own fixed phrases: *le escribo en relación con…*, *adjunto le remito…*, *quedo a la espera de su respuesta*, *sin otro particular, le saluda atentamente*, *agradecería que + subjunctive*.

Two grammatical markers of formality: **usted** with its third-person verb, and the **future tense** where speech would use *ir a*.

And formal Spanish is markedly more **impersonal and elaborate** than formal English. *Se ruega no fumar* is a sign; the English equivalent is *No smoking*. Translating English concision directly into Spanish reads as curt.

examples.target: Le escribo en relación con su solicitud.
examples.native: I am writing regarding your application.

examples.target: Agradecería que me facilitara los datos.
examples.native: I would be grateful if you could provide me with the data.

examples.target: Quedo a la espera de su respuesta.
examples.native: I look forward to your reply.

theory.watch_out: 'Agradecería que' takes the imperfect subjunctive: 'que me enviara', not 'que me envía'.

theory.title: Nominal style
theory.summary: Formal Spanish prefers nouns where English style guides now push for verbs.
theory.body:
Turning verbs into nouns is a mark of good formal Spanish — the opposite of current English advice, which treats nominalisation as a fault.

*Analizamos los datos* → **el análisis de los datos**
*Implementaron el sistema* → **la implementación del sistema**
*Cuando llegó* → **a su llegada**

Common suffixes: **-ción** (*implementación*), **-miento** (*seguimiento*), **-dad** (*complejidad*), **-eza** (*certeza*), **-anza** (*enseñanza*), **-aje** (*aprendizaje*).

The verbs that carry these nouns are worth learning as pairs, because a wrong pairing sounds instantly foreign: *llevar a cabo* un análisis, *tomar* una decisión, *plantear* una hipótesis, *establecer* una relación, *poner de manifiesto* un problema, *dar lugar a* un cambio.

Also characteristic: **a + noun** replacing a whole time clause — *a su llegada* (on his arrival), *tras su publicación* (after its publication), *ante la falta de datos* (given the lack of data). These compress a subordinate clause into three words and are everywhere in formal prose.

The risk is overuse: a paragraph built entirely of nouns becomes unreadable in any language.

examples.target: El análisis de los datos revela un patrón.
examples.native: Analysis of the data reveals a pattern.

examples.target: Se llevó a cabo una revisión completa.
examples.native: A full review was carried out.

examples.target: Ante la falta de pruebas, se archivó el caso.
examples.native: Given the lack of evidence, the case was closed.

theory.watch_out: The verb must match the noun. It's 'tomar una decisión', never 'hacer una decisión'.

theory.title: Impersonal structures in formal writing
theory.summary: Academic Spanish avoids 'yo' entirely, and there are four standard ways to do it.
theory.body:
Formal Spanish removes the writer from the sentence far more thoroughly than English, which now tolerates *I argue that*.

**Se + verb**: *se observa que, se concluye que, se ha demostrado que*. The default.
**First person plural**: *consideramos que, proponemos*. The plural of modesty, still standard.
**Impersonal frames**: *es preciso que, resulta necesario que, conviene que, procede que* — all with the **subjunctive**.
**Nominal style**: *el análisis de los datos revela…* rather than *analizamos los datos y vemos…*

**Cabe + infinitive** belongs here too: *cabe suponer que*, *cabe destacar que*.

Mood note: the assertive frames (*se observa que, se ha demostrado que, resulta evidente que*) take the **indicative**; the evaluative ones (*es preciso que, conviene que, resulta llamativo que*) take the **subjunctive**. The same asserting-versus-evaluating split that governs the whole mood system.

Negating an assertive frame flips it: *no se ha demostrado que **exista** relación*.

examples.target: Se observa una tendencia al alza.
examples.native: An upward trend is observed.

examples.target: Conviene que se revisen los datos.
examples.native: The data should be reviewed.

examples.target: No se ha demostrado que exista relación.
examples.native: No relationship has been shown to exist.

theory.watch_out: 'Se ha demostrado que existe' but 'no se ha demostrado que exista'. Negation flips it here too.

theory.title: Cleft sentences with ser
theory.summary: Spanish clefts agree in tense and in person, which English clefts never do.
theory.body:
A cleft sentence isolates one element for emphasis: **fue Juan quien lo hizo** — it was Juan who did it.

The structure is **ser + element + que/quien/donde/cuando**.

Two things differ from English. First, **ser agrees in tense** with the main verb: *fue él quien **lo hizo*** (past), *es él quien **lo hace*** (present). English keeps *it is* frozen.

Second, **the relative agrees**: *quien/quienes* for people, *donde* for place, *cuando* for time, *como* for manner, and *el que / la que / los que* when the article matters.

*Fue en Madrid **donde** nos conocimos.*
*Fue entonces **cuando** lo entendí.*
*Fue así **como** empezó todo.*

With a preposition, it repeats on both sides: *fue **con** ella **con** quien hablé*. That doubling looks redundant to an English speaker and is required.

And the verb may agree with the person: *soy yo quien **tiene** la culpa* is the safer form, though *quien **tengo*** is also heard.

examples.target: Fue ella quien me lo dijo.
examples.native: It was she who told me.

examples.target: Fue en Sevilla donde nos conocimos.
examples.native: It was in Seville that we met.

examples.target: Fue con él con quien hablé.
examples.native: It was him I spoke to.

theory.watch_out: 'Ser' matches the tense of the main verb: 'fue él quien lo hizo', not 'es él quien lo hizo'.

theory.title: Concession: the full range
theory.summary: Six ways to concede, sorted by register and by the mood each one demands.
theory.body:
Pulling the concessive structures together:

**Aunque** + indicative (real) / subjunctive (hypothetical or dismissed). The general-purpose one.
**A pesar de que** + either mood, same logic. **A pesar de + infinitive** when there is one subject.
**Si bien** + indicative, formal writing only: *si bien el método es sólido…*
**Por más/mucho que** + subjunctive normally.
**Por muy + adjective + que** + subjunctive.
**Aun + gerund**: *aun sabiéndolo, no dijo nada*.
**Y eso que** + indicative, spoken, always about something real.
**Pese a que** — a compact synonym of *a pesar de que*.

The doubled-verb constructions belong here too: *diga lo que diga*, *pase lo que pase*, *sea como sea*.

The spelling trap returns: **aun** (even) has no accent; **aún** (still, yet) does. *Aun así* versus *aún no*.

In a C1 exam, varying these rather than repeating *aunque* is precisely what is being assessed.

examples.target: Si bien el proyecto es ambicioso, es realista.
examples.native: While the project is ambitious, it is realistic.

examples.target: Aun sabiéndolo, no dijo nada.
examples.native: Even knowing it, he said nothing.

examples.target: Pese a que llovía, salimos a caminar.
examples.native: Despite the rain, we went out walking.

theory.watch_out: 'Si bien' is written register and takes the indicative. It is not a spoken option.

theory.title: Marking an opinion
theory.summary: Whether the marker takes the subjunctive depends on whether it is affirmative or negative.
theory.body:
**Personal**: *en mi opinión, a mi juicio, desde mi punto de vista, personalmente, por mi parte, a mi modo de ver*

**Attenuated**: *me parece que, diría que, tengo la impresión de que, si no me equivoco, hasta donde yo sé*

**Emphatic**: *estoy convencido de que, no me cabe duda de que, sin lugar a dudas, es innegable que*

**Distancing**: *dicen que, al parecer, según parece, por lo visto*

The mood follows the usual logic. Affirmative opinion verbs take the **indicative**: *me parece que **tiene** razón*. Negated, they take the **subjunctive**: *no me parece que **tenga** razón*.

A usage note: **a mi parecer** and **a mi modo de ver** belong to formal writing; **yo creo que** and **para mí** to speech. *Para mí que…* is markedly colloquial: *para mí que no viene*.

And **desde mi punto de vista** is the safe register-neutral option — it works in an essay and in a meeting alike.

examples.target: Desde mi punto de vista, el plan es viable.
examples.native: From my point of view, the plan is workable.

examples.target: No me parece que sea la mejor opción.
examples.native: It doesn't seem to me the best option.

examples.target: No me cabe duda de que funcionará.
examples.native: I have no doubt it will work.

theory.watch_out: 'Me parece que es' but 'no me parece que sea'. Negating the opinion flips the mood.

theory.title: Clefts with lo que
theory.summary: The version that emphasises an action or a whole idea rather than a person or a place.
theory.body:
When what you want to highlight is an **action or an abstract idea**, use **lo que**:

*Lo que me molesta es su actitud.*
*Lo que hizo fue marcharse sin decir nada.*
*Lo que necesitamos es más tiempo.*

With a verb, the pattern **lo que + hacer + ser + infinitive** is very idiomatic: *lo que hizo fue **irse***. English has the same shape (*what he did was leave*), so it transfers well.

Related emphatic structures:

**Lo + adjective + que**: *no sabes **lo cansado que** estoy*.
**Lo mucho/poco que**: *no imaginas **lo mucho que** me costó*.
**Todo lo que**: *todo lo que dijo era mentira*.

A mood point: when the highlighted element is a wish or something not yet real, the subordinate clause goes **subjunctive**: *lo que quiero es que **vengas***.

And note that *lo que* also functions as an ordinary relative meaning *what*: *no entiendo lo que dices*. The cleft use is distinguished by the *ser* that follows.

examples.target: Lo que me molesta es su actitud.
examples.native: What bothers me is his attitude.

examples.target: Lo que hizo fue irse sin avisar.
examples.native: What he did was leave without saying anything.

examples.target: No sabes lo cansado que estoy.
examples.native: You've no idea how tired I am.

theory.watch_out: 'Lo' + adjective still agrees with the person: 'lo cansada que estoy' if you're female.

theory.title: Reported speech in the media
theory.summary: Journalistic Spanish marks unverified information with a tense, where English uses an adverb.
theory.body:
Press Spanish has conventions worth recognising as a reader.

**The conditional of rumour**: *el ministro **habría dimitido*** — the minister has reportedly resigned. This conditional does **not** mean *would*; it flags that the paper has not confirmed the claim. English marks this with *reportedly* or *allegedly*; Spanish does it with a tense, and a reader who misses it takes a rumour for a fact.

**Sources**: *según fuentes cercanas al caso, de acuerdo con el informe, en declaraciones a este diario, tal y como adelantó…*

**Attributing verbs** carry the same stance load as in academic writing: *aseguró, matizó, puntualizó, negó, admitió, se limitó a decir*. *Se limitó a decir* is quietly damning.

**Presunto** is the legal *alleged*: *el presunto autor*. It is compulsory before a conviction, and using *el autor* instead is a legal risk, not just a style choice.

Mood: *negó que* + subjunctive; *admitió que* + indicative; *matizó que* + indicative.

examples.target: El ministro habría presentado su dimisión.
examples.native: The minister has reportedly tendered his resignation.

examples.target: El presunto autor fue detenido ayer.
examples.native: The alleged perpetrator was arrested yesterday.

examples.target: Negó que hubiera recibido el dinero.
examples.native: He denied having received the money.

theory.watch_out: A conditional in a news report means 'reportedly'. It is not a claim the paper is standing behind.

theory.title: Cuanto as a relative
theory.summary: A compact literary equivalent of 'todo lo que', plus the correlative 'cuanto más… más'.
theory.body:
**Cuanto** without an accent is a relative meaning *all that*: *te daré **cuanto** necesites* = *todo lo que necesites*. It belongs to formal or literary register; in speech *todo lo que* is normal.

It agrees when it refers to countable things: *invitó a **cuantos** conocía* — all those he knew.

The construction that is genuinely everyday is the correlative: **cuanto más… (tanto) más…**

*Cuanto más lo pienso, menos lo entiendo.*
*Cuanto antes, mejor.*
*Cuanto más practiques, más rápido aprenderás.*

This is the equivalent of English *the more… the more…*, and note two differences: Spanish uses **cuanto**, not the article, and the second half normally drops *tanto*.

If the clause refers to the future, it takes the **subjunctive**: *cuanto más **practiques***.

With a noun, *cuanto* agrees: *cuantas más personas vengan, mejor*.

And **cuánto** with an accent is the question word — *¿cuánto cuesta?* — a different word entirely.

examples.target: Cuanto más lo pienso, menos lo entiendo.
examples.native: The more I think about it, the less I understand.

examples.target: Cuanto antes lo hagas, mejor.
examples.native: The sooner you do it, the better.
