examples.target: Cuantas más personas vengan, más divertido será.
examples.native: The more people come, the more fun it will be.

theory.watch_out: Referring to the future, it takes the subjunctive: 'cuanto más practiques', not 'practicas'.

theory.title: The many jobs of se
theory.summary: Five distinct grammars share one syllable, and telling them apart is what makes advanced Spanish readable.
theory.body:
**Se** does five different jobs:

**Reflexive** — the subject acts on itself: *se lava*.
**Reciprocal** — they act on each other: *se abrazaron*. Clarified with *el uno al otro* or *mutuamente*.
**Impersonal** — no subject at all: *se vive bien aquí*. Verb always singular.
**Passive (pasiva refleja)** — *se venden pisos*. Verb agrees with the thing.
**Substitute for le/les** — before *lo/la/los/las*: *se lo di*.

And a sixth, the **dative of interest**, which changes the flavour without changing the meaning: *me comí toda la pizza* — the *me* adds relish and completion. *Se bebió la botella entera*.

The **accidental se** belongs here: *se me cayó el vaso*, *se me olvidó*. Spanish presents mishaps as things that happened to you rather than things you did. It is not evasion; it is the unmarked way to report an accident, and using *dejé caer el vaso* sounds like a confession.

Some verbs simply change meaning with *se*: *ir/irse*, *dormir/dormirse*, *quedar/quedarse*, *acordar/acordarse*, *parecer/parecerse*.

examples.target: Se me olvidaron las llaves.
examples.native: I forgot the keys.

examples.target: Se querían mucho.
examples.native: They loved each other very much.

examples.target: Me comí toda la tarta.
examples.native: I ate the whole cake.

theory.watch_out: 'Se me cayó' is the normal way to report an accident. 'Dejé caer' sounds like you meant to.

theory.title: Indefinite pronouns
theory.summary: Ninguno has no real plural, and cualquiera shortens before a noun.
theory.body:
**alguien / nadie** (people), **algo / nada** (things), **alguno / ninguno** (of a known set), **cualquiera** (any at all), **cada** (each), **todo** (all), **varios, demás, cierto, tal**.

Things worth knowing:

**Ninguno** is normally **singular**, even where English is plural: *no tengo **ningún** problema*, *no vino **ninguno** de ellos*. A plural *ningunos* exists only with nouns that have no singular (*ningunas tijeras*).

**Alguno/ninguno shorten** to *algún/ningún* before a masculine singular noun.

**Cualquiera** shortens to **cualquier** before any noun, of either gender: *cualquier día*, *cualquier cosa*. As a pronoun it keeps the -a: *cualquiera puede hacerlo*. Its plural is the odd *cualesquiera*, which is formal and rare.

**Cada** is invariable and never takes a plural noun: *cada día*, never *cada días*. For *every* in the sense of *all*, use *todos los*: *todos los días*.

And the double negative rule persists: *no vino **nadie***, *no hay **nada***.

examples.target: No tengo ningún problema con eso.
examples.native: I have no problem with that.

examples.target: Cualquier persona puede participar.
examples.native: Anyone can take part.

examples.target: Cada día aprendo algo nuevo.
examples.native: Every day I learn something new.

theory.watch_out: 'Ninguno' is singular: 'no tengo ningún amigo allí', not 'ningunos amigos'.

theory.title: Stressed possessives: mío, tuyo, suyo
theory.summary: The long forms go after the noun or stand alone, and they carry emphasis the short ones cannot.
theory.body:
Alongside *mi, tu, su* there is a stressed set: **mío, tuyo, suyo, nuestro, vuestro, suyo**, agreeing in gender and number.

They are used:

**After the noun**, for emphasis or in set phrases: *un amigo **mío***, *¡Dios **mío***!, *de parte **suya***.
**Alone with an article**, as a pronoun: *este libro es **el mío***.
**After ser**, with no article: *este libro es **mío***.

The difference between *mi amigo* and *un amigo mío* is real: the first is a specific friend already in view, the second is *a friend of mine*, one of several. English marks it with *of mine*; Spanish with position.

Formal correspondence uses them heavily: *de mi consideración*, *muy señor mío*, *un cordial saludo de su parte*.

**Suyo** inherits the ambiguity of *su* — his, hers, theirs, yours — and is disambiguated the same way: *de él*, *de ellos*, *de usted*.

And **lo mío / lo tuyo** means *my thing, my area*: *la informática no es lo mío*.

examples.target: Un amigo mío trabaja allí.
examples.native: A friend of mine works there.

examples.target: Este abrigo no es el mío.
examples.native: This coat isn't mine.

examples.target: Las matemáticas no son lo mío.
examples.native: Maths isn't my thing.

theory.watch_out: 'Mi amigo' is a specific friend; 'un amigo mío' is one of several. The position carries the meaning.

theory.title: Indefinite expressions with the subjunctive
theory.summary: The doubled-verb constructions that let you dismiss every possibility at once.
theory.body:
A set of fixed structures built by **repeating the verb in the subjunctive**:

*digas lo que **digas*** — whatever you say
*pase lo que **pase*** — whatever happens
*sea como **sea*** — however it may be
*sea quien **sea*** — whoever it may be
*vayas donde **vayas*** — wherever you go
*cueste lo que **cueste*** — whatever it costs

And the *-quiera* family: **quienquiera que**, **dondequiera que**, **comoquiera que**, **cuandoquiera que** — all with the subjunctive, all more literary than the doubled forms.

The doubled construction has no structural equivalent in English, which uses *-ever* words instead. That is why learners almost never produce it unprompted, and why using it correctly is a strong marker of advanced Spanish.

The same shape appears in emphatic concessions: *por mucho que **insistas***, *por muy tarde que **sea***.

A note on register: *pase lo que pase* and *sea como sea* are entirely everyday. *Quienquiera que sea* is not — it belongs to written or ceremonial language.

examples.target: Pase lo que pase, cuenta conmigo.
examples.native: Whatever happens, you can count on me.

examples.target: Digas lo que digas, no voy a cambiar de opinión.
examples.native: Whatever you say, I'm not changing my mind.

examples.target: Lo terminaré, cueste lo que cueste.
examples.native: I'll finish it, whatever it takes.

theory.watch_out: Both verbs go in the subjunctive: 'diga lo que diga', not 'dice lo que diga'.

theory.title: C1 review: register and precision
theory.summary: At this level the errors are no longer grammatical — they are errors of register.
theory.body:
A C1 speaker rarely conjugates wrongly. What separates them from a native is **register control**.

The recurring failures:

**Repeating one connector.** *Sin embargo* three times in a paragraph. Vary, or use punctuation.
**Speech markers in writing.** *O sea*, *bueno*, *pues* belong in conversation, not in an essay.
**Formal markers in speech.** *No obstante* in a bar sounds like a parody.
**Too little connection.** Spanish formal prose signposts more than English; a bare sequence of sentences reads as unfinished.
**Over-using *yo*.** Formal Spanish removes the writer: *se observa*, *cabe señalar*, *consideramos*.
**Translating English concision.** *No smoking* is *se ruega no fumar*, not *no fumar* on a formal notice.

The grammatical points still worth checking: *dequeísmo* (*pienso de que*), *queísmo* (*me alegro que*), *laísmo* and *leísmo*, the *sino/pero* split, *aun/aún*, and *porque / por qué / porqué / por que*.

And the sequence of tenses: a past main verb requires the imperfect subjunctive below it.

examples.target: Cabe señalar que el planteamiento resulta discutible.
examples.native: It should be noted that the approach is debatable.

examples.target: Me alegro de que hayas venido.
examples.native: I'm glad you came.

examples.target: No es que no quiera, es que no puedo.
examples.native: It's not that I don't want to, it's that I can't.

theory.watch_out: 'No es que' always takes the subjunctive: 'no es que no quiera', never 'no quiero'.

theory.title: Estar + participle: the resulting state
theory.summary: It describes the state left behind, not the action — and that is why it is not a passive.
theory.body:
**Ser + participle** reports the **action**: *la puerta **fue cerrada** a las diez* — someone closed it.
**Estar + participle** describes the **resulting state**: *la puerta **está cerrada*** — it is shut.

In both cases the participle agrees, but only the first is a passive. *Estar cerrada* has no agent and no event; it is a description.

This is why *la puerta está cerrada por el portero* is odd — a state does not have an agent. If you want the doer, you need the action: *fue cerrada por el portero*.

Common in instructions and reports: *el plazo **está** vencido*, *la cuenta **está** bloqueada*, *el documento **está** firmado*.

Related resultative structures:

**tener + participle** — accumulated result, with agreement: *tengo **escritas** tres cartas*.
**llevar + participle** — progress so far: *llevo **leídas** cien páginas*.
**quedar + participle** — a state fixed by agreement: *queda **aprobado** el acta*.

That last one is standard in minutes and legal proceedings, where it formally records that something is now settled.

examples.target: La tienda está cerrada los domingos.
examples.native: The shop is closed on Sundays.

examples.target: Tengo escritas tres páginas.
examples.native: I've got three pages written.

examples.target: Queda aprobada la propuesta.
examples.native: The proposal is hereby approved.

theory.watch_out: A state takes no agent. 'Está cerrada por el portero' should be 'fue cerrada por el portero'.

theory.title: Formal connectors: review
theory.summary: Which ones demand the subjunctive, gathered in one place.
theory.body:
The connectors that **always take the subjunctive**:

*para que, a fin de que, con el objeto de que* (purpose)
*antes de que* (time)
*a menos que, a no ser que, salvo que, con tal de que, siempre y cuando, en caso de que* (condition)
*sin que* (negative circumstance)
*de ahí que* (consequence)
*por mucho que, por muy… que* (concession, normally)

The ones that **always take the indicative**:

*porque, ya que, puesto que, dado que* (cause)
*así que, por lo tanto, por consiguiente, de modo que* — when stating a real result
*si bien, y eso que* (concession about a fact)

The ones that **take either**, with a change of meaning:

*aunque, a pesar de que* — real versus hypothetical
*cuando, mientras, hasta que, en cuanto* — habitual versus future
*de modo que, de manera que* — result (indicative) versus purpose (subjunctive)
*siempre que* — whenever (indicative) versus provided that (subjunctive)

And the one-subject rule applies throughout: *para llegar* rather than *para que yo llegue*.

examples.target: Te lo explico para que lo entiendas.
examples.native: I'm explaining it so that you understand.

examples.target: Salió sin que nadie lo viera.
examples.native: He left without anyone seeing him.

examples.target: Lo hice para llegar a tiempo.
examples.native: I did it in order to arrive on time.

theory.watch_out: 'Sin que' always takes the subjunctive; with one subject it becomes 'sin' + infinitive.

theory.title: Obligation in formal and legal language
theory.summary: Legal Spanish has its own obligation vocabulary, and 'deber de' means the opposite of obligation.
theory.body:
Everyday obligation is *tener que* and *deber*. Formal and legal Spanish uses a different set:

**deberá + infinitive** — the standard legal obligation: *el solicitante **deberá** presentar…* Future tense, not present.
**estar obligado a**
**quedar obligado a / queda prohibido**
**ser preceptivo / ser de obligado cumplimiento**
**corresponder a alguien + infinitive** — it falls to someone: *corresponde al juez decidir*.
**proceder a + infinitive** — to proceed to.

The distinction that matters: **deber** = obligation, **deber de** = probability.

*Debe presentar el documento* — he must submit it.
*Debe de estar en casa* — he's probably at home.

In speech the two blur constantly and nobody minds. In a legal or formal text the *de* is the difference between an obligation and a guess, so it is one of the few places where the distinction is genuinely enforced.

Prohibition: **se prohíbe**, **queda terminantemente prohibido**, **está prohibido** — and *se ruega no…* for the polite version on a sign.

examples.target: El solicitante deberá presentar la documentación.
examples.native: The applicant must submit the documentation.

examples.target: Queda prohibido el acceso a personal no autorizado.
examples.native: Access is prohibited to unauthorised personnel.

examples.target: Debe de haber un error.
examples.native: There must be a mistake.

theory.watch_out: 'Debe estar' is an obligation; 'debe de estar' is a guess. In legal text the 'de' matters.

theory.title: Formal conditional structures
theory.summary: Formal Spanish states conditions without 'si', using a set of conjunctions that all take the subjunctive.
theory.body:
Beyond *si*, formal Spanish has a full set of conditional conjunctions, and they all take the **subjunctive**:

**siempre que / siempre y cuando** — provided that: *te ayudo **siempre que** me avises*.
**a condición de que**
**con tal de que** — as long as, often with a hint of impatience.
**a no ser que / a menos que / salvo que** — unless.
**en caso de que** — in case.
**como** + subjunctive — a spoken threat: *como llegues tarde, me voy*.

Note **siempre que** is ambiguous by design: with the indicative it means *whenever* (*siempre que vengo, llueve*); with the subjunctive it means *provided that*. Same words, two conjunctions.

More compact formal alternatives: **de + infinitive** (*de haberlo sabido…*), **caso de + infinitive**, **en el supuesto de que + subjunctive**, and the gerund (*siendo así, procedemos*).

**Como + subjunctive** deserves care: it is a warning, and in the indicative the same word means *because*. Register and mood together do all the work.

examples.target: Te lo presto siempre que me lo devuelvas.
examples.native: I'll lend it to you provided you give it back.

examples.target: No iré a menos que me inviten.
examples.native: I won't go unless they invite me.

examples.target: En caso de que llueva, lo aplazamos.
examples.native: In case it rains, we'll postpone it.

theory.watch_out: 'Siempre que vengo' means whenever; 'siempre que vengas' means provided that. The mood is the conjunction.

theory.title: Fronting for emphasis
theory.summary: Spanish word order is flexible, and moving an element to the front is a deliberate act — with one obligatory consequence.
theory.body:
Spanish allows almost any element to move to the front for emphasis: *a mí no me lo dijo*, *muy bien lo sabes*, *de eso no quiero hablar*.

The rule that comes with it: when a **direct or indirect object is fronted**, the corresponding pronoun **must** be repeated:

*El libro **lo** compré ayer.*
*A Juan **le** di el dinero.*
*Esa película **la** vi el año pasado.*

Leaving out that pronoun is a real error, not a stylistic choice. English has no equivalent, which is why fronted sentences from learners come out incomplete.

Other emphatic moves:

**Sí que** — contradicts a denial: *sí que lo sabía*.
**Ni + noun** — not even: *ni una palabra dijo*.
**Bien que / vaya que** — spoken intensifiers.
**Adverb first**: *nunca lo había visto*, *raramente ocurre*.

When a negative element is fronted, the *no* disappears: *nunca lo he visto*, not *nunca no lo he visto*.

examples.target: El libro lo compré ayer.
examples.native: The book, I bought yesterday.

examples.target: A ella no le dije nada.
examples.native: To her I said nothing.

examples.target: Ni una palabra dijo en toda la tarde.
examples.native: He didn't say a single word all afternoon.

theory.watch_out: A fronted object needs its pronoun repeated: 'el libro LO compré', not 'el libro compré'.

theory.title: Persuading without pressing
theory.summary: The grammar of sounding reasonable: conditionals, impersonals and questions that are not questions.
theory.body:
Persuasive Spanish rarely commands. Its tools:

**Conditional** — softens a proposal: *sería conveniente revisar el plan*, *convendría plantearlo de otro modo*.
**Impersonal** — removes the accuser: *se podría considerar…*, *cabría preguntarse si…*
**Rhetorical question** — makes the reader reach the conclusion: *¿no sería más sensato esperar?*
**Understated concession** — *no deja de ser cierto que…*, *hasta cierto punto…*
**Mitigators** — *en cierto modo, en principio, a priori, en la medida en que*

**Cabría + infinitive** is characteristic and worth acquiring: *cabría matizar que*, *cabría preguntarse si*. It proposes a thought without owning it.

And **no deja de ser** is a very Spanish double negative used as praise or concession: *no deja de ser interesante* — it is, after all, interesting.

The overall difference from English persuasion is that Spanish hedges through **grammar** — conditional, impersonal, subjunctive — more than through vocabulary like *perhaps* or *somewhat*.

examples.target: Cabría preguntarse si es realmente necesario.
examples.native: One might ask whether it is really necessary.

examples.target: Sería conveniente revisar el presupuesto.
examples.native: It would be advisable to review the budget.

examples.target: No deja de ser un argumento válido.
examples.native: It is, after all, a valid argument.

theory.watch_out: 'Cabría preguntarse si' takes the indicative after 'si'. The hedge is in 'cabría', not the mood.

theory.title: Parallel structures
theory.summary: Spanish rhetoric leans on symmetry, and breaking the pattern is read as an error rather than variety.
theory.body:
Parallelism — repeating the same grammatical shape across a list — is a hallmark of good Spanish prose, and it is enforced more strictly than in English.

*Ni el dinero, ni el tiempo, ni el esfuerzo bastaron.*
*Vine, vi, vencí.*
*Tanto los alumnos como los profesores participaron.*

The correlative pairs must be completed: **ni… ni…**, **tanto… como…**, **no solo… sino también…**, **o… o…**, **ya… ya…** (literary), **sea… sea…**

**No solo… sino también** is worth care: the second element must be the same grammatical category as the first. *No solo **escribió** el libro sino que también lo **ilustró*** — note *sino que* before a conjugated verb, *sino también* before a noun or adjective.

When the list is of verbs, keep the same form throughout: *hay que analizar, comparar y concluir* — not *analizar, comparación y concluir*.

And **ni** requires the doubled negative when it follows the verb: *no vino **ni** llamó*.

examples.target: No solo escribió el libro, sino que también lo ilustró.
examples.native: He not only wrote the book, he illustrated it too.

examples.target: Tanto los alumnos como los profesores asistieron.
examples.native: Both the students and the teachers attended.

examples.target: Ni me llamó ni me escribió.
examples.native: He neither called nor wrote to me.

theory.watch_out: Before a conjugated verb it's 'sino que', not 'sino': 'sino que también lo ilustró'.

theory.title: Rhetorical questions
theory.summary: A negative question in Spanish expects a yes, and that asymmetry is what makes it persuasive.
theory.body:
A rhetorical question states something in the form of a question, so the reader supplies the conclusion themselves.

**Negative questions expect agreement**: *¿No es evidente que…?*, *¿Acaso no lo sabíamos ya?* The listener is being invited to say yes.

**¿Acaso…?** marks the question as rhetorical outright — it means roughly *surely you don't think that…*: *¿Acaso creías que era fácil?*

**¿Cómo no…?** — how could one not: *¿cómo no iba a enfadarse?*

**¿Qué sentido tiene…?** — what's the point of.

**¿No será que…?** — introduces an alternative explanation, often pointedly: *¿no será que no quieres?*

Answering a negative question is where Spanish and English diverge. To *¿no vienes?*, Spanish answers **sí** to mean *yes, I am coming*. English speakers hesitate between *yes* and *no*; Spanish does not — **sí** always affirms the verb, regardless of the negative in the question.

Register note: these belong to argument and to speech. In academic writing, one or two carry weight; more reads as haranguing.

examples.target: ¿Acaso no lo sabíamos ya?
examples.native: Did we not already know this?

examples.target: ¿Qué sentido tiene discutirlo ahora?
examples.native: What's the point of arguing about it now?

examples.target: ¿No será que no quieres venir?
examples.native: Could it be that you don't want to come?

theory.watch_out: To '¿no vienes?', 'sí' means you ARE coming. Spanish answers the verb, not the negative.

theory.title: Conceding in order to win the point
theory.summary: Granting your opponent's point first is a rhetorical move, and Spanish has a fixed grammar for it.
theory.body:
In argument, conceding before objecting is stronger than denying outright, and Spanish marks the move grammatically.

**Es cierto que… ahora bien…** — the classic frame: *es cierto que el coste es alto; ahora bien, el beneficio lo justifica*.
**Si bien es verdad que… no lo es menos que…** — a formal balance.
**Admitiendo que + subjunctive** — *admitiendo que sea difícil, no es imposible*.
**Por más que + subjunctive** — dismissing in advance.
**No es que… sino que…** — corrects a misreading: *no es que no quiera, sino que no puedo*.

Note the mood split: *es cierto que* takes the **indicative** because it asserts; *no es que* takes the **subjunctive** because it denies an interpretation rather than a fact.

**Aun cuando** is the formal *even if*, always subjunctive: *aun cuando fuera cierto…*

This structure — concede, pivot, assert — is the backbone of Spanish argumentative writing, and examiners look for it specifically. Simply stacking objections reads as unsophisticated.

examples.target: Es cierto que es caro; ahora bien, dura años.
examples.native: It's true that it's expensive; that said, it lasts for years.

examples.target: No es que no me guste, sino que no lo necesito.
examples.native: It's not that I don't like it, it's that I don't need it.

examples.target: Aun cuando fuera cierto, no cambiaría nada.
examples.native: Even if it were true, it would change nothing.

theory.watch_out: 'Es cierto que es' but 'no es que sea'. Asserting and denying take opposite moods.

theory.title: Adjective position as a stylistic choice
theory.summary: After the noun it classifies; before it, it evaluates — and literary prose lives in the second.
theory.body:
The basic rule was in Unit 6: after the noun distinguishes, before it comments. At C2 the point is what writers do with it.

**After (specifying)**: *la nieve blanca* — this snow as opposed to dirty snow.
**Before (evaluating)**: *la blanca nieve* — snow, which is of course white. The adjective adds no information; it adds tone.

That second use, the **epíteto**, is the backbone of literary description: *la verde hierba*, *el ancho mar*, *la oscura noche*. It signals that the writer is evoking, not classifying.

Several adjectives change meaning outright by position, and these are exam material: *viejo, pobre, grande, nuevo, único, cierto, medio, simple, antiguo, mismo*.

*un simple error* (merely) / *un error simple* (uncomplicated)
*cierta noticia* (a certain) / *una noticia cierta* (a true one)
*el mismo director* (the very same) / *el director mismo* (himself)

With **two adjectives**, one may go each side: *la vieja casa **abandonada***. That distributes evaluation and classification, and it is a very Spanish rhythm.

examples.target: Fue un simple malentendido.
examples.native: It was just a misunderstanding.

examples.target: Es un problema simple de resolver.
examples.native: It's a simple problem to solve.

examples.target: La vieja casa abandonada seguía en pie.
examples.native: The old abandoned house was still standing.

theory.watch_out: 'Un simple error' means merely an error; 'un error simple' means an uncomplicated one.

theory.title: Diminutives and augmentatives
theory.summary: They rarely say anything about size — they carry affection, contempt or softening.
theory.body:
**Diminutives**: *-ito/-ita*, *-illo/-illa*, *-ico/-ica*, *-ín/-ina*. **Augmentatives**: *-ón/-ona*, *-azo/-aza*, *-ote/-ota*.

Size is almost never the point.

**Affection**: *abuelita*, *hermanito*, *cafecito*.
**Softening a request or a criticism**: *un momentito*, *está un poquito frío*. This is the commonest use of all, and its absence makes a learner sound blunt.
**Contempt**: *un abogadillo*, *un trabajillo*.
**Intensity**, with *-azo*: *un golpazo*, *un exitazo*.

And some are lexicalised into different words: *bolso/bolsillo*, *ventana/ventanilla*, *silla/sillón*, *pan/panecillo*, *palabra/palabrota* (swear word).

Regional preferences are strong: *-ico* in Colombia, Costa Rica and Aragón; *-illo* in Andalusia; *-ín* in Asturias. Latin America uses diminutives far more than Spain, and in Mexico they extend to adverbs (*ahorita*, *lueguito*) — where *ahorita* famously can mean anything from *right now* to *at some point*.

Using none at all is one of the clearest markers of foreign Spanish.

examples.target: Espera un momentito, por favor.
examples.native: Wait just a moment, please.

examples.target: Nos tomamos un cafecito y charlamos.
examples.native: We had a nice little coffee and chatted.

examples.target: Le dieron un golpazo tremendo.
examples.native: They gave him an almighty blow.

theory.watch_out: 'Un momentito' is politeness, not size. Never using diminutives is what marks you as foreign.

theory.title: Free indirect style
theory.summary: The narrator borrows the character's voice without quotation marks or a reporting verb.
theory.body:
Free indirect style (*estilo indirecto libre*) blends the narrator's third person with the character's own words and thoughts. There is no *dijo que*, no quotation marks, and yet the voice is clearly the character's.

*Miró el reloj. ¿Es que nadie iba a venir? Otra vez sola, otra vez esperando.*

The markers that give it away:

**Third person and past tense** kept from the narration.
**Questions and exclamations** that belong to the character, not the narrator.
**Deictics from the character's position**: *ahora, aquí, hoy* alongside past tenses — a combination impossible in plain narration.
**Colloquial vocabulary** and interjections in a formal narrative voice.
**Evaluative words** the narrator would not use: *maldito, dichoso, por supuesto*.

Spanish uses this far more than English realist fiction does, and it is the main reason a translated Spanish novel can feel oddly ambiguous about who is speaking.

As a reader, the practical skill is noticing that a sentence's judgements belong to the character, so the narrator is not vouching for them.

examples.target: Miró el reloj. ¿Es que nadie iba a venir?
examples.native: She looked at the clock. Was nobody going to come?

examples.target: Cerró la puerta. Ahora sí que estaba solo.
examples.native: He shut the door. Now he really was alone.

examples.target: ¡Qué frío hacía aquella mañana!
examples.native: How cold it was that morning!

theory.watch_out: 'Ahora' with a past tense is the giveaway: the deixis belongs to the character, not the narrator.

theory.title: Word order as style
theory.summary: Spanish word order is freer than English, and the freedom is used for emphasis and rhythm.
theory.body:
Spanish does not need a fixed subject-verb-object order, because the endings already mark who does what. The freedom is exploited stylistically.

**Verb before subject** is normal, not marked, with intransitive verbs: *llegó el invierno*, *sonó el teléfono*, *faltan dos días*. Putting the subject first (*el invierno llegó*) sounds emphatic.

**Adjective before noun** turns description into evaluation — covered earlier, and in literary prose it is used constantly: *la blanca nieve*, where *blanca* is not distinguishing but evoking.

**Fronting a complement** foregrounds it: *de eso no quiero hablar*, *muy caro me salió*.

**Postponing the subject to the end** gives it weight, especially in a long sentence — Spanish naturally puts the newest information last.

**Hyperbaton** — breaking up a phrase — belongs to poetry and elevated prose: *de la mano el destino nos llevaba*.

The rule to hold on to: in Spanish, **the end of the sentence is the strong position**, whereas in English it is often the beginning. Rearranging accordingly is what makes a translated sentence stop sounding translated.

examples.target: Llegó el invierno antes de tiempo.
examples.native: Winter came early.

examples.target: De eso no quiero hablar.
examples.native: That I don't want to talk about.

examples.target: Muy caro me salió aquel error.
examples.native: That mistake cost me dearly.

theory.watch_out: 'Sonó el teléfono' is neutral; 'el teléfono sonó' is emphatic. The order is not free of meaning.

theory.title: Tense as a narrative device
theory.summary: In literature the tense is chosen for effect, not for chronology.
theory.body:
Once the tenses are mastered as grammar, they become tools of style.

**Historical present** — a past event narrated in the present to bring the reader inside it: *en 1492 Colón **llega** a América*. Common in history writing, journalism and anecdotes.

**Imperfect for description** — a narrator opening a scene uses the imperfect to suspend time: *llovía, la calle **estaba** desierta, nadie **hablaba***. The preterite would start the plot; the imperfect holds it.

**Narrative imperfect** — an imperfect used for a completed action, to soften its impact: *al día siguiente **moría** el rey*. Journalistic and literary; it presents the event as part of a flow rather than a blow.

**Preterite for the turning point** — after pages of imperfect, a single preterite marks the moment everything changed.

**Conditional for a future seen from the past**: *no lo sabía entonces, pero aquel día **cambiaría** su vida*.

The pattern to internalise: **imperfect paints, preterite moves**. A page of only preterites reads as a report; a page of only imperfects never begins.

examples.target: Llovía y la calle estaba desierta.
examples.native: It was raining and the street was deserted.

examples.target: En 1605 Cervantes publica el Quijote.
examples.native: In 1605 Cervantes publishes Don Quixote.

examples.target: No lo sabía, pero aquel día cambiaría su vida.
examples.native: He didn't know it, but that day would change his life.

theory.watch_out: The imperfect paints the scene, the preterite moves the plot. Only preterites reads as a police report.

theory.title: Diminutives for humour
theory.summary: Shrinking a word that cannot be shrunk is a standing joke in Spanish.
theory.body:
Applying a diminutive to something large, serious or abstract creates humour by mismatch.

*Un problemita* — said of a disaster.
*Una multita de trescientos euros.*
*Un favorcito* — announcing something enormous.
*Un examencito de tres horas.*

The joke is that the suffix minimises what obviously cannot be minimised, and both speakers know it. It softens bad news and defuses a request at the same time.

Diminutives also attach to words that grammatically resist them, which is funny in itself: **adverbs** (*ahorita, cerquita, prontito, despacito*), **gerunds** (*callandito*), and even **nada** (*nadita*).

The augmentative does the mirror job: *un problemón*, *un fiestón*, *un cochazo*, *un golazo*. Here the exaggeration is admiring rather than dismissive.

Regional note: Mexican Spanish takes this furthest, to the point where *ahorita* has become genuinely ambiguous about time. River Plate Spanish uses *-ito* heavily too, often with *che* and voseo, and Andalusian favours *-illo* for the same ironic purpose.

Using one of these correctly signals that you are inside the joke rather than translating it.

examples.target: Tengo un problemita: perdí el pasaporte.
examples.native: I've got a tiny problem: I lost my passport.

examples.target: Te pido un favorcito, ¿me prestas el coche?
examples.native: Just a little favour: can I borrow your car?

examples.target: Nos metieron un golazo increíble.
examples.native: They scored an absolutely stunning goal against us.

theory.watch_out: 'Un problemita' usually announces a big problem. The suffix is the joke, not the size.

theory.title: Exaggeration
theory.summary: Hyperbole is conventional in Spanish; taken literally it produces constant misunderstandings.
theory.body:
Spanish exaggerates as a matter of routine, and the expressions are fixed rather than invented on the spot.

**Quantity**: *un montón de, la mar de, un sinfín de, mil veces, cien mil cosas, todo el mundo*
**Intensity**: *muerto de hambre/frío/risa, harto de, hasta las narices, no poder más*
**Comparisons**: *más viejo que Matusalén, más lento que una tortuga, más claro que el agua, más feo que un pecado*
**With -ísimo**: *carísimo, muchísimo, malísimo*
**Time**: *hace un siglo que no te veo, tardó una eternidad*

*Me muero de hambre* is not a medical statement; *hace un siglo que no te veo* is not a claim about a century. English does this too, but Spanish does it more, and in registers where English would be literal.

**Ni + noun** is the negative version: *ni un euro*, *ni una palabra*, *ni de broma*, *ni harto de vino* (absolutely not).

And **para + infinitive** as a hyperbolic result: *un frío **para morirse***.

The learner risk is answering hyperbole literally — replying to *me muero de hambre* with concern rather than lunch.

examples.target: Hace un siglo que no te veo.
examples.native: I haven't seen you in ages.

examples.target: Estoy muerto de hambre.
examples.native: I'm starving.

examples.target: No pienso ir, ni de broma.
examples.native: There's no way I'm going.

theory.watch_out: 'Me muero de hambre' means he's hungry. Answering it literally is the giveaway.

theory.title: Recognising irony
theory.summary: Spanish irony is signalled by fixed phrases more than by tone, which is what makes it learnable.
theory.body:
Irony is where advanced learners misread most often, because the words say the opposite of the meaning.

The fixed markers:

**¡Qué bien!** after bad news.
**Sí, claro / ya, ya / ya te digo** — sarcastic agreement.
**Encima** — on top of everything: *y encima llegó tarde*.
**Menos mal que…** — sometimes genuine relief, sometimes bitter.
**Vaya + noun** — *¡vaya ayuda!* means it was no help at all.
**Pues sí que…** — *pues sí que empezamos bien*.
**Lo que faltaba / era lo único que faltaba** — that's all we needed.
**Como para…** — *está como para salir con este frío*.

Grammatical signals: an exaggerated diminutive, an unexpected formal register in a casual setting, or the **future of conjecture** used dismissively (*será muy listo, pero…*).

That last frame is worth learning: **será… pero…** concedes a quality only to demolish it. *Será muy guapo, pero es insoportable.*

The cultural point: Spanish irony is often warmer than English sarcasm and less hostile than it sounds in translation. Reading it as an attack is a common foreign misreading.

examples.target: Y encima llegó tarde. ¡Qué bien!
examples.native: And on top of that he arrived late. Wonderful!

examples.target: Vaya ayuda me has dado.
examples.native: Some help you've been.

examples.target: Será muy listo, pero no lo demuestra.
examples.native: He may be very clever, but he doesn't show it.

theory.watch_out: 'Será muy listo, pero…' concedes only to demolish. It is not agreement.

theory.title: Questions used for humour
theory.summary: A question that expects no answer, used to complain or to mock without saying so directly.
theory.body:
Beyond argument, rhetorical questions carry a great deal of Spanish humour and complaint.

**¿Tú qué crees?** — obviously.
**¿Y a mí qué me cuentas?** — not my problem.
**¿Pero qué dices?** — disbelief.
**¿Desde cuándo…?** — since when: *¿desde cuándo sabes tú de coches?*
**¿No te fastidia?** — the nerve of it.
**¿Qué más da?** — what difference does it make.
**¿Y qué?** — so what.
**¿Para qué te crees que…?** — what do you think… is for.

These are formulaic, so they can be learned as blocks — which matters, because improvising a rhetorical question in a second language usually lands as a real question.

A structural note: **¿Cómo que…?** repeats the other person's words back in disbelief: *— No voy a ir. — ¿Cómo que no vas a ir?* This has no English structural equivalent and is extremely common.

Register: all of these are spoken and informal. In writing they appear only in dialogue, opinion columns and comedy.

examples.target: ¿Cómo que no vienes?
examples.native: What do you mean you're not coming?

examples.target: ¿Desde cuándo sabes tú de fútbol?
examples.native: Since when do you know anything about football?

examples.target: ¿Y a mí qué me cuentas?
examples.native: And what's that got to do with me?

theory.watch_out: '¿Cómo que…?' repeats what was just said in disbelief. It is not asking how.

theory.title: Understatement
theory.summary: Spanish understates with double negatives, where English uses adverbs like 'rather'.
theory.body:
Spanish has its own understatement, and it works grammatically rather than lexically.

**Double negative as praise**: *no está nada mal*, *no deja de ser interesante*, *no es poca cosa*, *no le falta razón*. These are warmer than they look — *no está nada mal* is real approval.

**Mitigators**: *un poco, algo, más bien, digamos que, por así decirlo, en cierto modo, tirando a*

*Es **más bien** caro* — it's on the expensive side.
*Está **algo** cansado* — he's rather tired.

**Negating the opposite**: *no es precisamente barato* (it's expensive), *no es que sea feo* (it is).

**Tampoco es que…** dismisses an exaggeration: *tampoco es que sea tan difícil*.

**Digamos que** flags that a euphemism is coming: *digamos que no fue su mejor día*.

The practical reading skill: *no está mal* from a Spanish speaker is closer to *that's good* than to *it's acceptable*. Reading it as lukewarm — the way an English speaker reads *not bad* — undersells the compliment.

examples.target: No está nada mal tu propuesta.
examples.native: Your proposal is really rather good.

examples.target: No es precisamente barato.
examples.native: It's not exactly cheap.

examples.target: Digamos que no fue su mejor día.
examples.native: Let's say it wasn't his finest day.

theory.watch_out: 'No está nada mal' is genuine praise in Spanish, warmer than English 'not bad'.

theory.title: Academic and technical register
theory.summary: Precision here is about hedging correctly, not about sounding certain.
theory.body:
Academic Spanish rewards **calibrated claims**. Overstating is the commonest register error at C2.

**Strong**: *demuestra que, evidencia que, confirma que, pone de manifiesto*
**Moderate**: *indica que, sugiere que, apunta a que, parece indicar*
**Weak**: *podría indicar, no cabe descartar que* (+ subjunctive), *cabría suponer que*

**Structuring**: *el presente trabajo, a lo largo del artículo, como se ha señalado, en el apartado anterior, a modo de síntesis*

**Limiting**: *en la medida en que, siempre que se cumpla, dentro de los límites de, con las debidas reservas*

Characteristic grammar: impersonal *se*, the plural of modesty (*consideramos*), nominal style, and the present tense for general truths even about past studies (*el estudio **muestra***).

Two false friends worth flagging: **actualmente** means *currently*, not *actually* (*en realidad*); and **eventualmente** means *possibly*, not *eventually* (*finalmente*). Both appear constantly in translated academic prose and both are wrong.

**No cabe descartar que** takes the subjunctive: *no cabe descartar que **exista** otra causa*.

examples.target: Los datos sugieren una correlación moderada.
examples.native: The data suggest a moderate correlation.

examples.target: No cabe descartar que existan otros factores.
examples.native: Other factors cannot be ruled out.

examples.target: Actualmente se investigan otras vías.
examples.native: Other avenues are currently being investigated.

theory.watch_out: 'Actualmente' is currently, not actually. 'Eventualmente' is possibly, not eventually.

theory.title: Colloquial markers
theory.summary: The filler words that make speech sound native, and that no textbook sentence contains.
theory.body:
Spoken Spanish is held together by small words that carry no dictionary meaning but a great deal of function.

**Opening**: *bueno, pues, mira, oye, a ver, vamos a ver*
**Filling**: *o sea, es que, en plan, tipo, ¿sabes?, ¿no?*
**Agreeing**: *claro, ya, exacto, desde luego, hombre*
**Closing**: *nada, en fin, total, y ya está, y punto*
**Softening**: *un poco, más o menos, o algo así, por así decirlo*

**Es que** is the workhorse of everyday justification: *es que no me dio tiempo*.

**Total, que…** resumes a story after a digression: *total, que al final no fuimos*.

**Hombre** is not gendered in this use — it is said to women too — and softens disagreement: *hombre, tampoco es para tanto*.

Regional variation is heavy: *tío/tía* and *vale* in Spain, *che* and *dale* in Argentina, *güey* and *órale* in Mexico, *pues* and *listo* in Colombia. Mixing them randomly sounds odder than using none.

And the register rule: none of these belong in formal writing, where they are the clearest sign of an essay written as if spoken.

examples.target: Es que no me dio tiempo, en serio.
examples.native: The thing is I didn't have time, honestly.

examples.target: Total, que al final no fuimos.
examples.native: Anyway, in the end we didn't go.

examples.target: Hombre, tampoco es para tanto.
examples.native: Come on, it's not that big a deal.

theory.watch_out: 'Hombre' as a softener is said to women too. It isn't addressing anyone as a man.

theory.title: Diplomatic language
theory.summary: Disagreeing, refusing and complaining without closing the door.
theory.body:
Diplomatic Spanish protects the relationship while still saying the difficult thing.

**Disagreeing**: *entiendo su punto de vista, si bien…*, *no comparto del todo…*, *quizá convendría matizar…*, *permítame discrepar…*

**Refusing**: *me temo que no va a ser posible*, *lamento comunicarle que…*, *en esta ocasión no podremos…*, *no está en nuestra mano*

**Complaining**: *quisiera trasladarle mi preocupación por…*, *me gustaría llamar su atención sobre…*, *entiendo que puede haber sido un malentendido, pero…*

**Asking for a change**: *agradecería que + imperfect subjunctive*, *¿sería posible…?*, *convendría revisar…*

The grammar doing the work: the **conditional** (*sería, convendría, agradecería*), the **imperfect subjunctive** after *agradecería que*, the **impersonal** to avoid accusing (*parece que ha habido un error* rather than *usted se equivocó*), and **passive or se** to remove the culprit.

That last move is the most useful: *se ha producido un retraso* blames nobody, where *usted se retrasó* blames someone. Choosing between them is a diplomatic decision expressed as grammar.

examples.target: Agradecería que revisaran el expediente.
examples.native: I would be grateful if you could review the file.

examples.target: Me temo que no va a ser posible en esta ocasión.
examples.native: I'm afraid it won't be possible on this occasion.

examples.target: Parece que ha habido un malentendido.
examples.native: It seems there has been a misunderstanding.

theory.watch_out: 'Se ha producido un retraso' blames nobody; 'usted se retrasó' blames someone. Pick deliberately.

theory.title: Legal and bureaucratic Spanish
theory.summary: A register with its own grammar, including tenses that survive nowhere else.
theory.body:
Administrative Spanish is a distinct dialect, and reading it is a practical skill — contracts, forms and official letters all use it.

**Fixed verbs**: *deberá, procederá, quedará, corresponderá, se resolverá, surtirá efecto*
**Archaic forms**: the **future subjunctive** — *si alguien **tuviere** derecho…* — extinct everywhere else but alive in legal texts and a few proverbs (*donde fueres, haz lo que vieres*).
**Fossilised phrases**: *a los efectos oportunos, sin perjuicio de, en su caso, a tenor de lo dispuesto, de conformidad con, salvo error u omisión*
**Formal nouns**: *el/la solicitante, el/la interesado/a, la parte, el otorgante*

Characteristic features: heavy nominalisation, the passive with *se*, extremely long sentences, and **no first person** at all.

**Sin perjuicio de** is worth knowing precisely: it means *without this affecting…*, not *without harming*.

**En su caso** means *where applicable*, not *in his case* — a false friend that changes the sense of a clause completely.

As a writer, the goal at C2 is to **read** this register accurately and to be able to convert it into plain Spanish for someone else, which is the mediation skill of Unit 30.

examples.target: El interesado deberá aportar la documentación requerida.
examples.native: The applicant must provide the required documentation.

examples.target: Sin perjuicio de lo anterior, se mantendrá el plazo.
examples.native: Notwithstanding the above, the deadline will remain.

examples.target: Se adjuntará, en su caso, el justificante de pago.
examples.native: Proof of payment shall be attached where applicable.

theory.watch_out: 'En su caso' means 'where applicable', not 'in his case'. It changes the whole clause.

theory.title: Converting between registers
theory.summary: Saying the same thing twice, once for a form and once for a friend.
theory.body:
Converting register is a C2 skill in itself, and it changes far more than vocabulary.

*Solicito que se me facilite…* → *¿Me puedes dar…?*
*Se ruega no fumar* → *No fumes*
*Le comunico que no podré asistir* → *Oye, que no puedo ir*
*Adjunto le remito el documento* → *Te mando el archivo*

What changes:

**Verbs**: Latinate to plain — *solicitar/pedir*, *comunicar/decir*, *remitir/mandar*, *finalizar/acabar*.
**Structure**: nominal to verbal — *la finalización del proyecto* → *cuando acabemos*.
**Person**: impersonal to personal — *se ruega* → *por favor*.
**Address**: *usted* to *tú*.
**Tense**: future to *ir a* — *le informaré* → *te aviso*.
**Connectors**: *no obstante* → *pero*.

The frequent mistake is converting only the vocabulary and leaving the syntax formal, which produces a sentence with the wrong shape and casual words — instantly recognisable as translated.

Going the other way, the risk is over-formalising: piling up *no obstante* and *cabe señalar* in a simple email reads as pompous rather than polite.

examples.target: Le comunico que no podré asistir a la reunión.
examples.native: I am writing to inform you that I will be unable to attend.

examples.target: Oye, que al final no puedo ir.
examples.native: Listen, I can't make it after all.

examples.target: Se ruega no fumar en las instalaciones.
examples.native: Smoking is not permitted on the premises.

theory.watch_out: Change the syntax too, not just the words. Formal structure with casual vocabulary reads as translated.

theory.title: Collocations
theory.summary: Which verb goes with which noun is arbitrary, and getting it wrong is the last thing to sound foreign.
theory.body:
A collocation is a pairing that native speakers use and that no rule predicts. This is the final layer of fluency, because every word is already known.

**tomar** una decisión (never *hacer*) · **cometer** un error · **prestar** atención · **hacer** una pregunta · **dar** un paseo · **tener** ganas · **echar** de menos · **poner** un ejemplo · **guardar** silencio · **correr** un riesgo · **sacar** una foto · **hacer** caso · **llevar a cabo** un proyecto · **plantear** una hipótesis · **surtir** efecto

With adjectives: *un error **garrafal***, *una diferencia **abismal***, *un silencio **sepulcral***, *una lluvia **torrencial***, *un **rotundo** éxito*.

The errors are predictable because they come from English: *hacer una decisión* (from *make a decision*), *hacer un error* (*make a mistake*), *pagar atención* (*pay attention*), *tomar una foto* (*take a photo* — Spanish says *sacar*, though *tomar* is accepted in Latin America).

There is no rule to derive these. They are learned in pairs, from reading, and they are exactly what a dictionary does not tell you.

examples.target: Tenemos que tomar una decisión hoy.
examples.native: We have to make a decision today.

examples.target: Cometí un error garrafal.
examples.native: I made a terrible mistake.

examples.target: Presta atención a los detalles.
examples.native: Pay attention to the details.

theory.watch_out: 'Hacer una decisión' and 'pagar atención' are direct from English. It's 'tomar' and 'prestar'.

theory.title: Choosing between synonyms
theory.summary: Dictionary synonyms are almost never interchangeable, and the difference is usually register or attitude.
theory.body:
At C2 the vocabulary work is no longer about learning new words but about choosing between ones you already know.

*Delgado* (neutral) / *flaco* (blunt, sometimes negative) / *esbelto* (flattering) / *escuálido* (unhealthy).

*Barato* (cheap in price) / *económico* (kinder) / *asequible* (affordable) / *cutre* (shoddy).

*Viejo* (can offend of people) / *mayor* (the polite word) / *anciano* (respectful, formal) / *antiguo* (of things).

*Trabajo* (neutral) / *empleo* (formal) / *curro* (slang) / *puesto* (position).

*Decir* / *comentar* / *afirmar* / *soltar* (blurt) / *espetar* (snap).

The rule of thumb for people: **mayor**, not *viejo*. *Un hombre mayor* is respectful; *un hombre viejo* is not.

And the **connotation of Latinate versus everyday words** runs opposite to English. In English, plain Anglo-Saxon words often sound warmer and Latinate ones colder — and in Spanish the everyday word usually *is* the Latinate one, so the effect is neutral. Reaching for a rarer synonym to sound educated usually just sounds odd.

examples.target: Es un señor mayor muy amable.
examples.native: He's a very kind elderly gentleman.

examples.target: Buscamos una opción más asequible.
examples.native: We're looking for a more affordable option.

examples.target: Soltó la noticia sin avisar.
examples.native: He blurted out the news without warning.

theory.watch_out: For people use 'mayor', not 'viejo'. 'Un hombre viejo' can land as an insult.

theory.title: Idioms in context
theory.summary: Idioms are register-marked, and using one in the wrong setting is worse than not using it.
theory.body:
Spanish idioms are plentiful, but the C2 skill is knowing **where** each belongs.

**Neutral, usable almost anywhere**: *dar en el clavo* (hit the nail on the head), *estar al día*, *tener en cuenta*, *a grandes rasgos*, *en líneas generales*.

**Clearly colloquial**: *estar hasta las narices*, *irse por las ramas*, *tomar el pelo*, *no tener ni idea*, *ser pan comido*, *costar un ojo de la cara*.

**Formal or written**: *sentar un precedente*, *poner de manifiesto*, *dejar constancia*, *salvando las distancias*.

The common failure is dropping a colloquial idiom into a formal text because it was the only one that came to mind. *El proyecto es pan comido* in a report reads badly — worse than the plain *el proyecto es sencillo*.

A second risk: idioms date and travel badly. Many are regional (*ponerse las pilas*, *estar en la luna de Valencia*, *hacerse el sueco*), and a Spanish idiom used in Buenos Aires can simply not be understood.

The safe practice for a learner is to use idioms you have **heard in that exact setting**, and otherwise to say the plain thing well.

examples.target: Has dado en el clavo con esa observación.
examples.native: You've hit the nail on the head with that remark.

examples.target: No te vayas por las ramas, ve al grano.
examples.native: Don't beat about the bush, get to the point.

examples.target: Ese coche cuesta un ojo de la cara.
examples.native: That car costs an arm and a leg.

theory.watch_out: Only use an idiom you've heard in that setting. A colloquial one in a report reads worse than plain words.

theory.title: Everyday idiomatic verbs
theory.summary: A handful of verbs cover an enormous range of meanings, and each one is a small system.
theory.body:
Spanish leans on a few very productive verbs, and learning their combinations is worth more than learning many rare verbs.

**Dar**: *dar igual* (not matter), *darse cuenta* (realise), *dar con* (find), *dar la lata* (pester), *dar por hecho* (assume), *darse prisa* (hurry).

**Echar**: *echar de menos* (miss), *echar una mano* (help), *echar un vistazo* (glance), *echarse a llorar* (burst out), *echar la culpa* (blame).

**Poner**: *ponerse a* (start), *ponerse + adjective* (become — *se puso rojo*), *poner al día* (update), *ponerse de acuerdo* (agree).

**Quedar**: *quedar con* (arrange to meet), *quedarse* (stay), *quedar en* (agree to), *quedar bien/mal* (make a good/bad impression), *quedarse con* (keep).

**Llevar**: *llevarse bien* (get on), *llevar + time + gerund* (have been doing), *llevar a cabo* (carry out).

**Darse cuenta** is worth flagging: it means *to realise*, and it needs **de** before a clause — *me di cuenta **de que** llegaba tarde*. Dropping the *de* is *queísmo* and is noticed.

examples.target: Me di cuenta de que llegaba tarde.
examples.native: I realised I was running late.

examples.target: ¿Me echas una mano con esto?
examples.native: Can you give me a hand with this?

examples.target: Nos llevamos muy bien desde el principio.
examples.native: We got on very well from the start.

theory.watch_out: 'Darse cuenta' needs 'de': 'me di cuenta de que'. Without it, it's the classic queísmo error.

theory.title: Verb plus preposition
theory.summary: Spanish has no phrasal verbs, but it has verbs that demand a specific preposition — and the choice is not negotiable.
theory.body:
Spanish has nothing like English phrasal verbs, where a particle changes the meaning entirely. What it has is verbs that **require** a particular preposition, and using the wrong one is a clear error.

**a**: *acostumbrarse a, atreverse a, negarse a, comprometerse a, aprender a, ayudar a, empezar a, volver a*
**de**: *acordarse de, olvidarse de, darse cuenta de, alegrarse de, depender de, tratarse de, encargarse de, quejarse de*
**en**: *insistir en, confiar en, fijarse en, pensar en, tardar en, consistir en*
**con**: *contar con, soñar con, casarse con, enfadarse con, encontrarse con*
**por**: *preocuparse por, interesarse por, optar por, esforzarse por*

Some verbs change meaning with the preposition: *pensar en* (think about) / *pensar de* (have an opinion of) / *pensar* + infinitive (plan to). *Contar con* (rely on) / *contar* (tell).

A note for English speakers: *depender **de***, not *depender en*; *soñar **con***, not *soñar de*; *consistir **en***, not *consistir de*. All three are direct interference from English and all three are frequent.

examples.target: No me acuerdo de su nombre.
examples.native: I can't remember his name.

examples.target: Todo depende de lo que decidan.
examples.native: It all depends on what they decide.

examples.target: Puedes contar conmigo.
examples.native: You can count on me.

theory.watch_out: 'Depender de', 'soñar con', 'consistir en'. Translating the English preposition gets all three wrong.

theory.title: C2 review: what is left
theory.summary: At this point the remaining work is judgement, not knowledge.
theory.body:
By C2 the grammar is not the obstacle. What separates a very advanced learner from a native is a set of judgements.

**Register.** Matching the level of formality to the situation, and keeping it consistent through a whole text — the commonest remaining failure is a formal essay with one colloquial sentence in it.

**Collocation.** *Tomar* a decision, *cometer* an error, *prestar* attention. No rule predicts these; only reading does.

**Connotation.** *Mayor* rather than *viejo*. *Asequible* rather than *barato*. Choosing between words you already know.

**Idiomatic density.** Using enough idiom to sound natural and not so much that it sounds performed.

**Regional awareness.** Knowing that *coger* is unremarkable in Spain and vulgar in much of Latin America; that *vos* is standard in Argentina; that *ahorita* means different things in different countries.

**Mediation.** Reading a legal or technical text accurately and rendering it for someone who cannot.

The grammar points still worth checking after all this: *dequeísmo* and *queísmo*, *sino* versus *pero*, *aun* versus *aún*, the sequence of tenses in the subjunctive, and the pronoun that a fronted object requires.

examples.target: Me di cuenta de que no era el momento.
examples.native: I realised it wasn't the moment.

examples.target: No es que no esté de acuerdo, sino que lo veo distinto.
examples.native: It's not that I disagree, it's that I see it differently.

examples.target: Esa decisión la tomamos entre todos.
examples.native: That decision we made together.

theory.watch_out: At this level the errors are register, not grammar. One colloquial sentence ruins a formal text.

theory.title: The verbs of mediation
theory.summary: Each one commits you to a different degree of faithfulness to the original.
theory.body:
The verb you use to describe what you are doing sets the expectation.

**resumir** — shorter, same content, same order.
**sintetizar** — combines sources, reorganised by idea.
**parafrasear** — same length, different words.
**explicar** — adds what the reader lacks.
**aclarar** — removes an ambiguity.
**matizar** — adds a qualification the original implied.
**interpretar** — states what it means, going beyond the words.
**traducir** — another language, same content.
**adaptar** — changes the form for a different audience.
**trasladar** — conveys to someone else, often a complaint or a message.

The distinction that matters most is **explicar** versus **interpretar**. Explaining stays inside the text; interpreting adds the mediator's reading. Presenting an interpretation as an explanation is where mediation becomes distortion.

**Trasladar** is worth having: *quisiera trasladarle nuestra preocupación* is the standard formal way of passing on a complaint without owning it personally.

And note *matizar*, which has no single English equivalent — it means to add the nuance that makes a blunt statement accurate, and it appears constantly in Spanish argument and journalism.

examples.target: Permítame matizar esa afirmación.
examples.native: Allow me to qualify that statement.

examples.target: Quisiera trasladarle nuestra preocupación.
examples.native: I would like to convey our concern to you.

examples.target: Voy a resumirte lo que dice el informe.
examples.native: I'll summarise for you what the report says.

theory.watch_out: Explaining stays inside the text; interpreting adds your reading. Passing one off as the other is distortion.

theory.title: Paraphrasing
theory.summary: Saying it again differently — the skill that proves you understood rather than memorised.
theory.body:
Paraphrase restates content in different words while keeping the meaning and, crucially, the **stance** of the original.

**Markers**: *es decir, o sea, dicho de otro modo, en otras palabras, lo que quiere decir es que, esto es, dicho con otras palabras*

**Techniques**:

**Change the word class**: *analizaron los datos* → *el análisis de los datos*.
**Change the voice**: *el comité aprobó la propuesta* → *la propuesta fue aprobada* / *se aprobó la propuesta*.
**Change the connector**: *aunque llovía, salimos* → *llovía; sin embargo, salimos*.
**Substitute with a synonym of the same register**: *solicitar* → *pedir* only if the register allows it.
**Explain rather than replace**: for a technical term, define it.

The two failures are opposite: staying **too close** to the original — changing only a word or two — and drifting **too far**, adding a judgement the source did not make.

That second one matters most. If the original says *sugiere que*, the paraphrase must not say *demuestra que*. Preserving the strength of a claim is part of paraphrasing it accurately.

examples.target: Es decir, el proyecto no es viable a corto plazo.
examples.native: That is, the project isn't viable in the short term.

examples.target: Dicho de otro modo, faltan recursos.
examples.native: In other words, resources are lacking.

examples.target: Lo que quiere decir es que necesitamos más tiempo.
examples.native: What he means is that we need more time.

theory.watch_out: Keep the strength of the claim. If the source 'sugiere', your paraphrase cannot 'demuestra'.

theory.title: Mediating between registers
theory.summary: Explaining an official text to someone who cannot read it — the most practical skill in the level.
theory.body:
Mediation means taking a text one person cannot use and making it usable, without changing what it says.

A legal notice: *deberá aportar la documentación acreditativa en el plazo de diez días hábiles, surtiendo efecto la notificación desde su recepción.*

Mediated: *tenés que llevar los papeles que lo demuestren. Tenés diez días de trabajo — sin contar fines de semana — desde que te llegó la carta.*

What changed: *aportar* → *llevar*, *documentación acreditativa* → *los papeles que lo demuestren*, *días hábiles* → explained rather than translated, *surtir efecto* → *desde que te llegó*, and the impersonal became a *tú*.

What did **not** change: the deadline, the requirement, the starting point. Mediation simplifies the language, never the content.

The hardest part is judging **how much the other person knows**. Explaining too much is condescending; too little mediates nothing. This is why a good mediator asks a question before starting, and why the same explanation works for one person and fails with the next.

And a term with no equivalent — *días hábiles*, *empadronamiento* — is **explained**, not translated.

examples.target: Tenés diez días hábiles, o sea sin contar sábados ni domingos.
examples.native: You have ten working days, meaning weekends don't count.

examples.target: Lo que pide el papel es que demuestres dónde vivís.
examples.native: What the form is asking for is proof of where you live.

examples.target: En resumen: llevá el DNI y una factura reciente.
examples.native: In short: bring your ID and a recent bill.

theory.watch_out: Simplify the language, never the content. A dropped deadline is a mediation failure, not a simplification.

theory.title: Synthesising several sources
theory.summary: The connectors that let you show where sources agree, differ and contradict each other.
theory.body:
Synthesis means combining sources into one account that shows their relationship — not summarising each in turn.

**Agreement**: *ambos autores coinciden en que…*, *en la misma línea…*, *asimismo, X sostiene que…*, *este planteamiento es compartido por…*

**Difference**: *frente a X, Y sostiene que…*, *por su parte, Y matiza que…*, *mientras que X sostiene…, Y considera…*, *en contraste con…*

**Contradiction**: *X afirma que…, si bien Y lo niega*, *estos resultados contradicen los de…*

**Gap**: *ninguno de los estudios aborda…*, *queda por determinar si…*, *la bibliografía no recoge…*

**Own conclusion**: *a la luz de lo anterior…*, *todo ello permite concluir que…*, *cabe deducir que…*

The structural point: a synthesis is organised **by idea**, not by author. A text that goes *X dice… Y dice… Z dice…* is a list, not a synthesis, and that is precisely what a C2 exam penalises.

Grammar note: *coincidir en que* takes the indicative; *negar que* and *poner en duda que* take the subjunctive.

examples.target: Ambos autores coinciden en que el método es válido.
examples.native: Both authors agree that the method is valid.

examples.target: Frente a Pérez, López niega que exista tal relación.
examples.native: In contrast to Pérez, López denies such a relationship exists.

examples.target: Queda por determinar si el efecto se mantiene.
examples.native: It remains to be determined whether the effect persists.

theory.watch_out: Organise by idea, not by author. 'X dice, Y dice, Z dice' is a list, not a synthesis.
